extraction.body: Nvidia stock closed 4.27% lower on Monday after the tech giant launched an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. U.S. intelligence agencies said Alice Huang, an executive at cloud company Megaspeed, has been passing information to Beijing, according to reports in The New York Times and the Financial Times . Nvidia said its board has launched an independent investigation following the reports that Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it," the company said in a Sunday statement . The co-founder and CEO told staff in an email that he had "fallen short" of his responsibility to serve his colleagues, the board, partners and shareholders around the world. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," Huang said in the email. China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said Monday that the "so-called Chinese spy narrative" was unsubstantiated, Reuters reported. The probe has sparked questions about Huang's future as CEO of the company. But any talk of replacing Huang is "comedy," Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNBC's " Squawk Box Europe ." While the probe and affair are a "game changer" for the CEO and company, it doesn't alter the view that Nvidia remains two to three years ahead of China in artificial intelligence chips, Ives said. "You're talking about what I would view as a torchbearer — the leader of AI technology — not just in the U.S. but globally. So I think the fact that we're in this situation, from an investor perspective, the clear worry is, does Jensen stay on as CEO? The Street would say probably likely, but given the board investigation, anything could happen, and that creates a huge uncertainty." Tech stocks took a hammering last week as investors reassessed the data center buildout after Democrats won control of Congress. Asian tech stocks rose across the region on Monday, rebounding from Friday's losses. Shares of U.S. chipmakers also climbed, with Marvell adding 9.49%, Arm Holdings gaining 6.69% Intel adding 5.49% and Qualcomm rising 3.66% on Monday. Broadcom added 8.78% and Nvidia AI chip rival Advanced Micro Devices gained 13.26%. Joachim Klement, investment strategist at Panmure Liberum, said the impact is currently contained to Nvidia. But if Huang's position is "endangered," then "Nvidia might cut back on supporting other companies, whether it's in Asia or in the U.S., that might then spread a little bit more into the other semiconductor names," he said. U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday praised Huang's leadership but said he hadn't spoken to the CEO about the investigation. "I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it," the president told reporters. "He's done an amazing job for our country," Trump added. Shaun Maguire, partner at Sequoia, also defended the tech giant CEO, saying in a post on X that Huang is "one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation." He added, "two mistakes don't make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership." SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk reshared Maguire's post, adding that he agrees with the venture capitalist's statements. Nvidia is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17 and will hold a major conference in Washington, D.C., at the end of the month. — CNBC's Kif Leswing and Kamaron McNair helped contribute to this report. sources.title: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny
passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology.
The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.
Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake.

Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.

Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.

The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024.
At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.
The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia.
Historically, China has been a big market for the company.
It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives.
In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue.
Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China.
Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead.
Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers .
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang, the billionaire chief executive of US chipmaker Nvidia, has built a reputation as one of the most influential figures in the global artificial intelligence industry. But the man behind the technology powering AI tools such as ChatGPT is now at the centre of a controversy involving an alleged Chinese spy, an extramarital affair and questions over the movement of advanced computer chips to China.Media reports last week said US intelligence officials believe Huang grew close to a Chinese executive who was funneling information to Beijing. The woman, identified as Alice Huang, is alleged to have been recruited by China to gather intelligence on the Nvidia chief.Nvidia's board said on Sunday it had opened a probe into its CEO and co-founder. Huang, 63, acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and told employees he was "deeply sorry".The allegations have drawn attention to the intersection of personal relationships, corporate espionage and the increasingly sensitive technology rivalry between the United States and China.While the alleged relationship has put Huang's personal life under scrutiny, questions have also emerged over Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data centre company where Alice Huang reportedly held a senior position. The company has been linked to investigations into the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China, which faces US restrictions on acquiring some of the most advanced processors.Here is what we know about the people, companies and allegations involved.Who is Jensen Huang?Born in Taipei in 1963, Jensen Huang, originally named Jen-Hsun, is one of the most recognisable figures in the global technology industry.Little known to the wider public until a few years ago, the 63-year-old has become a prominent face of the artificial intelligence boom. He regularly draws stadium-sized crowds at technology events, where he presents Nvidia's latest products and computing systems.His company makes Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), specialised processors that were initially developed to handle complex graphics but have since become essential to training and running advanced AI systems.Nvidia's rapid rise has pushed its market valuation to around $4.5 trillion, making it one of the world's most valuable companies. Huang, who owns roughly four per cent of the company, has an estimated fortune of $160 billion, according to Forbes.He founded Nvidia in 1993 with two friends after meeting them at a Silicon Valley diner. The company created the first GPU in 1999 and went on to benefit from the growth of video games, data centres, cloud computing and, more recently, generative AI.Huang has also developed a close informal relationship with US President Donald Trump, advising him on artificial intelligence. He travelled with Trump aboard Air Force One during the president's visit to Beijing earlier this year. His influence over an industry increasingly viewed as critical to national security has made the latest allegations particularly sensitive..China dismisses spy plot claim involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as smear campaign.How did Jensen Huang rise to prominence?Huang's journey to the top of the technology industry began with an unconventional childhood. At the age of nine, he was sent with his brother to a boarding school in Kentucky after his uncle recommended the institution to their Taiwanese parents, believing it to be a prestigious school. It was, in fact, a school for troubled youth.Too young to enrol as a student, Huang boarded there but attended a nearby public school alongside the children of tobacco farmers. Struggling with English, he was bullied and made to clean toilets during what he later described as a difficult two-year period."We worked really hard, we studied really hard, and the kids were really tough," he recounted in an interview with US broadcaster NPR.But "the ending of the story is I loved the time I was there," Huang said.His parents later brought him home after settling in Oregon in the northwestern United States. He graduated from university at the age of 20 and went on to work at chipmakers AMD and LSI Logic.Huang eventually decided to establish his own company, with a focus on developing processors capable of handling computing tasks beyond the capabilities of conventional computers.Nvidia was founded in 1993 to "solve problems that normal computers can't," he said during an interview on the "No Priors" podcast.Shaping Nvidia's AI ambitionsHuang is known for his distinctive public image, almost always appearing in a black T-shirt and leather jacket. He also has a Nvidia logo tattoo and a fondness for sports cars.One former senior Nvidia employee described him to AFP as "the most driven person" he had ever met.His approach to artificial intelligence has also attracted attention. While some technology insiders have warned that unchecked AI development could pose an existential threat to humanity within a decade, Huang has rejected calls to deliberately slow the industry down."That kind of narrative is dramatic, it gets a lot of attention," but "it's not grounded on facts," he told CBS News in September."We should go as fast as we can" on AI, but labs should not release products that are not safe, he said.In Taiwan, where he was born, Huang is treated almost like a celebrity. Fans regularly crowd around him for photographs and autographs, while journalists have followed him to his barber shop and favourite night market."He has created the phenomena because of his personal charm," noted Wayne Lin of Witology Market Trend Research Institute."A person like him must be very busy and his schedule should be full every day meeting big bosses. But he remembers to eat street food when he comes to Taiwan," he said, calling Huang "unusually friendly."However, his public image has not always reflected the atmosphere inside the company. While Nvidia has maintained a largely drama-free image around its chief, a former employee described Huang as a "very paradoxical" individual who was fiercely protective of his employees but could also, within the executive circle, be capable of "ripping people to shreds" over major mistakes or poor decisions..As the world debates the risks of AI, China closes the technology gap with US.Who is Alice Huang?Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is the Chinese national identified in media reports as the woman allegedly recruited by Beijing to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang.Despite sharing the same surname, the two are not related.Public information about Alice Huang remains limited. According to the New York Times, she was a senior executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that rents out computing power to businesses seeking to train and operate AI systems.The newspaper, citing people briefed on the surveillance operation, reported that she was well connected at the highest levels of the global AI chip industry and spoke good English.An online search also brought up a short profile of Alice Huang, accompanied by a photograph, on a Chinese fund database. It listed previous employment at HSBC bank and as a reporter for Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV.US intelligence officials reportedly concluded last year that Alice Huang was targeting the Nvidia chief. The alleged relationship has since become a focus of media reports.What is known about their alleged relationship?Reports about the pair's relationship emerged last week, with Huang acknowledging to Nvidia employees on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Photographs and videos from industry gatherings have also drawn attention to their association.One photograph from an industry party in 2024, posted on LinkedIn, appears to show Huang sitting next to a long-haired woman wearing elaborate jewellery, believed to be Alice Huang.The following year, both attended a dinner hosted by the Nvidia chief at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei during Computex, Taiwan's leading technology exhibition.Journalists filmed through the restaurant's glass windows and doors as Huang and a woman identified as Alice Huang, wearing a pink dress, mingled with other guests.At one point, Huang is seen putting his arm around her as she kisses him on the right cheek, according to press livestreams.She is also seen following the Nvidia chief as he re-enters the restaurant after speaking to journalists outside, running her fingers down his lower back. The two later leave in the same car.The reports have brought renewed scrutiny to Huang's personal life, although the alleged espionage operation has potentially wider implications for the global technology industry..China's spy chief warns 'hostile forces' using AI to threaten national security.What is Megaspeed and why is it under scrutiny?Megaspeed International is a Singapore-based data centre company that rents out computing power to other businesses for training and running AI systems. These chips are also considered strategically important because of their potential military applications.The United States has imposed restrictions on exports of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China, citing national security concerns. The restrictions are also part of Washington's broader effort to maintain its technological advantage over Beijing in artificial intelligence.The measures have made access to advanced computing hardware a sensitive issue for companies operating across international markets.The New York Times reported that the US government had been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over concerns that it may have helped direct Nvidia chips to China. The newspaper also reported that Singapore authorities had investigated the company and questioned Alice Huang in 2025.Last year, Bloomberg News separately reported on the Singapore investigation into Megaspeed over the alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips to China. The claims have not been independently established, while the investigations into Megaspeed and the Nvidia chief's conduct could have significant implications for one of the most powerful companies in the technology industry.(With inputs from AFP and AP).Washington accuses Chinese AI firms of 'systematic' theft from US rivals.As the US and China form AI blocs, countries are increasingly torn between them.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.

U.S. officials had earlier suspected that Alice Huang , an executive at a Singapore-based data-center company, was helping China evade restrictions on advanced AI chipe, while maintaining a close relationship with Jensen Huang.

Meanwhile, the company's head of public policy communications said that Huang would continue to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption.
Nvidia stock closed 4.27% lower on Monday after the tech giant launched an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.

But if Huang's position is "endangered," then "Nvidia might cut back on supporting other companies, whether it's in Asia or in the U.S., that might then spread a little bit more into the other semiconductor names," he said.
Nvidia said its board has launched an independent investigation following the reports that Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said Monday that the "so-called Chinese spy narrative" was unsubstantiated, Reuters reported.
While the probe and affair are a "game changer" for the CEO and company, it doesn't alter the view that Nvidia remains two to three years ahead of China in artificial intelligence chips, Ives said.
But any talk of replacing Huang is "comedy," Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNBC's " Squawk Box Europe ."
Joachim Klement, investment strategist at Panmure Liberum, said the impact is currently contained to Nvidia.
Nvidia is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings on Nov.
17 and will hold a major conference in Washington, D.C., at the end of the month.
— CNBC's Kif Leswing and Kamaron McNair helped contribute to this report.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology.
The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.
Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake.

Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.

Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.

The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024.

extraction.body: Nvidia stock closed 4.27% lower on Monday after the tech giant launched an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. U.S. intelligence agencies said Alice Huang, an executive at cloud company Megaspeed, has been passing information to Beijing, according to reports in The New York Times and the Financial Times . Nvidia said its board has launched an independent investigation following the reports that Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it," the company said in a Sunday statement . The co-founder and CEO told staff in an email that he had "fallen short" of his responsibility to serve his colleagues, the board, partners and shareholders around the world. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," Huang said in the email. China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said Monday that the "so-called Chinese spy narrative" was unsubstantiated, Reuters reported. The probe has sparked questions about Huang's future as CEO of the company. But any talk of replacing Huang is "comedy," Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNBC's " Squawk Box Europe ." While the probe and affair are a "game changer" for the CEO and company, it doesn't alter the view that Nvidia remains two to three years ahead of China in artificial intelligence chips, Ives said. "You're talking about what I would view as a torchbearer — the leader of AI technology — not just in the U.S. but globally. So I think the fact that we're in this situation, from an investor perspective, the clear worry is, does Jensen stay on as CEO? The Street would say probably likely, but given the board investigation, anything could happen, and that creates a huge uncertainty." Tech stocks took a hammering last week as investors reassessed the data center buildout after Democrats won control of Congress. Asian tech stocks rose across the region on Monday, rebounding from Friday's losses. Shares of U.S. chipmakers also climbed, with Marvell adding 9.49%, Arm Holdings gaining 6.69% Intel adding 5.49% and Qualcomm rising 3.66% on Monday. Broadcom added 8.78% and Nvidia AI chip rival Advanced Micro Devices gained 13.26%. Joachim Klement, investment strategist at Panmure Liberum, said the impact is currently contained to Nvidia. But if Huang's position is "endangered," then "Nvidia might cut back on supporting other companies, whether it's in Asia or in the U.S., that might then spread a little bit more into the other semiconductor names," he said. U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday praised Huang's leadership but said he hadn't spoken to the CEO about the investigation. "I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it," the president told reporters. "He's done an amazing job for our country," Trump added. Shaun Maguire, partner at Sequoia, also defended the tech giant CEO, saying in a post on X that Huang is "one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation." He added, "two mistakes don't make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership." SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk reshared Maguire's post, adding that he agrees with the venture capitalist's statements. Nvidia is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17 and will hold a major conference in Washington, D.C., at the end of the month. — CNBC's Kif Leswing and Kamaron McNair helped contribute to this report. The co-founder and CEO told staff in an email that he had "fallen short" of his responsibility to serve his colleagues, the board, partners and shareholders around the world.
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," Huang said in the email.
China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said Monday that the "so-called Chinese spy narrative" was unsubstantiated, Reuters reported.
The probe has sparked questions about Huang's future as CEO of the company.
But any talk of replacing Huang is "comedy," Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNBC's " Squawk Box Europe ."
While the probe and affair are a "game changer" for the CEO and company, it doesn't alter the view that Nvidia remains two to three years ahead of China in artificial intelligence chips, Ives said.

"You're talking about what I would view as a torchbearer — the leader of AI technology — not just in the U.S. but globally. So I think the fact that we're in this situation, from an investor perspective, the clear worry is, does Jensen stay on as CEO? The Street would say probably likely, but given the board investigation, anything could happen, and that creates a huge uncertainty."
Tech stocks took a hammering last week as investors reassessed the data center buildout after Democrats won control of Congress.

Asian tech stocks rose across the region on Monday, rebounding from Friday's losses. Shares of U.S. chipmakers also climbed, with Marvell adding 9.49%, Arm Holdings gaining 6.69% Intel adding 5.49% and Qualcomm rising 3.66% on Monday. Broadcom added 8.78% and Nvidia AI chip rival Advanced Micro Devices gained 13.26%.
Joachim Klement, investment strategist at Panmure Liberum, said the impact is currently contained to Nvidia.

But if Huang's position is "endangered," then "Nvidia might cut back on supporting other companies, whether it's in Asia or in the U.S., that might then spread a little bit more into the other semiconductor names," he said.
U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday praised Huang's leadership but said he hadn't spoken to the CEO about the investigation.
"I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it," the president told reporters.
"He's done an amazing job for our country," Trump added.
Shaun Maguire, partner at Sequoia, also defended the tech giant CEO, saying in a post on X that Huang is "one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation."
He added, "two mistakes don't make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership."
SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk reshared Maguire's post, adding that he agrees with the venture capitalist's statements.
Nvidia is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17 and will hold a major conference in Washington, D.C., at the end of the month.
— CNBC's Kif Leswing and Kamaron McNair helped contribute to this report.

sources.title: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny
passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology.
The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.
Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake.

Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.

Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.

The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024.
At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.
The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia.
Historically, China has been a big market for the company.
It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives.
In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue.
Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China.
Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead.
Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers .
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang, the billionaire chief executive of US chipmaker Nvidia, has built a reputation as one of the most influential figures in the global artificial intelligence industry. But the man behind the technology powering AI tools such as ChatGPT is now at the centre of a controversy involving an alleged Chinese spy, an extramarital affair and questions over the movement of advanced computer chips to China.Media reports last week said US intelligence officials believe Huang grew close to a Chinese executive who was funneling information to Beijing. The woman, identified as Alice Huang, is alleged to have been recruited by China to gather intelligence on the Nvidia chief.Nvidia's board said on Sunday it had opened a probe into its CEO and co-founder. Huang, 63, acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and told employees he was "deeply sorry".The allegations have drawn attention to the intersection of personal relationships, corporate espionage and the increasingly sensitive technology rivalry between the United States and China.While the alleged relationship has put Huang's personal life under scrutiny, questions have also emerged over Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data centre company where Alice Huang reportedly held a senior position. The company has been linked to investigations into the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China, which faces US restrictions on acquiring some of the most advanced processors.Here is what we know about the people, companies and allegations involved.Who is Jensen Huang?Born in Taipei in 1963, Jensen Huang, originally named Jen-Hsun, is one of the most recognisable figures in the global technology industry.Little known to the wider public until a few years ago, the 63-year-old has become a prominent face of the artificial intelligence boom. He regularly draws stadium-sized crowds at technology events, where he presents Nvidia's latest products and computing systems.His company makes Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), specialised processors that were initially developed to handle complex graphics but have since become essential to training and running advanced AI systems.Nvidia's rapid rise has pushed its market valuation to around $4.5 trillion, making it one of the world's most valuable companies. Huang, who owns roughly four per cent of the company, has an estimated fortune of $160 billion, according to Forbes.He founded Nvidia in 1993 with two friends after meeting them at a Silicon Valley diner. The company created the first GPU in 1999 and went on to benefit from the growth of video games, data centres, cloud computing and, more recently, generative AI.Huang has also developed a close informal relationship with US President Donald Trump, advising him on artificial intelligence. He travelled with Trump aboard Air Force One during the president's visit to Beijing earlier this year. His influence over an industry increasingly viewed as critical to national security has made the latest allegations particularly sensitive..China dismisses spy plot claim involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as smear campaign.How did Jensen Huang rise to prominence?Huang's journey to the top of the technology industry began with an unconventional childhood. At the age of nine, he was sent with his brother to a boarding school in Kentucky after his uncle recommended the institution to their Taiwanese parents, believing it to be a prestigious school. It was, in fact, a school for troubled youth.Too young to enrol as a student, Huang boarded there but attended a nearby public school alongside the children of tobacco farmers. Struggling with English, he was bullied and made to clean toilets during what he later described as a difficult two-year period."We worked really hard, we studied really hard, and the kids were really tough," he recounted in an interview with US broadcaster NPR.But "the ending of the story is I loved the time I was there," Huang said.His parents later brought him home after settling in Oregon in the northwestern United States. He graduated from university at the age of 20 and went on to work at chipmakers AMD and LSI Logic.Huang eventually decided to establish his own company, with a focus on developing processors capable of handling computing tasks beyond the capabilities of conventional computers.Nvidia was founded in 1993 to "solve problems that normal computers can't," he said during an interview on the "No Priors" podcast.Shaping Nvidia's AI ambitionsHuang is known for his distinctive public image, almost always appearing in a black T-shirt and leather jacket. He also has a Nvidia logo tattoo and a fondness for sports cars.One former senior Nvidia employee described him to AFP as "the most driven person" he had ever met.His approach to artificial intelligence has also attracted attention. While some technology insiders have warned that unchecked AI development could pose an existential threat to humanity within a decade, Huang has rejected calls to deliberately slow the industry down."That kind of narrative is dramatic, it gets a lot of attention," but "it's not grounded on facts," he told CBS News in September."We should go as fast as we can" on AI, but labs should not release products that are not safe, he said.In Taiwan, where he was born, Huang is treated almost like a celebrity. Fans regularly crowd around him for photographs and autographs, while journalists have followed him to his barber shop and favourite night market."He has created the phenomena because of his personal charm," noted Wayne Lin of Witology Market Trend Research Institute."A person like him must be very busy and his schedule should be full every day meeting big bosses. But he remembers to eat street food when he comes to Taiwan," he said, calling Huang "unusually friendly."However, his public image has not always reflected the atmosphere inside the company. While Nvidia has maintained a largely drama-free image around its chief, a former employee described Huang as a "very paradoxical" individual who was fiercely protective of his employees but could also, within the executive circle, be capable of "ripping people to shreds" over major mistakes or poor decisions..As the world debates the risks of AI, China closes the technology gap with US.Who is Alice Huang?Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is the Chinese national identified in media reports as the woman allegedly recruited by Beijing to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang.Despite sharing the same surname, the two are not related.Public information about Alice Huang remains limited. According to the New York Times, she was a senior executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that rents out computing power to businesses seeking to train and operate AI systems.The newspaper, citing people briefed on the surveillance operation, reported that she was well connected at the highest levels of the global AI chip industry and spoke good English.An online search also brought up a short profile of Alice Huang, accompanied by a photograph, on a Chinese fund database. It listed previous employment at HSBC bank and as a reporter for Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV.US intelligence officials reportedly concluded last year that Alice Huang was targeting the Nvidia chief. The alleged relationship has since become a focus of media reports.What is known about their alleged relationship?Reports about the pair's relationship emerged last week, with Huang acknowledging to Nvidia employees on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Photographs and videos from industry gatherings have also drawn attention to their association.One photograph from an industry party in 2024, posted on LinkedIn, appears to show Huang sitting next to a long-haired woman wearing elaborate jewellery, believed to be Alice Huang.The following year, both attended a dinner hosted by the Nvidia chief at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei during Computex, Taiwan's leading technology exhibition.Journalists filmed through the restaurant's glass windows and doors as Huang and a woman identified as Alice Huang, wearing a pink dress, mingled with other guests.At one point, Huang is seen putting his arm around her as she kisses him on the right cheek, according to press livestreams.She is also seen following the Nvidia chief as he re-enters the restaurant after speaking to journalists outside, running her fingers down his lower back. The two later leave in the same car.The reports have brought renewed scrutiny to Huang's personal life, although the alleged espionage operation has potentially wider implications for the global technology industry..China's spy chief warns 'hostile forces' using AI to threaten national security.What is Megaspeed and why is it under scrutiny?Megaspeed International is a Singapore-based data centre company that rents out computing power to other businesses for training and running AI systems. These chips are also considered strategically important because of their potential military applications.The United States has imposed restrictions on exports of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China, citing national security concerns. The restrictions are also part of Washington's broader effort to maintain its technological advantage over Beijing in artificial intelligence.The measures have made access to advanced computing hardware a sensitive issue for companies operating across international markets.The New York Times reported that the US government had been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over concerns that it may have helped direct Nvidia chips to China. The newspaper also reported that Singapore authorities had investigated the company and questioned Alice Huang in 2025.Last year, Bloomberg News separately reported on the Singapore investigation into Megaspeed over the alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips to China. He regularly draws stadium-sized crowds at technology events, where he presents Nvidia's latest products and computing systems.His company makes Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), specialised processors that were initially developed to handle complex graphics but have since become essential to training and running advanced AI systems.Nvidia's rapid rise has pushed its market valuation to around $4.5 trillion, making it one of the world's most valuable companies.

Huang, who owns roughly four per cent of the company, has an estimated fortune of $160 billion, according to Forbes.He founded Nvidia in 1993 with two friends after meeting them at a Silicon Valley diner.

The company created the first GPU in 1999 and went on to benefit from the growth of video games, data centres, cloud computing and, more recently, generative AI.Huang has also developed a close informal relationship with US President Donald Trump, advising him on artificial intelligence.
He travelled with Trump aboard Air Force One during the president's visit to Beijing earlier this year.

His influence over an industry increasingly viewed as critical to national security has made the latest allegations particularly sensitive..China dismisses spy plot claim involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as smear campaign.How did Jensen Huang rise to prominence?Huang's journey to the top of the technology industry began with an unconventional childhood.
At the age of nine, he was sent with his brother to a boarding school in Kentucky after his uncle recommended the institution to their Taiwanese parents, believing it to be a prestigious school.
It was, in fact, a school for troubled youth.Too young to enrol as a student, Huang boarded there but attended a nearby public school alongside the children of tobacco farmers.

Struggling with English, he was bullied and made to clean toilets during what he later described as a difficult two-year period."We worked really hard, we studied really hard, and the kids were really tough," he recounted in an interview with US broadcaster NPR.But "the ending of the story is I loved the time I was there," Huang said.His parents later brought him home after settling in Oregon in the northwestern United States.

He graduated from university at the age of 20 and went on to work at chipmakers AMD and LSI Logic.Huang eventually decided to establish his own company, with a focus on developing processors capable of handling computing tasks beyond the capabilities of conventional computers.Nvidia was founded in 1993 to "solve problems that normal computers can't," he said during an interview on the "No Priors" podcast.Shaping Nvidia's AI ambitionsHuang is known for his distinctive public image, almost always appearing in a black T-shirt and leather jacket.

He also has a Nvidia logo tattoo and a fondness for sports cars.One former senior Nvidia employee described him to AFP as "the most driven person" he had ever met.His approach to artificial intelligence has also attracted attention.

While some technology insiders have warned that unchecked AI development could pose an existential threat to humanity within a decade, Huang has rejected calls to deliberately slow the industry down."That kind of narrative is dramatic, it gets a lot of attention," but "it's not grounded on facts," he told CBS News in September."We should go as fast as we can" on AI, but labs should not release products that are not safe, he said.In Taiwan, where he was born, Huang is treated almost like a celebrity.

Fans regularly crowd around him for photographs and autographs, while journalists have followed him to his barber shop and favourite night market."He has created the phenomena because of his personal charm," noted Wayne Lin of Witology Market Trend Research Institute."A person like him must be very busy and his schedule should be full every day meeting big bosses.
But he remembers to eat street food when he comes to Taiwan," he said, calling Huang "unusually friendly."However, his public image has not always reflected the atmosphere inside the company.

While Nvidia has maintained a largely drama-free image around its chief, a former employee described Huang as a "very paradoxical" individual who was fiercely protective of his employees but could also, within the executive circle, be capable of "ripping people to shreds" over major mistakes or poor decisions..As the world debates the risks of AI, China closes the technology gap with US.Who is Alice Huang?Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is the Chinese national identified in media reports as the woman allegedly recruited by Beijing to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang.Despite sharing the same surname, the two are not related.Public information about Alice Huang remains limited.

According to the New York Times, she was a senior executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that rents out computing power to businesses seeking to train and operate AI systems.The newspaper, citing people briefed on the surveillance operation, reported that she was well connected at the highest levels of the global AI chip industry and spoke good English.An online search also brought up a short profile of Alice Huang, accompanied by a photograph, on a Chinese fund database.

It listed previous employment at HSBC bank and as a reporter for Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV.US intelligence officials reportedly concluded last year that Alice Huang was targeting the Nvidia chief.

The alleged relationship has since become a focus of media reports.What is known about their alleged relationship?Reports about the pair's relationship emerged last week, with Huang acknowledging to Nvidia employees on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife.

Photographs and videos from industry gatherings have also drawn attention to their association.One photograph from an industry party in 2024, posted on LinkedIn, appears to show Huang sitting next to a long-haired woman wearing elaborate jewellery, believed to be Alice Huang.The following year, both attended a dinner hosted by the Nvidia chief at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei during Computex, Taiwan's leading technology exhibition.Journalists filmed through the restaurant's glass windows and doors as Huang and a woman identified as Alice Huang, wearing a pink dress, mingled with other guests.At one point, Huang is seen putting his arm around her as she kisses him on the right cheek, according to press livestreams.She is also seen following the Nvidia chief as he re-enters the restaurant after speaking to journalists outside, running her fingers down his lower back.

The two later leave in the same car.The reports have brought renewed scrutiny to Huang's personal life, although the alleged espionage operation has potentially wider implications for the global technology industry..China's spy chief warns 'hostile forces' using AI to threaten national security.What is Megaspeed and why is it under scrutiny?Megaspeed International is a Singapore-based data centre company that rents out computing power to other businesses for training and running AI systems.

These chips are also considered strategically important because of their potential military applications.The United States has imposed restrictions on exports of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China, citing national security concerns.

The restrictions are also part of Washington's broader effort to maintain its technological advantage over Beijing in artificial intelligence.The measures have made access to advanced computing hardware a sensitive issue for companies operating across international markets.The New York Times reported that the US government had been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over concerns that it may have helped direct Nvidia chips to China.

The newspaper also reported that Singapore authorities had investigated the company and questioned Alice Huang in 2025.Last year, Bloomberg News separately reported on the Singapore investigation into Megaspeed over the alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips to China.

The claims have not been independently established, while the investigations into Megaspeed and the Nvidia chief's conduct could have significant implications for one of the most powerful companies in the technology industry.(With inputs from AFP and AP).Washington accuses Chinese AI firms of 'systematic' theft from US rivals.As the US and China form AI blocs, countries are increasingly torn between them.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

sources.title: Nvidia earnings call drama: Will Jensen Huang talk 'Trump' and China chips after Xi summit? - CNBC
passages: On its conference call, traders on prediction markets platform Kalshi think the company might talk about President Donald Trump after CEO Jensen Huang joined him on his trip to China .
Trump has 50-50 odds of being mentioned on the call, with the chances rising recently.
Huang joined Trump for his summit in Beijing with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
After the U.S.-China summit, neither country revealed if Trump or Xi discussed Taiwan , which is home to critical chip manufacturers.
Traders now only place 15% odds that the company discusses Taiwan Semiconductor Company , down from previously a 78% chance.
And there's a 55% chance the company will discuss humanoid robots.
In his keynote address at the CES Trade Show in January, Huang said he expects to see robots with some human-level capabilities this year.
This would be a new feature of the Nvidia calls as that topic didn't come up in the company's February earnings call.
In January, Trump cleared the way for Chinese purchases of the chip model.
That came with a 25% tariff on imports for chips that will be sent to China.
Huang's presence on the trip came as the status of Nvidia's H200 chip sales in China remains uncertain.
China, though, hasn't allowed firms to purchase the chip, Trump claimed to reporters.
All eyes are on Nvidia , the world's most valuable company and artificial intelligence trade darling, as it is set to report fiscal first-quarter earnings on Wednesday after the closing bell.

sources.title: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny - TechCrunch
passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology.
The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.
Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake.

Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.

Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.

The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024.
At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.
The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia.
Historically, China has been a big market for the company.
It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives.
In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue.
Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China.
Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead.
Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers .
Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence.
Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

coreStoryFacts.text: On its conference call, traders on prediction markets platform Kalshi think the company might talk about President Donald Trump after CEO Jensen Huang joined him on his trip to China .
Trump has 50-50 odds of being mentioned on the call, with the chances rising recently.
Huang joined Trump for his summit in Beijing with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
After the U.S.-China summit, neither country revealed if Trump or Xi discussed Taiwan , which is home to critical chip manufacturers.
Traders now only place 15% odds that the company discusses Taiwan Semiconductor Company , down from previously a 78% chance.
And there's a 55% chance the company will discuss humanoid robots.
In his keynote address at the CES Trade Show in January, Huang said he expects to see robots with some human-level capabilities this year.
This would be a new feature of the Nvidia calls as that topic didn't come up in the company's February earnings call.
In January, Trump cleared the way for Chinese purchases of the chip model.
That came with a 25% tariff on imports for chips that will be sent to China.
Huang's presence on the trip came as the status of Nvidia's H200 chip sales in China remains uncertain.
China, though, hasn't allowed firms to purchase the chip, Trump claimed to reporters.
All eyes are on Nvidia , the world's most valuable company and artificial intelligence trade darling, as it is set to report fiscal first-quarter earnings on Wednesday after the closing bell.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology.
The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.
Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake.

Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.

Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.

The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024.
At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.

relevantPassages.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology.
The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.
Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake.

Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.

Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.

The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024.
At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.
The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia.
Historically, China has been a big market for the company.
It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives.
In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue.
Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China.
Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead.
Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers .

Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

The company’s chips are the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built, and demand has consistently outpaced supply for years. Nvidia has also been an influential investor in a wide range of up-and-coming AI companies in recent years, with about $99 billion worth of equity investments in frontier AI labs, neoclouds, infrastructure companies, and more. Its chief executive has even become close with President Donald Trump. This is why, as both cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry. Huang is in hot water after news broke of his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud provider and a top Nvidia customer. Questions are swirling around how the affair may have influenced Huang’s reported push to sell advanced chips to China — and potentially even influenced President Trump’s own decisions surrounding AI export controls. US officials believe the Megaspeed executive is a foreign intelligence asset that has funneled information straight to the Chinese government, per The New York Times — in particular, officials reportedly believe that Megaspeed is related to a convoluted web of Chinese companies working together to access chips in bulk and perhaps even illegally get some of those chips into China. The transaction sizes were outside the norm for a small company, particularly when Nvidia chips are so difficult to get. Nvidia spokespeople had said Huang’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive was strictly business. Their interactions were described as “not unusual or unexpected” in statements to the press. Nvidia’s line was, “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.” But at some point, their relationship became personal. In June 2024, just before Megaspeed became an Nvidia customer, photos show the two with other AI executives at a bar in Taipei after a local trade show; the following year, they reportedly had a business dinner in Taipei with others as well. But in private, according to US officials cited by the Times, the two’s relationship raised alarm bells for the US government — they had reportedly been surveilling the Megaspeed executive for months, if not longer, and that’s how it came out that she was in close contact with Huang. The revelation is particularly concerning because of Huang’s lobbying role. He’d been trying to convince the Trump administration and Congress to loosen export controls for sending advanced semiconductors to China, ostensibly so that Nvidia could sell more chips. We now know this was happening around the same time that Huang was spotted at the Taiwan dinner with Alice Huang in May 2025, according to Culper Research, which shorted Nvidia’s stock earlier this year. That dinner occurred shortly after Nvidia had shared the Trump administration’s new restrictions on its China-specific H20 chips in April. Just a couple months after the Taiwan dinner, Huang reportedly met with Trump in the Oval Office in July 2025 to plead his case for loosening export restrictions on Nvidia’s advanced semiconductors. Days later, the company announced that the administration had blessed sales of its H20 chips to China. Huang had argued that spreading American chips to China would help establish US technology as the standard, rather than allowing for Chinese chips to grow, according to The New York Times. After setbacks earlier in the second Trump term in export policy to China, Huang began speaking with then-White House AI czar David Sacks in 2025, who became the key advocate for Nvidia’s view that selling American chips to China would be beneficial, the Times reported. By October 2025, Huang was lobbying Trump to allow Nvidia to sell more advanced chips to China, ahead of Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, per the Times; but after Trump considered the proposal, he ultimately decided not to move forward. (That same month, Huang hired an external PR firm known for handling sex scandals, Wired reported.) Months later, in December 2025, Trump changed course slightly, allowing Nvidia to sell H20 chips to a greenlit list of “approved customers” in China, with the US government taking a 25 percent cut of those sales. CSET’s Dohmen said that during the past two years, the US has seen a light loosening of AI export control regulations under the Trump administration, driven partly by Huang’s own lobbying. But it’s important to note, she said, that “even without any kind of intelligence operations from the Chinese side, it is in Nvidia’s interest and in Jensen Huang’s interest to lobby for looser export control restrictions.” Any restrictions by definition stifle Nvidia’s business expansion and cut off potential sales to help it grow its already stunning market cap — which is currently about $4.25 trillion, second only to Apple. Huang’s relationship with Trump is also particularly relevant here. The president lavished praise on Huang during a speech last year, saying that until recently, he hadn’t even heard of Nvidia, and then he wanted to break it up. But after meeting Huang, he said, he understood why it would be difficult to re-create the company he’d built. More recently, Huang put Trump on speakerphone when the president called him during an appearance onstage at the All-In Summit, publicly displaying his close access to the Oval Office. This past spring, a classified memo — the writing of which was overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, per the Times — circulated among Trump administration officials ahead of the president’s trip to China in May, warning of the Megaspeed executive’s alleged involvement in surveillance on behalf of China’s Ministry of State Security. Her reported goal was to learn about advanced AI chips in the US and try to influence them being made available to China on a large scale. Asked if he had known about the memo reviewed by Rubio at a press briefing on Monday, Trump said, “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” Earlier in the briefing, he said he was unaware of the alleged spy connection ahead of his trip to China. Huang was initially left off the list of executives joining Trump on the trip, but the president later asked him to join. Trump had been briefed about a year ago that US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive to be a China intelligence operative, according to the Times, and that she had a close relationship with a US citizen who turned out to be Nvidia’s CEO. So far, the allegations haven’t affected Huang’s future at Nvidia.

sources.title: Ring, known for its doorbell cameras, launches a home security drone and an enterprise security robot - TechCrunch
passages: Automated security is one space the tech industry has never quite cracked.
In 2021, Amazon launched its own home security robot, known as Astro.

Astro, which resembles Ring’s new robot (the company says that it was inspired to create the bot because of “feedback from Amazon Astro customers”), was first announced as a kind of nebulous domestic helper before being repurposed as an enterprise security product.
Ring calls the device a “flying indoor security camera” — which should give you a pretty good idea of what it’s supposed to do and how it’s supposed to work.
Ring Drone Cam is designed to fly from room to room, inspecting what is happening in a user’s house and, if there’s trouble, to alert them.
The first new device is a home security drone that users will be able to deploy to patrol their domiciles when they’re out.

It also comes with a periscope camera, which can be adjusted to see over specific obstacles, and it also includes two-way audio — meaning that, should the remote user need to communicate with a person at the store (be that an employee or a burglar), they can speak to them through the robot.
The company announced Ring Robotics on Tuesday, debuting two new devices that are sure to stir more than a little bit of controversy.
Ring says that both robots are powered by the same proprietary AI system, known as AI Pilot.

The company says this system leverages “specialized vision models, sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” Both devices, using this software, are designed to develop a detailed schematic of your house or office purely by exploring the space for themselves, the company says.
However, Ring claims that both devices have been built with “privacy and security” baked into them.
Ring cameras generally record their videos to the cloud.

extraction.body: Ring, the Amazon-owned home security company, is launching its own robotics division, with an eye toward automating security at both the home and the office. The company announced Ring Robotics on Tuesday, debuting two new devices that are sure to stir more than a little bit of controversy. The first new device is a home security drone that users will be able to deploy to patrol their domiciles when they’re out. The other item that the company is launching is a roving enterprise security robot, designed for businesses. First, the drone. Ring calls the device a “flying indoor security camera” — which should give you a pretty good idea of what it’s supposed to do and how it’s supposed to work. Ring Drone Cam is designed to fly from room to room, inspecting what is happening in a user’s house and, if there’s trouble, to alert them. It has been built to integrate with Ring’s other home security devices so, for instance, if a Ring alarm goes off in a particular part of the home (say, the backdoor), the bot will supposedly fly to that location and investigate. When it’s not in use, the drone stays inactive in a docking bay. The drone shoots video in 2K and it also comes equipped with LED lights so that it can keep watch at night and record video in low light. It can be controlled via Amazon’s Alexa Home Map , and the bot can also be scheduled to patrol the house at specific times — so, if you know you’re going to be out for the night or even on vacation, the drone can keep you apprised of what’s happening while you’re away. Now, let’s turn to Ring Rover Cam. Like the drone, this roving robot can be set to patrol specific routes, at specific times, within the user’s business. The robot streams video in continuous 4K, which is viewable via Ring’s mobile app, and a trigger can be set to automatically record if it detects a human. It also comes with a periscope camera, which can be adjusted to see over specific obstacles, and it also includes two-way audio — meaning that, should the remote user need to communicate with a person at the store (be that an employee or a burglar), they can speak to them through the robot. Ring says that both robots are powered by the same proprietary AI system, known as AI Pilot. The company says this system leverages “specialized vision models, sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” Both devices, using this software, are designed to develop a detailed schematic of your house or office purely by exploring the space for themselves, the company says. “Together, it’s like having a guard on patrol who never clocks out,” the company claims, of its new devices. “Ring Rover can do a sweep of the floor after close and investigate when sensor trips at 2 a.m. — streaming it all to your phone, wherever you are.” Automated security is one space the tech industry has never quite cracked. In 2021, Amazon launched its own home security robot, known as Astro. Astro, which resembles Ring’s new robot (the company says that it was inspired to create the bot because of “feedback from Amazon Astro customers”), was first announced as a kind of nebulous domestic helper before being repurposed as an enterprise security product. The device never took off, however, and seven months into the robot’s glow-up as a small business security guard, Amazon put the device out to pasture . Privacy concerns have long dogged Ring — with critics frequently alleging that the company’s cameras have created unofficial surveillance networks that police departments can (and routinely do) tap into. It seems natural to assume that similar complaints will be lodged about the company’s newest products, given the invasive potential of both. However, Ring claims that both devices have been built with “privacy and security” baked into them. The company notes that the videos recorded by both devices are protected by TAKE (Throw Away the Key Encryption), which the company calls its “strongest default encryption yet.” It’s unclear whether there will be an option for local video storage. Ring cameras generally record their videos to the cloud. The Rover is being made available starting on December 16 and it will retail at a whopping $1,000. The drone, meanwhile, won’t launch until next year, on January 27, and will be made available for $270. Automated security is one space the tech industry has never quite cracked. In 2021, Amazon launched its own home security robot, known as Astro. Astro, which resembles Ring’s new robot (the company says that it was inspired to create the bot because of “feedback from Amazon Astro customers”), was first announced as a kind of nebulous domestic helper before being repurposed as an enterprise security product. The device never took off, however, and seven months into the robot’s glow-up as a small business security guard, Amazon put the device out to pasture .

Privacy concerns have long dogged Ring — with critics frequently alleging that the company’s cameras have created unofficial surveillance networks that police departments can (and routinely do) tap into. It seems natural to assume that similar complaints will be lodged about the company’s newest products, given the invasive potential of both.

However, Ring claims that both devices have been built with “privacy and security” baked into them. The company notes that the videos recorded by both devices are protected by TAKE (Throw Away the Key Encryption), which the company calls its “strongest default encryption yet.” It’s unclear whether there will be an option for local video storage. Ring cameras generally record their videos to the cloud.

The Rover is being made available starting on December 16 and it will retail at a whopping $1,000. The drone, meanwhile, won’t launch until next year, on January 27, and will be made available for $270.

sources.title: Amazon announces Astro the home robot - BBC
passages: Amazon is launching Astro, its first household robot, powered by its Alexa smart home technology.
"Astro is a bold move by Amazon, but a logical step given its expertise in robots and desire to become more integrated into consumers' daily lives,"said Ben Wood, chief analyst at CCS Insight.
The robot will ship later this year, Amazon said - but only in the US.
And after the initial, limited run, its price will go up to $1,449.99, it said.
"I'm just gutted that it won't be shipping in the UK in the foreseeable future."
At last year's event, Amazon turned heads with a flying indoor alarm drone .
The Always Home Cam launches from its deployment bay if it detects a potential intrusion, and can fly around a home to check with a video feed.
But it was not launched and no more details were released in the past year.
Amazon said it was more than "Alexa with wheels" and had been programmed with a range of movements and expressions to give it personality.
It demonstrated asking Astro to "beatbox" - and the robot bopped its head and made expressions while playing hip-hop beats.
It said Astro can be set with "out of bounds" zones, so it cannot go into certain areas, or could be set to "do not disturb".
It also features buttons to turn off cameras and microphones - though it loses its ability to move around when they are switched off.
The small robot also comes equipped with an extendable "periscope" camera that pops up from its head.
Amazon showed an example of using it to check if a gas hob had been left on after leaving the house.
Unlike some rivals, Amazon "is willing to bring highly experimental products to market" and see how customers react, he said.
"Offering products resembling something from a science fiction novel positions Amazon as an innovative company in the eyes of consumers and investors," he said.
This is largely because the price tag means it will be a toy for the rich for some time to come.
Amazon wants a slice of the robotics market, boldly stating that it believes all homes will have one in five to 10 years.
This first foray offers Amazon a chance to hone its skills.
And arguably, there is no company already as firmly embedded in our homes as Amazon.
In one example, Amazon said children could "scan" a favourite toy using the Glow's camera, and turn it into a jigsaw puzzle to reassemble.
Amazon was also keen to pre-empt privacy concerns.

extraction.body: Amazon is launching Astro, its first household robot, powered by its Alexa smart home technology. The company said it can be remote-controlled when not at home, to check on pets, people, or home security. It can also patrol a home automatically and send owners a notification if it detects something unusual. Amazon said it was more than "Alexa with wheels" and had been programmed with a range of movements and expressions to give it personality. It demonstrated asking Astro to "beatbox" - and the robot bopped its head and made expressions while playing hip-hop beats. Amazon was also keen to pre-empt privacy concerns. It said Astro can be set with "out of bounds" zones, so it cannot go into certain areas, or could be set to "do not disturb". It also features buttons to turn off cameras and microphones - though it loses its ability to move around when they are switched off. The small robot also comes equipped with an extendable "periscope" camera that pops up from its head. Amazon showed an example of using it to check if a gas hob had been left on after leaving the house. The technology and retail giant suggested that the $999.99 (£740) robot could be a help to the elderly. "Astro is a bold move by Amazon, but a logical step given its expertise in robots and desire to become more integrated into consumers' daily lives,"said Ben Wood, chief analyst at CCS Insight. Unlike some rivals, Amazon "is willing to bring highly experimental products to market" and see how customers react, he said. "Offering products resembling something from a science fiction novel positions Amazon as an innovative company in the eyes of consumers and investors," he said. The robot will ship later this year, Amazon said - but only in the US. And after the initial, limited run, its price will go up to $1,449.99, it said. "I believe the Astro robot will sell out in minutes when it becomes available in the US market," Mr Wood said. "I'm just gutted that it won't be shipping in the UK in the foreseeable future." Amazon wants a slice of the robotics market, boldly stating that it believes all homes will have one in five to 10 years. It wants Astro to be that must-have new member of the household, and there is no denying that the little wheeled robot is pretty cute - although the periscope that pops out of its head is a little creepy. But we have seen other cute humanoid robots - such as Pepper - fail to make a mark. This is largely because the price tag means it will be a toy for the rich for some time to come. And while Amazon was keen to convince us that for that you get more than "Alexa on wheels", it was hard to see a compelling use case for this other than to curb that ever-present paranoia that you left the oven on. But building robots is hard. And if the home robotics market is ever going to take off, people will have to be convinced to spend a lot of money. This first foray offers Amazon a chance to hone its skills. And arguably, there is no company already as firmly embedded in our homes as Amazon. The company is known for occasionally making unusual smart home tech such as its Alexa-controlled microwave from 2018. At last year's event, Amazon turned heads with a flying indoor alarm drone . The Always Home Cam launches from its deployment bay if it detects a potential intrusion, and can fly around a home to check with a video feed. But it was not launched and no more details were released in the past year. Instead, Amazon on Tuesday said it was opening up the invite list for early adopters to buy the drone on a limited basis - but did not give dates for widespread availability. Among the other devices unveiled at the event was the the Amazon Glow: a video calling device that has the ability to project an interactive "touchscreen" on the floor or table in front of it. The idea is to engage children during long video calls, as they can play games or draw on the 19-inch projected "screen" while on the video call. Relatives on the other end can also interact with the projection through a tablet app. In one example, Amazon said children could "scan" a favourite toy using the Glow's camera, and turn it into a jigsaw puzzle to reassemble. Royal Berkshire Hospital patients can get scans, discuss results and a treatment plan the same day. Police have launched an investigation on suspicion of sexual harassment after the robot's owner, 16, and his companion are said to have streamed the incident. The £3.67m Yorkshire Robotics Hub at the University of Bradford is hoping to bridge the "automation gap".

sources.title: Amazon turned its Alexa robot into a Ring security patrol bot
passages: As part of a new brand called Ring Robotics — designed to take a more proactive approach to security instead of just monitoring — a new rolling mobile security camera was announced by Amazon, called the Ring Rover Cam.
It borrows a lot of the design and functionality from the Astro home robot that Amazon first debuted in 2021.

It can be manually dispatched to a specific room or any point along a pre-programmed patrol route to investigate a disturbance, and it will also automatically head to a location where an alarm on another Ring device is triggered.

It now features 4K resolution, and you can set the camera to raise and lower to specific heights while programming a scheduled patrol route so the robot can see over counters, shelving, or other raised obstacles.
The Rover Cam is targeted at businesses in need of an affordable security solution that can patrol and investigate concerns in large facilities, and it comes with a few upgrades.
