It borrows a lot of the design and functionality from the Astro home robot that Amazon first debuted in 2021. The Rover Cam is targeted at businesses in need of an affordable security solution that can patrol and investigate concerns in large facilities, and it comes with a few upgrades. As with Astro, the Rover Cam rolls around on a pair of large wheels that help it navigate small obstacles or uneven terrain. It can be manually dispatched to a specific room or any point along a pre-programmed patrol route to investigate a disturbance, and it will also automatically head to a location where an alarm on another Ring device is triggered. It now features 4K resolution, and you can set the camera to raise and lower to specific heights while programming a scheduled patrol route so the robot can see over counters, shelving, or other raised obstacles. Astro’s cupholder has been replaced with a permanent stubby tower featuring a built-in siren and a flashing red light that both function as deterrents. Instead of displaying a cute pair of eyes to encourage engagement, the Rover Cam’s screen is used to display status messages, including when it’s actively recording. Battery life is estimated to be about 30 minutes, allowing the robot to cover facilities around 5,000 square feet, but it’s limited to a single floor. In 2023, it launched the $2,349.99 Astro for Business but discontinued it just a year later. The Ring Rover Cam is now available for preorder for $999.99 and is expected to ship starting on December 16th.

extraction.body: Ring, the Amazon-owned home security company, is launching its own robotics division, with an eye toward automating security at both the home and the office. The company announced Ring Robotics on Tuesday, debuting two new devices that are sure to stir more than a little bit of controversy. The first new device is a home security drone that users will be able to deploy to patrol their domiciles when they’re out. The other item that the company is launching is a roving enterprise security robot, designed for businesses. First, the drone. Ring calls the device a “flying indoor security camera” — which should give you a pretty good idea of what it’s supposed to do and how it’s supposed to work. Ring Drone Cam is designed to fly from room to room, inspecting what is happening in a user’s house and, if there’s trouble, to alert them. It has been built to integrate with Ring’s other home security devices so, for instance, if a Ring alarm goes off in a particular part of the home (say, the backdoor), the bot will supposedly fly to that location and investigate. When it’s not in use, the drone stays inactive in a docking bay. The drone shoots video in 2K and it also comes equipped with LED lights so that it can keep watch at night and record video in low light. It can be controlled via Amazon’s Alexa Home Map , and the bot can also be scheduled to patrol the house at specific times — so, if you know you’re going to be out for the night or even on vacation, the drone can keep you apprised of what’s happening while you’re away. Now, let’s turn to Ring Rover Cam. Like the drone, this roving robot can be set to patrol specific routes, at specific times, within the user’s business. The robot streams video in continuous 4K, which is viewable via Ring’s mobile app, and a trigger can be set to automatically record if it detects a human. It also comes with a periscope camera, which can be adjusted to see over specific obstacles, and it also includes two-way audio — meaning that, should the remote user need to communicate with a person at the store (be that an employee or a burglar), they can speak to them through the robot. Ring says that both robots are powered by the same proprietary AI system, known as AI Pilot. The company says this system leverages “specialized vision models, sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” Both devices, using this software, are designed to develop a detailed schematic of your house or office purely by exploring the space for themselves, the company says. “Together, it’s like having a guard on patrol who never clocks out,” the company claims, of its new devices. “Ring Rover can do a sweep of the floor after close and investigate when sensor trips at 2 a.m. — streaming it all to your phone, wherever you are.” Automated security is one space the tech industry has never quite cracked. In 2021, Amazon launched its own home security robot, known as Astro. Astro, which resembles Ring’s new robot (the company says that it was inspired to create the bot because of “feedback from Amazon Astro customers”), was first announced as a kind of nebulous domestic helper before being repurposed as an enterprise security product. The device never took off, however, and seven months into the robot’s glow-up as a small business security guard, Amazon put the device out to pasture . Privacy concerns have long dogged Ring — with critics frequently alleging that the company’s cameras have created unofficial surveillance networks that police departments can (and routinely do) tap into. It seems natural to assume that similar complaints will be lodged about the company’s newest products, given the invasive potential of both. However, Ring claims that both devices have been built with “privacy and security” baked into them. The company notes that the videos recorded by both devices are protected by TAKE (Throw Away the Key Encryption), which the company calls its “strongest default encryption yet.” It’s unclear whether there will be an option for local video storage. Ring cameras generally record their videos to the cloud. The Rover is being made available starting on December 16 and it will retail at a whopping $1,000. The drone, meanwhile, won’t launch until next year, on January 27, and will be made available for $270. sources.title: Amazon turned its Alexa robot into a Ring security patrol bot
passages: As part of a new brand called Ring Robotics — designed to take a more proactive approach to security instead of just monitoring — a new rolling mobile security camera was announced by Amazon, called the Ring Rover Cam.
It borrows a lot of the design and functionality from the Astro home robot that Amazon first debuted in 2021.

It can be manually dispatched to a specific room or any point along a pre-programmed patrol route to investigate a disturbance, and it will also automatically head to a location where an alarm on another Ring device is triggered.

It now features 4K resolution, and you can set the camera to raise and lower to specific heights while programming a scheduled patrol route so the robot can see over counters, shelving, or other raised obstacles.
The Rover Cam is targeted at businesses in need of an affordable security solution that can patrol and investigate concerns in large facilities, and it comes with a few upgrades.

extraction.body: As part of a new brand called Ring Robotics — designed to take a more proactive approach to security instead of just monitoring — a new rolling mobile security camera was announced by Amazon, called the Ring Rover Cam. It borrows a lot of the design and functionality from the Astro home robot that Amazon first debuted in 2021. The Rover Cam is targeted at businesses in need of an affordable security solution that can patrol and investigate concerns in large facilities, and it comes with a few upgrades. As with Astro, the Rover Cam rolls around on a pair of large wheels that help it navigate small obstacles or uneven terrain. It can be manually dispatched to a specific room or any point along a pre-programmed patrol route to investigate a disturbance, and it will also automatically head to a location where an alarm on another Ring device is triggered. It now features 4K resolution, and you can set the camera to raise and lower to specific heights while programming a scheduled patrol route so the robot can see over counters, shelving, or other raised obstacles. Astro’s cupholder has been replaced with a permanent stubby tower featuring a built-in siren and a flashing red light that both function as deterrents. Instead of displaying a cute pair of eyes to encourage engagement, the Rover Cam’s screen is used to display status messages, including when it’s actively recording. Battery life is estimated to be about 30 minutes, allowing the robot to cover facilities around 5,000 square feet, but it’s limited to a single floor. In 2023, it launched the $2,349.99 Astro for Business but discontinued it just a year later. The Ring Rover Cam is now available for preorder for $999.99 and is expected to ship starting on December 16th.

One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting an investigation. US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing , according to a New York Times report. On Sunday, Huang admitted , external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the reports. The firm said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is also investigating the affair . The FBI declined to comment further when contacted by the BBC. Trump said he spoke with Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. "I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - pictured at an event US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . Her current whereabouts are unknown. Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked. However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday at a regular daily press briefing: "We have already responded to this. The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China." The New York Times reported in late October that Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf. Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Huang. Last spring, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman, according to the New York Times. Nvidia shares slide as US tech giant investigates CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China . Huang has soared to international importance with his company Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" , he has a reputation as a workaholic and perfectionist with incredibly high standards for his staff. He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang. His children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez work at Nvidia in senior roles. passages: So far, Nvidia and Jensen Huang have said that they have “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that hasn’t settled things as the investigation continues.

extraction.body: When you go poking neighbours garden and picking fruits nothing good comes out of it The CEO of tech giant Nvidia is under scrutiny by both his own company and politicians amid reports he was the target of an alleged Chinese spy. As a result of the allegations and investigation, Nvidia’s stock fell four per cent on Monday. The New York Times reported on Oct. 29 that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been involved in a relationship with Alice Huang , a former executive of Nvidia Cloud partner Megaspeed. Eight days later on Nov. 6, the New York Times reported U.S. intelligence had alleged she was a spy for Beijing. Huang acknowledged his affair in a letter to his family and the company this weekend. Here’s what is known so far about Huang, his relationship with the Megaspeed former executive and what this means for the Nvidia going forward. Jensen Huang is the president and CEO of Nvidia and co-founded the multi-national technology company in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. The 63-year-old was born in Taiwan then moved to Thailand with his family as a child before being sent by his parents to live in the U.S. at age nine. He graduated from Oregon State University as an electrical engineer and received a master’s degree in the same field from Stanford University. Ranked the eighth richest man in the world by Forbes and sometimes known as “Daddy Huang,” he’s been also recognized for his trademark leather jackets and high-profile launches. Huang also has a close relationship with President Donald Trump, having travelled to China in May as part of a state visit. He’s also pushed Trump to ease export restrictions on Nvidia chips. He’s been married to his wife Lori Huang since 1985 and has two children. Their daughter Madison is a senior director of product and technical marketing for physical AI platforms at Nvidia, while son Spencer manages robotics software products. The Nvidia CEO apologized to both his wife and children in a letter the company posted Sunday, admitting he was unfaithful. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote. “My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy. But Beijing has been interested in AI microchips from Nvidia for several years. Its most advanced chips are barred from sale in China, but the Trump administration gave permission for Nvidia to sell its H200 chips to 10 approved Chinese firms last year. China has imposed its own restrictions over concerns of dependence on U.S. technology, with Reuters reporting about 600,000 of the company’s chips are stored in Hong Kong awaiting shipment. “We know for a fact that China has engaged in espionage particularly in those areas it has identified as strategic and one of those areas right now is going to be frontier AI,” said Stephanie Carvin, a former national security analyst and associate professor at Carleton University. “It absolutely needs and wants the chips that are produced by Nvidia and other companies to further its ambitions in this kind of geopolitical race.” Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen and former executive of Megaspeed, an AI company that calls itself a specialized Cloud provider and a partner of Nvidia in the Asia-Pacific region. The company has been under investigation by the U.S. government over suspicions it helped Beijing gain access to the U.S. tech giant’s advanced AI chips that are currently barred. In December 2025, Megaspeed posted a message that its company had undergone multiple inspections by U.S. government departments, as well as Nvidia. “These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company,” the statement reads. Global News has requested comment on the latest investigation involving its former executive. It is not known at this time when the pair started their relationship, but Reuters reported the two were previously pictured at a bar together in Taipei in 2025 during a technology conference. The affair appears to have hallmarks of what security experts call a “honey pot.” “They could be convincing you to try and give up information that you have or to make certain decisions and try to persuade you in some way,” she said. “But even just the affair itself can be harmful, right, because it can be used as blackmail.” Chinese industrial espionage has been a significant concern for officials over recent decades in both Canada and the U.S. “The long-term cost to the American economy and national security cannot be precisely measured, but estimates run into the billions of dollars for commercial and technological espionage.” Following Huang’s apology, Nvidia announced Sunday it was launching an investigation led by a committee of independent directors and assisted by outside counsel. The company said it prioritizes national and economic security, though adds it has “no reason to believe” either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. The board said it has confidence in Huang and his leadership team. Nvidia appears to be backing its CEO for now, but Jeffrey Sonnenfeld at Yale University’s School of Management said while Huang has no successor at this time and has been praised for his work with the company, his future is “50-50.” “It’s 50-50 whether or not he can hold onto his position,” Sonnenfeld told Global News. “There’s a blow to his credibility though already that he would put the company at risk … Even if exonerated, he certainly has a permanent black eye for the recklessness.” U.S. lawmakers have launched their own investigation, with three Republican House committee chairs requesting Huang appear before them for a joint, closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang. They’ve asked him to appear on Nov. 18 or to provide an alternative date by Nov. 11. Trump said Monday that the FBI was investigating the affair between Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, adding he didn’t think the CEO would have anything to worry about. “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” Trump told reporters.

Here’s how it works . Third time may be the charm for Ring's long-gestating security drone efforts — and Ring CEO Jamie Simioff insists that the new Ring Drone Cam is just what his customers want. "When people stop me on the street, it's what they ask, 'Where's the drone?'" Simioff told me. After a decade of effort, which traces back to before Ring became a part of the giant Amazon device family, Ring is finally ready to deliver a home security drone that makes sense. Sure, perhaps we've heard this before, and Siminoff wasn't shy about recounting Ring's abortive drone history. That history started with an idea in 2016, which led to a drone that Siminoff said launched in 2021 but not to customers. "They were in boxes and ready to go," he added (design trade-offs, limited flight time, privacy concerns, and other issues ultimately scuttled that launch ). By 2025, Ring was ready with another attempt, but that drone also never shipped. As Sminioff described it, Ring was overcomplicating the drones, building in too many capabilities. A smart drone — basically a flying robot with all the attendant sensors — was the wrong approach. So Ring went back to the drawing board but with a critical learning: "The more sensors you take off, the lighter you can go, because you’re using less power." He said Ring decided to "take all the intelligence out" and shifted it to the cloud. The resulting security drone is ultra-light (around 160 grams) and has just a few native skills, which include knowing how to land and how to connect via Wi-Fi to the app. The App connects to Ring's new AI Pilot, which uses cloud-based, silicon-powered agents to control the drone. Not that the drone is flying blind. It has a front camera, a base camera, and the guidance of the AI Pilot, which is using a brand-new home map. Ring Drone Cam owners will be able to use the drone to walk through their home and build a detailed map, which Siminoff described as a "digital twin" of your space. If, for instance, you detect a rear door open or a window ajar in your home (via one of Ring's sensors that they assume you'll have throughout your home), you can tap on the location in the digital house map and the Ring Drone Cam will lift off from its home charge base and fly directly to it. The AI Pilot knows the map of your home, so it won't be bouncing off walls and, if someone does happen to be in the way, the Ring Drone Cam will know how to get around them. Siminoff admitted, though, that the drone is simply not smart enough to come up with an alternative route to get around, say, a group of people. A relatively simple and lightweight flyer, the Ring Drone Cam is quite loud, and Siminoff says that's intentional. "It’s loud — we think that’s a feature. This thing is not gonna sneak up on you." In fact, the use case he envisions is when nobody is home, though he agreed that if you're home asleep and there's movement downstairs, it could come in handy then, too. The sound alone might scare off intruders. The Ring Drone Cam is not designed to go outside, but it can peer out of a window. Imagine that someone approaches your front door, and the Ring Doorbell detects them. The Drone Cam could get the alert, lift off, and shine its LED spotlights out the window. I asked Siminoff if the Ring app would support split-screen, so you could see the Drone and Doorbell footage side-by-side. He said it didn't, but that he liked the idea. In the app, Ring Drone Cam owners can schedule automated home patrols that include multiple floors, since this drone can traverse stairways. The drone keeps track of the ground below but has no sensor for the ceiling. It also depends on that Wi-Fi connection for navigation. If your home internet cuts out, the Drone will basically land where it is, assuming it's safe to do so. Speaking of safety, all four propellers are inside cages, so even if the lightweight drone does somehow run into you, you're unlikely to get injured. Siminoff also said that the Drone Cam promises the same level of video privacy as you find on the brand's video doorbells, which includes two-factor authentication and encryption. Also, as soon as the drone lands, it stops filming, and the charging dock also covers the camera when the drone is settled inside. As you might expect for such a small and lightweight drone, the Ring Drone Cam doesn't offer much flight time, cruising for roughly five to eight minutes on a charge (consumer drones can often fly for up to 30 minutes). Charging could take between 40 minutes and an hour, though I imagine its patrol flights might just be a minute or two, after which the drone would return to its charging base. Assuming that this is the drone Ring finally ships, the Ring Drone Cam will be available in the US only (Ring hasn't announced any plans to expand the launch) from January 27 for $249.99 and will be available in dark gray. The white units I saw were all pre-production, and there are currently no plans to offer a white option. Remember Amazon Astro, the sort-of-cute patrol robot that Amazon launched in 2021 and discontinued in 2024 ? It's back, in a fashion. Using Astro as a base, Ring rebuilt it, added a light tower, and rechristened it the Ring Rover Cam. extraction.body: Ring is finally shipping a flying indoor drone camera. The Ring Drone Cam will arrive on January 27th, 2027, for $249.99, Ring founder Jamie Siminoff said at a launch event in New York City this week. If it does actually ship, it will arrive almost six years after the company announced its first flying camera, the Ring Always Home Cam. Designed to patrol inside your home when you’re not there, the Drone Cam is an AI-powered drone that can react to triggers from Ring sensors, such as detecting motion, a door opening, a water leak, or an alarm sounding. When triggered, it flies along pre-programmed routes to a set location, where it can livestream and record what’s happening in the Ring app. The drone can also run scheduled patrols around your home or be sent out on demand. It’s a completely different product from the Always Home Cam that was announced in 2020. It’s significantly smaller, about a quarter the size of the model I saw demoed at CES in 2023, weighing 165 grams. A small camera is integrated into its body, as opposed to dangling in the center. [Video: Ring Drone Cam Footage of Jen] Ring claims the Drone Cam can fly for 5 to 8 minutes on a charge, and for every minute of flight time takes 8 minutes of charging — meaning a five-minute flight needs about 40 minutes of charging. This short flight time suggests the product is better suited to quick check-ins than continuous monitoring, and whether it can really replace multiple stationary cameras remains to be seen. The drone apparently follows pre-planned flight paths you set up in the Ring app and will go around any obstacles it encounters along those routes. However, I didn’t get to see it interact with obstacles or anything unexpected — I’m particularly curious how pets will react to it. A long runway Siminoff said Ring has been developing the drone since 2016 and has come close to shipping two different models over that time, before landing on the current version. Siminoff explained that they struggled to pack all the technology needed for an autonomous drone to fly in your home into a practical design for less than $250. “Truly, it’s like an AI agent that’s controlling the robot,” said Siminoff. Rover also uses AI Pilot and is available for pre-order now, with shipping expected to begin on December 16th, 2026. Both security devices work like any other Ring camera, streaming and sending recorded video to the Ring app and require a Ring Protect plan for video storage and advanced features. They will also work with Amazon’s upcoming Alexa Home Map to understand your home and where sensors and other devices are located. [Image: Ring’s Drone Cam is slated to launch in January. Ring ushered in a world of new privacy questions when its cameras first started entering people’s homes more than a decade ago. Over the past year, the company’s new technologies have sparked fears that it could enable a surveillance state. An AI-piloted drone that can map your home, fly from room to room, and relies on the cloud to operate will certainly raise new privacy questions when it hits the market next year.

extraction.body: Amazon announced during its fall hardware event Tuesday that the Ring Always Home Cam — the flying drone camera announced during the same event last year — will begin selling this fall. Starting today, you can request an invitation to buy the Always Home Cam . The Ring Always Home Cam will cost $250, and it will be able to fly around your house following a preset flight path. You’ll be able to schedule a route around the house or trigger a trip manually. In addition, the camera will be able to respond to certain events — such as an armed door/window sensor in the Ring Alarm system being set off. The camera is not designed to cover multiple floors, so flying up or down stairs seems to be out, along with remote control, which Ring said will not be possible for security and privacy reasons. The Always Home Cam will not be able to record footage while it’s docked, and its loud propellers will make its presence known, in case you’re worried about its access to private spaces in your home. Ring’s privacy has been the subject of close scrutiny and sharp criticism — particularly for how it has shared user information with police, and how it has facilitated video sharing on its public app and with police. Despite some recent improvements to its policies, releasing a flying drone camera complicates already-difficult questions about where Ring stands on privacy. Indoor security cameras have contributed to serious privacy breaches as it is; to attach propellers to one and enable it to fly autonomously around a house potentially compounds the existing problems. (Ring’s indoor cameras, including the Always Home Cam, cannot be used to respond to Requests for Assistance posts by police.) Amazon’s strategy for rolling out the drone cam is perhaps more telling than it seems. The tech giant has relied on invite-only sales when a device’s uptake has been uncertain — the Echo Auto , Alexa Microwave and other so-called Day 1 devices spring to mind here. The strategy, in these cases, has been explicit: limit the initial release to measure market interest. (UK and Australian prices were not announced, but $250 is about £185 or AU$345.) The Always Home Cam has certainly grabbed headlines. The question is whether it will get people to pull out their credit cards — or their Prime cards . Or perhaps, eventually, to ask Alexa to order it for them. At Tuesday’s event, Amazon also announced the Ring Alarm Pro , Amazon Blink , the Astro , a new custom alerts feature and more. The company unveiled that Ring will soon let you hire virtual security guards to monitor your doorbell feed, as well. © 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

Here’s how it works . Third time may be the charm for Ring's long-gestating security drone efforts — and Ring CEO Jamie Simioff insists that the new Ring Drone Cam is just what his customers want. "When people stop me on the street, it's what they ask, 'Where's the drone?'" Simioff told me. After a decade of effort, which traces back to before Ring became a part of the giant Amazon device family, Ring is finally ready to deliver a home security drone that makes sense. Sure, perhaps we've heard this before, and Siminoff wasn't shy about recounting Ring's abortive drone history. That history started with an idea in 2016, which led to a drone that Siminoff said launched in 2021 but not to customers. "They were in boxes and ready to go," he added (design trade-offs, limited flight time, privacy concerns, and other issues ultimately scuttled that launch ). By 2025, Ring was ready with another attempt, but that drone also never shipped. As Sminioff described it, Ring was overcomplicating the drones, building in too many capabilities. A smart drone — basically a flying robot with all the attendant sensors — was the wrong approach. So Ring went back to the drawing board but with a critical learning: "The more sensors you take off, the lighter you can go, because you’re using less power." He said Ring decided to "take all the intelligence out" and shifted it to the cloud. The resulting security drone is ultra-light (around 160 grams) and has just a few native skills, which include knowing how to land and how to connect via Wi-Fi to the app. The App connects to Ring's new AI Pilot, which uses cloud-based, silicon-powered agents to control the drone. Not that the drone is flying blind. It has a front camera, a base camera, and the guidance of the AI Pilot, which is using a brand-new home map. Ring Drone Cam owners will be able to use the drone to walk through their home and build a detailed map, which Siminoff described as a "digital twin" of your space. If, for instance, you detect a rear door open or a window ajar in your home (via one of Ring's sensors that they assume you'll have throughout your home), you can tap on the location in the digital house map and the Ring Drone Cam will lift off from its home charge base and fly directly to it. The AI Pilot knows the map of your home, so it won't be bouncing off walls and, if someone does happen to be in the way, the Ring Drone Cam will know how to get around them. Siminoff admitted, though, that the drone is simply not smart enough to come up with an alternative route to get around, say, a group of people. A relatively simple and lightweight flyer, the Ring Drone Cam is quite loud, and Siminoff says that's intentional. "It’s loud — we think that’s a feature. This thing is not gonna sneak up on you." In fact, the use case he envisions is when nobody is home, though he agreed that if you're home asleep and there's movement downstairs, it could come in handy then, too. The sound alone might scare off intruders. The Ring Drone Cam is not designed to go outside, but it can peer out of a window. Imagine that someone approaches your front door, and the Ring Doorbell detects them. The Drone Cam could get the alert, lift off, and shine its LED spotlights out the window. I asked Siminoff if the Ring app would support split-screen, so you could see the Drone and Doorbell footage side-by-side. He said it didn't, but that he liked the idea. In the app, Ring Drone Cam owners can schedule automated home patrols that include multiple floors, since this drone can traverse stairways. The drone keeps track of the ground below but has no sensor for the ceiling. It also depends on that Wi-Fi connection for navigation. If your home internet cuts out, the Drone will basically land where it is, assuming it's safe to do so. Speaking of safety, all four propellers are inside cages, so even if the lightweight drone does somehow run into you, you're unlikely to get injured. Siminoff also said that the Drone Cam promises the same level of video privacy as you find on the brand's video doorbells, which includes two-factor authentication and encryption. Also, as soon as the drone lands, it stops filming, and the charging dock also covers the camera when the drone is settled inside. As you might expect for such a small and lightweight drone, the Ring Drone Cam doesn't offer much flight time, cruising for roughly five to eight minutes on a charge (consumer drones can often fly for up to 30 minutes). Charging could take between 40 minutes and an hour, though I imagine its patrol flights might just be a minute or two, after which the drone would return to its charging base. Assuming that this is the drone Ring finally ships, the Ring Drone Cam will be available in the US only (Ring hasn't announced any plans to expand the launch) from January 27 for $249.99 and will be available in dark gray. The white units I saw were all pre-production, and there are currently no plans to offer a white option. Remember Amazon Astro, the sort-of-cute patrol robot that Amazon launched in 2021 and discontinued in 2024 ? It's back, in a fashion. Using Astro as a base, Ring rebuilt it, added a light tower, and rechristened it the Ring Rover Cam. And while the Ring Rover Cam could be used in a home, it's really designed for medium-to-small businesses — and at $999.99 it's priced for those customers, too, Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds. If, for instance, you detect a rear door open or a window ajar in your home (via one of Ring's sensors that they assume you'll have throughout your home), you can tap on the location in the digital house map and the Ring Drone Cam will lift off from its home charge base and fly directly to it.

The AI Pilot knows the map of your home, so it won't be bouncing off walls and, if someone does happen to be in the way, the Ring Drone Cam will know how to get around them. Siminoff admitted, though, that the drone is simply not smart enough to come up with an alternative route to get around, say, a group of people.
A relatively simple and lightweight flyer, the Ring Drone Cam is quite loud, and Siminoff says that's intentional. "It’s loud — we think that’s a feature. This thing is not gonna sneak up on you."

In fact, the use case he envisions is when nobody is home, though he agreed that if you're home asleep and there's movement downstairs, it could come in handy then, too. The sound alone might scare off intruders.

The Ring Drone Cam is not designed to go outside, but it can peer out of a window. Imagine that someone approaches your front door, and the Ring Doorbell detects them. The Drone Cam could get the alert, lift off, and shine its LED spotlights out the window.
I asked Siminoff if the Ring app would support split-screen, so you could see the Drone and Doorbell footage side-by-side. He said it didn't, but that he liked the idea.

In the app, Ring Drone Cam owners can schedule automated home patrols that include multiple floors, since this drone can traverse stairways. The drone keeps track of the ground below but has no sensor for the ceiling. It also depends on that Wi-Fi connection for navigation. If your home internet cuts out, the Drone will basically land where it is, assuming it's safe to do so.

Speaking of safety, all four propellers are inside cages, so even if the lightweight drone does somehow run into you, you're unlikely to get injured. Siminoff also said that the Drone Cam promises the same level of video privacy as you find on the brand's video doorbells, which includes two-factor authentication and encryption. Also, as soon as the drone lands, it stops filming, and the charging dock also covers the camera when the drone is settled inside.

As you might expect for such a small and lightweight drone, the Ring Drone Cam doesn't offer much flight time, cruising for roughly five to eight minutes on a charge (consumer drones can often fly for up to 30 minutes). Charging could take between 40 minutes and an hour, though I imagine its patrol flights might just be a minute or two, after which the drone would return to its charging base.

Assuming that this is the drone Ring finally ships, the Ring Drone Cam will be available in the US only (Ring hasn't announced any plans to expand the launch) from January 27 for $249.99 and will be available in dark gray. The white units I saw were all pre-production, and there are currently no plans to offer a white option.
Remember Amazon Astro, the sort-of-cute patrol robot that Amazon launched in 2021 and discontinued in 2024 ? It's back, in a fashion.

Using Astro as a base, Ring rebuilt it, added a light tower, and rechristened it the Ring Rover Cam. And while the Ring Rover Cam could be used in a home, it's really designed for medium-to-small businesses — and at $999.99 it's priced for those customers, too,

extraction.body: Undeterred by a chorus of “what could go wrong?”, Ring pushed ahead. It’s now making the Always Home Cam available by invitation, requiring potential customers to apply to earn the ability to buy it. Last year, the company said it would be sold for $250, and it’s sticking with that price. That’s right: For less than $300, you can have a drone buzzing around your head inside your own home. To hear Amazon and Ring product execs tell it, the drone was designed to alleviate the burden of having multiple fixed cameras in different locations around your house. Instead, you can just push a button on the Ring Always Home Cam and send it flying around to survey the place, or you can program it to identify certain activities during specific windows of time—say, at night, while the family is sleeping. It streams the video to your smartphone or tablet, and clips can be stored for up to 60 days with a subscription fee. Since we haven’t been able to get our hands on the drone, it’s difficult to elaborate on its design. Ring has said it is lightweight, and we know that there are cameras mounted on its lower half. An onboard neural processing unit enables the drone to identify different scenarios, as well as objects within the home. It has plastic-tipped propellers, for safety, and its docking station has been designed to block the camera when the drone is in its resting state. Ring president Leila Rouhi tells WIRED the company has faced specific design challenges in building the drone. These have included “locating windows and how light is shining through windows, mirrors, chandeliers, kids, animals—just all of the objects that we have in our homes,” Rouhi said. “There is no blueprint that is universal.” The company may have been able to address some of these engineering challenges—and no doubt will keep iterating based on the data that its “invited” customers share—but some privacy and civil rights advocates expressed major concerns about the drone last year, to which Ring has offered some boilerplate statements. extraction.body: Ring is finally shipping a flying indoor drone camera. The Ring Drone Cam will arrive on January 27th, 2027, for $249.99, Ring founder Jamie Siminoff said at a launch event in New York City this week. If it does actually ship, it will arrive almost six years after the company announced its first flying camera, the Ring Always Home Cam. Designed to patrol inside your home when you’re not there, the Drone Cam is an AI-powered drone that can react to triggers from Ring sensors, such as detecting motion, a door opening, a water leak, or an alarm sounding. When triggered, it flies along pre-programmed routes to a set location, where it can livestream and record what’s happening in the Ring app. The drone can also run scheduled patrols around your home or be sent out on demand. It’s a completely different product from the Always Home Cam that was announced in 2020. It’s significantly smaller, about a quarter the size of the model I saw demoed at CES in 2023, weighing 165 grams. A small camera is integrated into its body, as opposed to dangling in the center. [Video: Ring Drone Cam Footage of Jen] Ring claims the Drone Cam can fly for 5 to 8 minutes on a charge, and for every minute of flight time takes 8 minutes of charging — meaning a five-minute flight needs about 40 minutes of charging. This short flight time suggests the product is better suited to quick check-ins than continuous monitoring, and whether it can really replace multiple stationary cameras remains to be seen. The drone apparently follows pre-planned flight paths you set up in the Ring app and will go around any obstacles it encounters along those routes. However, I didn’t get to see it interact with obstacles or anything unexpected — I’m particularly curious how pets will react to it. A long runway Siminoff said Ring has been developing the drone since 2016 and has come close to shipping two different models over that time, before landing on the current version. Siminoff explained that they struggled to pack all the technology needed for an autonomous drone to fly in your home into a practical design for less than $250. “Truly, it’s like an AI agent that’s controlling the robot,” said Siminoff. Rover also uses AI Pilot and is available for pre-order now, with shipping expected to begin on December 16th, 2026. Both security devices work like any other Ring camera, streaming and sending recorded video to the Ring app and require a Ring Protect plan for video storage and advanced features. They will also work with Amazon’s upcoming Alexa Home Map to understand your home and where sensors and other devices are located. [Image: Ring’s Drone Cam is slated to launch in January. Ring ushered in a world of new privacy questions when its cameras first started entering people’s homes more than a decade ago. Over the past year, the company’s new technologies have sparked fears that it could enable a surveillance state. An AI-piloted drone that can map your home, fly from room to room, and relies on the cloud to operate will certainly raise new privacy questions when it hits the market next year.

extraction.body: Amazon announced during its fall hardware event Tuesday that the Ring Always Home Cam — the flying drone camera announced during the same event last year — will begin selling this fall. Starting today, you can request an invitation to buy the Always Home Cam . The Ring Always Home Cam will cost $250, and it will be able to fly around your house following a preset flight path. You’ll be able to schedule a route around the house or trigger a trip manually. In addition, the camera will be able to respond to certain events — such as an armed door/window sensor in the Ring Alarm system being set off. The camera is not designed to cover multiple floors, so flying up or down stairs seems to be out, along with remote control, which Ring said will not be possible for security and privacy reasons. The Always Home Cam will not be able to record footage while it’s docked, and its loud propellers will make its presence known, in case you’re worried about its access to private spaces in your home. Ring’s privacy has been the subject of close scrutiny and sharp criticism — particularly for how it has shared user information with police, and how it has facilitated video sharing on its public app and with police. Despite some recent improvements to its policies, releasing a flying drone camera complicates already-difficult questions about where Ring stands on privacy. Indoor security cameras have contributed to serious privacy breaches as it is; to attach propellers to one and enable it to fly autonomously around a house potentially compounds the existing problems. (Ring’s indoor cameras, including the Always Home Cam, cannot be used to respond to Requests for Assistance posts by police.) Amazon’s strategy for rolling out the drone cam is perhaps more telling than it seems. The tech giant has relied on invite-only sales when a device’s uptake has been uncertain — the Echo Auto , Alexa Microwave and other so-called Day 1 devices spring to mind here. The strategy, in these cases, has been explicit: limit the initial release to measure market interest. (UK and Australian prices were not announced, but $250 is about £185 or AU$345.) The Always Home Cam has certainly grabbed headlines. The question is whether it will get people to pull out their credit cards — or their Prime cards . Or perhaps, eventually, to ask Alexa to order it for them. At Tuesday’s event, Amazon also announced the Ring Alarm Pro , Amazon Blink , the Astro , a new custom alerts feature and more. The Always Home Cam will not be able to record footage while it’s docked, and its loud propellers will make its presence known, in case you’re worried about its access to private spaces in your home.

Ring’s privacy has been the subject of close scrutiny and sharp criticism — particularly for how it has shared user information with police, and how it has facilitated video sharing on its public app and with police. Despite some recent improvements to its policies, releasing a flying drone camera complicates already-difficult questions about where Ring stands on privacy. Indoor security cameras have contributed to serious privacy breaches as it is; to attach propellers to one and enable it to fly autonomously around a house potentially compounds the existing problems. (Ring’s indoor cameras, including the Always Home Cam, cannot be used to respond to Requests for Assistance posts by police.)

Amazon’s strategy for rolling out the drone cam is perhaps more telling than it seems. The tech giant has relied on invite-only sales when a device’s uptake has been uncertain — the Echo Auto , Alexa Microwave and other so-called Day 1 devices spring to mind here. The strategy, in these cases, has been explicit: limit the initial release to measure market interest. (UK and Australian prices were not announced, but $250 is about £185 or AU$345.)

The Always Home Cam has certainly grabbed headlines. The question is whether it will get people to pull out their credit cards — or their Prime cards . Or perhaps, eventually, to ask Alexa to order it for them.

At Tuesday’s event, Amazon also announced the Ring Alarm Pro , Amazon Blink , the Astro , a new custom alerts feature and more. The company unveiled that Ring will soon let you hire virtual security guards to monitor your doorbell feed, as well.

Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies.

It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source.
U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.
The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.”
Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified.

U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.

passages: Six months before the Nvidia spy scandal emerged , the New York-based short seller firm Culper Research had already raised questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unusually close relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips.

Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies.

It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source.
U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.
The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.”
Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified.

extraction.body: It is a rough day for Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang. After media reports surfaced linking Jensen Huang to alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, the Nvidia chief has confessed his affair. But as it turns out, a US short seller was able to connect the dots and spot something between Jensen and Alice months ago.In May this year, US short seller Culper Research published a report, “NVIDIA (NVDA): The China Problem.” While the report did not allege an affair or attempt of espionage, the firm described Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice as “uncomfortably close.”Alice Huang is a former executive at Singapore’s Megaspeed, which buys computing resources such as advanced chips and then sells compute to clients. Its clients reportedly included Chinese giant Alibaba. Though US intelligence agencies believe that Alice may have managed to transfer confidential data from Jensen to Beijing.The report came as Culper Research announced plans to “short” Nvidia stocks. Shorting refers to betting against a company's stock, expecting the price to fall down within a certain time period.What did the short seller find?In its report, Culper highlighted two public sightings of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang. Nearly a year later, in May 2025, they were filmed dining in Taiwan with a Hong Kong executive, weeks after the US tightened trade restrictions on China. The report claimed that during the second sighting, Alice was reluctant to be seen with Jensen Huang in public, likely due to stricter US restrictions on China.As per the report, while the short seller did not find any evidence of an affair, it did find the relationship “uncomfortably close.” Culper Research's post from May.The Financial Times later reported that an intelligence-based memo said the two had been romantically involved and that she had been tasked with encouraging him to advocate looser export restrictions. The reporting did not establish that Jensen Huang knew of any alleged intelligence activity. Beijing denied that Alice Huang was an intelligence asset.Big transactions at Singapore firmThe report focused on Megaspeed, whose Singapore balance sheet rose from about $33 million at the end of 2023 to about $3 billion a year later, largely because of $2.9 billion in refundable deposits from an unnamed source. The report inferred that Alibaba-linked funds may have moved through Apex and Megaspeed to finance purchases of Nvidia-powered servers, but it did not document such a transfer.A current Megaspeed employee told Culper that Alice Huang remained effectively “our boss” despite reports that she had left the company. The employee claimed Jensen Huang visited Megaspeed-linked data centres every few months and that Alibaba representatives appeared around each visit. A former Nvidia employee said colleagues had wondered whether Megaspeed had a special relationship with the Nvidia chief.Culper’s broader case was that Chinese demand continued to drive more than 20 per cent of Nvidia’s FY2026 compute revenue after the company said its China data-centre business had fallen to zero following restrictions imposed in April 2025. It alleged that demand was routed through Southeast Asian intermediaries and illegal diversion, while Nvidia’s method of reporting revenue by customers’ headquarters obscured where equipment ultimately went.Trade records cited by Culper showed that Speedmatrix imported $4.6 billion of products between December 2024 and January 2026, including $4 billion from Nvidia partner Aivres. Another Nvidia partner, Giga Computing, shipped $511 million of equipment, largely to Speedmatrix and Novagate Cloud, which Culper described as an apparent Megaspeed offshoot.Jensen Huang comes clean, apologies for affairWhile the short seller disclosed concerns over Jensen and Alice publicly six months ago, US intelligence agencies had been investigating the connection for months. It is said that US President Donald Trump was first notified nearly a year ago.After reports surfaced, Jensen Huang confessed the affair in a memo to employees. I am deeply sorry.” The Nvidia chief said he would cooperate with the investigation and remained committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting American national security. The Nvidia board said it had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets had been compromised and expressed confidence in Huang.Three Republican committee chairs in the US House requested a closed-door briefing with Huang for November 18. extraction.body: Nvidia is probing whether Chinese intelligence targeted its CEO through an affair. Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted having an affair two days after the FT reported his alleged romantic relationship with a woman the US intelligence community believes was working as a spy for China. Huang revealed the affair in an internal message to employees on Sunday that was obtained by the FT. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang said in the message. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” In a separate statement, Nvidia said its board would open an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” Huang said he would fully cooperate. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust,” he said. “I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.” The FT reported on Friday that the US believed Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman who was recruited to spy for China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. American officials this year wrote a memo, based on information from US intelligence, which said the Nvidia boss had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of the chipmaker, according to people familiar with the document. The affair is a damaging blow to the Nvidia chief, who in recent years has become the face of the AI boom, one of the technology’s loudest champions, and transformed the Silicon Valley group into the first $5 trillion company. It also comes at a critical juncture for the wider AI sector, which faces a deepening political backlash in the US and growing investor concern over whether the hundreds of billions of dollars spent on infrastructure will pay off. Nvidia’s Frankfurt-listed shares were down more than 6 percent in early trading on Monday. Huang’s admission of an affair comes after Nvidia previously dismissed suggestions of an improper relationship with Alice Huang, saying the interactions were “nothing unusual or unexpected” when dealing with an Nvidia customer. The American government memo, which said US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive had been recruited by the MSS, was drafted just before President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping. Jensen Huang has developed a close relationship with Trump, which has frustrated US national security officials who believe he is too willing to sell advanced chips to China that could harm American security. Asked about Huang on Sunday, Trump told reporters he had done an “amazing job” for the US. Asked if he regretted not acting on the intelligence about the affair, Trump said: “No, I don’t think so. I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.” “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on,” Trump added. After broadly staying out of politics, Huang started to build relations with Trump after the president called him out of the blue on his birthday. He quickly became one of Trump’s favorite executives, accompanying him on state visits, including to China earlier this year and the UK last year. Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to adopt a more permissive approach to shipping Nvidia’s AI chips to China, after the company was entirely cut off from the critical market by new export controls in 2025. The resulting deal—with Trump permitting the export of Nvidia’s older-generation H200 chips to China, with the US government taking a cut of sales—had a minimal impact on the Silicon Valley company’s sales, as Beijing pushed back against its technology. But it further angered China hawks in the US administration. The US government had already been investigating Megaspeed over concerns that it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Nvidia on Sunday said a committee of independent directors, helped by external lawyers, would oversee the investigation. “The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders,” the company said. “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” Huang, who co-founded Nvidia as a video-game graphics card company in 1993, is one of the longest-serving founder-CEOs in Silicon Valley. More than most technology groups, Nvidia’s success is tethered to that of its CEO. Huang leads a close and loyal core team of about half a dozen executives, acting as its chief salesman on the international stage while directly managing dozens of direct reports who keep the company running. He has credited this “flat” organizational structure for the speed at which the company operates, helping it to stay ahead of rivals in the AI chip market and increasing its market valuation from roughly $1 trillion in 2023 to $4.5 trillion today. Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted having an affair two days after the FT reported his alleged romantic relationship with a woman the US intelligence community believes was working as a spy for China.
Huang revealed the affair in an internal message to employees on Sunday that was obtained by the FT.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang said in the message. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

In a separate statement, Nvidia said its board would open an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Huang said he would fully cooperate. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust,” he said. “I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.”
The FT reported on Friday that the US believed Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman who was recruited to spy for China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

American officials this year wrote a memo, based on information from US intelligence, which said the Nvidia boss had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of the chipmaker, according to people familiar with the document.

The affair is a damaging blow to the Nvidia chief, who in recent years has become the face of the AI boom, one of the technology’s loudest champions, and transformed the Silicon Valley group into the first $5 trillion company.

It also comes at a critical juncture for the wider AI sector, which faces a deepening political backlash in the US and growing investor concern over whether the hundreds of billions of dollars spent on infrastructure will pay off.
Nvidia’s Frankfurt-listed shares were down more than 6 percent in early trading on Monday.

Huang’s admission of an affair comes after Nvidia previously dismissed suggestions of an improper relationship with Alice Huang, saying the interactions were “nothing unusual or unexpected” when dealing with an Nvidia customer.

The American government memo, which said US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive had been recruited by the MSS, was drafted just before President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping.

Jensen Huang has developed a close relationship with Trump, which has frustrated US national security officials who believe he is too willing to sell advanced chips to China that could harm American security.

Asked about Huang on Sunday, Trump told reporters he had done an “amazing job” for the US. Asked if he regretted not acting on the intelligence about the affair, Trump said: “No, I don’t think so. I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.”
“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on,” Trump added.
After broadly staying out of politics, Huang started to build relations with Trump after the president called him out of the blue on his birthday.
He quickly became one of Trump’s favorite executives, accompanying him on state visits, including to China earlier this year and the UK last year.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to adopt a more permissive approach to shipping Nvidia’s AI chips to China, after the company was entirely cut off from the critical market by new export controls in 2025.

The resulting deal—with Trump permitting the export of Nvidia’s older-generation H200 chips to China, with the US government taking a cut of sales—had a minimal impact on the Silicon Valley company’s sales, as Beijing pushed back against its technology. But it further angered China hawks in the US administration.
The US government had already been investigating Megaspeed over concerns that it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.
Nvidia on Sunday said a committee of independent directors, helped by external lawyers, would oversee the investigation.

“The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders,” the company said. “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia as a video-game graphics card company in 1993, is one of the longest-serving founder-CEOs in Silicon Valley. More than most technology groups, Nvidia’s success is tethered to that of its CEO.

Huang leads a close and loyal core team of about half a dozen executives, acting as its chief salesman on the international stage while directly managing dozens of direct reports who keep the company running.

He has credited this “flat” organizational structure for the speed at which the company operates, helping it to stay ahead of rivals in the AI chip market and increasing its market valuation from roughly $1 trillion in 2023 to $4.5 trillion today.

Elon Musk, a close ally of Huang, was among the first to offer support, agreeing with a social media post that he was “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation” and “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.”

But John Moolenaar, the Republican head of the House China committee who, with other lawmakers, has requested Huang to testify before Congress, said: “It is vital that Jensen Huang address our national security concerns in Congress related to China’s access to sensitive technology and information.”

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to being unfaithful to his wife, following reports about his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US intelligence agencies of working for Beijing. The controversy has prompted Nvidia's board to launch an independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. It has also brought renewed attention to the increasingly sensitive relationship between the United States, China and the global artificial intelligence industry. Who is the woman at the centre of the controversy? According to reports, Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. Alice Huang reportedly came under the scrutiny of US intelligence agencies, which suspected that she was working with Chinese intelligence. Reports suggest that she was recruited by China to gather information about Nvidia and its CEO. The connection becomes particularly significant because Megaspeed is an Nvidia customer. The company has also faced scrutiny over suspicions that it helped Chinese entities obtain advanced Nvidia AI chips despite US export restrictions. US intelligence reportedly believed that Alice Huang's proximity to Jensen Huang could provide an opportunity to gather information about Nvidia's business plans and its discussions with the American government. It is important to note that these are reported intelligence assessments and allegations, not established findings of Nvidia's investigation. Why would China be interested in Nvidia's CEO? To understand the significance, one needs to understand Nvidia's position in the global technology industry. Nvidia is the world's leading supplier of advanced AI computing chips, accounting for about 80% of all GPU chips in the world. Its GPUs power some of the world's largest data centres and artificial intelligence models, for more than 66% of AI computing capacity in use worldwide by Q4 2025. The company has consequently become central to America's efforts to maintain its technological advantage over China. Jensen Huang is also more than just a corporate executive. He has been actively involved in discussions with the US government over restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China. Any access to Nvidia's internal business strategy, future product development, customer relationships or discussions with American policymakers could potentially be valuable to a foreign intelligence agency. However, there is currently no established evidence that Huang shared classified information or that Nvidia's trade secrets were compromised. The bigger picture: America's AI chip war with China The controversy comes at a time when Washington is increasingly concerned about China's access to advanced semiconductor technology. Since 2022, the US government has introduced restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China, citing national security concerns. The restrictions are intended to limit China's access to computing capabilities that could have military and strategic applications. Nvidia has repeatedly found itself caught between American export controls and the enormous Chinese market. Huang has previously argued that restricting access to American chips could accelerate China's efforts to develop its own semiconductor industry. The Megaspeed controversy therefore raises a larger question: Can the US protect its technological advantage when the global AI supply chain involves customers, companies and intermediaries operating across multiple countries? Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation on November 8. The company said it had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia's trade secrets had been compromised. Huang has agreed to cooperate with the investigation and is expected to continue as CEO during the review. The controversy has also attracted the attention of US lawmakers. Republican leaders from three House committees have sought a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18, including questions about the company's safeguards against foreign intelligence operations. US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has publicly defended the Nvidia chief. "I think he's an honourable guy," Trump told reporters on November 8, adding that Huang had "done an amazing job for our country." Trump also said he had not discussed the allegations with Huang, but added, "I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it." When asked whether he would take Huang on his upcoming Asia trip, Trump responded that he would certainly consider it. Did the relationship provide an opportunity for Chinese intelligence to access sensitive commercial information?

November 9, 2026 "Dear Mr. Huang: We are writing to request that you appear before our committees for a joint, closed-door briefing on NVIDIA’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People’s Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang," the letter begins. Less than 24 hours after he admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese spy , Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been asked to appear before the House Select Committee on China. The Committee issued a letter today, signed by Rep. Brian J. Mast (R-FL), Rep. John Moolenaar (R-MI), and Rep. Eric A. Crawford (R-AK). An X post featuring the letter states that the letter "expresses concerns over NVIDIA’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and Mr. Huang’s reported ties to a Chinese intelligence-linked executive of a Singapore-based data center company."

ICYMI: Chairman @RepMoolenaar, Chairman @RepBrianMast, and Chairman @RepRickCrawford have sent a letter to NVIDIA CEO @JensenHuang asking him to appear before their three committees this month. The letter expresses concerns over NVIDIA’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and Mr. Huang’s reported ties to a Chinese intelligence-linked executive of a Singapore-based data center company. November 9, 2026

"Dear Mr. Huang: We are writing to request that you appear before our committees for a joint, closed-door briefing on NVIDIA’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People’s Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang," the letter begins.

It goes on to say that recent reports surrounding the affair "raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information. "The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk."

The closed-door hearing is set for November 18, 2026; whether Huang will attend remains unclear. The letter also allows for Huang to set an alternative date during while the 119th Congress is still in session.

On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed. It is alleged that the latter was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information and help China get its hands on Nvidia's AI GPUs, the most powerful of which are banned from export to the country by Washington. Megaspeed has been accused of smuggling $2 billion of AI chips into China .

In a statement to Nvidia employees, Jensen Huang said, "To my colleagues at NVIDIA, I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." As Huang's statement noted, Nvidia has opened an independent investigation into its CEO's conduct regarding the national security concerns the story has laid bare. The board of directors stated, "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information."

Nvidia shares dropped by around 5% in early trading, but have since recovered some of their losses. The company has rocketed to a market capitalization of over $4 trillion as the global hardware leader of the AI boom. Its powerful GPUs are in high demand for both the training of AI models and inference.
