extraction.body: Nvidia is probing whether Chinese intelligence targeted its CEO through an affair. Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted having an affair two days after the FT reported his alleged romantic relationship with a woman the US intelligence community believes was working as a spy for China. Huang revealed the affair in an internal message to employees on Sunday that was obtained by the FT. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang said in the message. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” In a separate statement, Nvidia said its board would open an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” Huang said he would fully cooperate. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust,” he said. “I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.” The FT reported on Friday that the US believed Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman who was recruited to spy for China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. American officials this year wrote a memo, based on information from US intelligence, which said the Nvidia boss had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of the chipmaker, according to people familiar with the document. The affair is a damaging blow to the Nvidia chief, who in recent years has become the face of the AI boom, one of the technology’s loudest champions, and transformed the Silicon Valley group into the first $5 trillion company. It also comes at a critical juncture for the wider AI sector, which faces a deepening political backlash in the US and growing investor concern over whether the hundreds of billions of dollars spent on infrastructure will pay off. Nvidia’s Frankfurt-listed shares were down more than 6 percent in early trading on Monday. Huang’s admission of an affair comes after Nvidia previously dismissed suggestions of an improper relationship with Alice Huang, saying the interactions were “nothing unusual or unexpected” when dealing with an Nvidia customer. The American government memo, which said US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive had been recruited by the MSS, was drafted just before President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping. Jensen Huang has developed a close relationship with Trump, which has frustrated US national security officials who believe he is too willing to sell advanced chips to China that could harm American security. Asked about Huang on Sunday, Trump told reporters he had done an “amazing job” for the US. Asked if he regretted not acting on the intelligence about the affair, Trump said: “No, I don’t think so. I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.” “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on,” Trump added. After broadly staying out of politics, Huang started to build relations with Trump after the president called him out of the blue on his birthday. He quickly became one of Trump’s favorite executives, accompanying him on state visits, including to China earlier this year and the UK last year. Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to adopt a more permissive approach to shipping Nvidia’s AI chips to China, after the company was entirely cut off from the critical market by new export controls in 2025. The resulting deal—with Trump permitting the export of Nvidia’s older-generation H200 chips to China, with the US government taking a cut of sales—had a minimal impact on the Silicon Valley company’s sales, as Beijing pushed back against its technology. But it further angered China hawks in the US administration. The US government had already been investigating Megaspeed over concerns that it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Nvidia on Sunday said a committee of independent directors, helped by external lawyers, would oversee the investigation. “The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders,” the company said. “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” Huang, who co-founded Nvidia as a video-game graphics card company in 1993, is one of the longest-serving founder-CEOs in Silicon Valley. More than most technology groups, Nvidia’s success is tethered to that of its CEO. Huang leads a close and loyal core team of about half a dozen executives, acting as its chief salesman on the international stage while directly managing dozens of direct reports who keep the company running. He has credited this “flat” organizational structure for the speed at which the company operates, helping it to stay ahead of rivals in the AI chip market and increasing its market valuation from roughly $1 trillion in 2023 to $4.5 trillion today. Elon Musk, a close ally of Huang, was among the first to offer support, agreeing with a social media post that he was “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation” and “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” But John Moolenaar, the Republican head of the House China committee who, with other lawmakers, has requested Huang to testify before Congress, said: “It is vital that Jensen Huang address our national security concerns in Congress related to China’s access to sensitive technology and information.” © 2026 The Financial Times Ltd . "I love our country and our company," Jensen Huang said.
"I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security."
In a letter to Nvidia employees obtained by The Associated Press, Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologized to his family and colleagues.
He said he took "full responsibility" for his actions.

Alice Huang was previously a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia.
Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to the Times.
Nvidia's board said it has "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.

"Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption."
Asked whether he wished he had acted on intelligence when he was briefed about spying, Trump again praised Huang: "I think he's an honorable guy.

The Times reported last month that U.S. intelligence agencies had discovered that Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and chip buyer, and determined that she was feeding information directly to Beijing.

"I just can't comment because of the nature of it," he told reporters.
"Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life," Huang wrote.
He did, however, refer to the national security concerns raised in news reports and said he supported the board's investigation and would cooperate fully.

extraction.body: What began as a controversy surrounding the personal life of one of the world's most powerful technology executives has now become a matter of national security scrutiny in the United States. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to being unfaithful to his wife, following reports about his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US intelligence agencies of working for Beijing. The controversy has prompted Nvidia's board to launch an independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. It has also brought renewed attention to the increasingly sensitive relationship between the United States, China and the global artificial intelligence industry. Who is the woman at the centre of the controversy? According to reports, Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. Alice Huang reportedly came under the scrutiny of US intelligence agencies, which suspected that she was working with Chinese intelligence. Reports suggest that she was recruited by China to gather information about Nvidia and its CEO. The connection becomes particularly significant because Megaspeed is an Nvidia customer. The company has also faced scrutiny over suspicions that it helped Chinese entities obtain advanced Nvidia AI chips despite US export restrictions. US intelligence reportedly believed that Alice Huang's proximity to Jensen Huang could provide an opportunity to gather information about Nvidia's business plans and its discussions with the American government. It is important to note that these are reported intelligence assessments and allegations, not established findings of Nvidia's investigation. Why would China be interested in Nvidia's CEO? To understand the significance, one needs to understand Nvidia's position in the global technology industry. Nvidia is the world's leading supplier of advanced AI computing chips, accounting for about 80% of all GPU chips in the world. Its GPUs power some of the world's largest data centres and artificial intelligence models, for more than 66% of AI computing capacity in use worldwide by Q4 2025. The company has consequently become central to America's efforts to maintain its technological advantage over China. Jensen Huang is also more than just a corporate executive. He has been actively involved in discussions with the US government over restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China. Any access to Nvidia's internal business strategy, future product development, customer relationships or discussions with American policymakers could potentially be valuable to a foreign intelligence agency. However, there is currently no established evidence that Huang shared classified information or that Nvidia's trade secrets were compromised. The bigger picture: America's AI chip war with China The controversy comes at a time when Washington is increasingly concerned about China's access to advanced semiconductor technology. Since 2022, the US government has introduced restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China, citing national security concerns. The restrictions are intended to limit China's access to computing capabilities that could have military and strategic applications. Nvidia has repeatedly found itself caught between American export controls and the enormous Chinese market. Huang has previously argued that restricting access to American chips could accelerate China's efforts to develop its own semiconductor industry. The Megaspeed controversy therefore raises a larger question: Can the US protect its technological advantage when the global AI supply chain involves customers, companies and intermediaries operating across multiple countries? Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation on November 8. The company said it had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia's trade secrets had been compromised. Huang has agreed to cooperate with the investigation and is expected to continue as CEO during the review. The controversy has also attracted the attention of US lawmakers. Republican leaders from three House committees have sought a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18, including questions about the company's safeguards against foreign intelligence operations. US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has publicly defended the Nvidia chief. "I think he's an honourable guy," Trump told reporters on November 8, adding that Huang had "done an amazing job for our country." Trump also said he had not discussed the allegations with Huang, but added, "I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it." When asked whether he would take Huang on his upcoming Asia trip, Trump responded that he would certainly consider it. Did the relationship provide an opportunity for Chinese intelligence to access sensitive commercial information?

sources.title: Amazon launches home robot Astro and giant Alexa display - The Guardian
passages: Amazon has launched its long-awaited home robot, named Astro, that can autonomously drive around your home packed with cameras and a screen.
The robot can handle video calls, recognising you and coming to find you when someone calls, and provides all the features of Alexa on wheels.
Disney has used Amazon’s custom assistant technology to create its own voice assistant called “Hey Disney”.

It can be used alongside Alexa on compatible devices at home in the US later this year, with characters from Disney, Pixar or Star Wars, but is primarily designed for use across Disney’s parks and resorts, where it will be in hotel rooms to act as a guide and digital service agent.
Relatives and friends can call into the Glow and play with children as they interact with the projected display on the floor, and with digital and physical objects such as finishing puzzles.
Amazon also launched a super-sized version of its smart display with a 15.6in screen designed to be wall-mounted.
It is linked with the doorbell firm Ring’s Protect Pro service, and can patrol your home, investigate disturbances and send an alert if it detects an unrecognised person.
Astro also processes images and sensor data on the device to help preserve privacy.
Amazon’s Ring flying drone security camera, the Always Home Cam, announced this time last year , will finally be available for invitation-only purchase.
The security camera can fly about your home along set patrol routes, or move to disturbances detected by other sensors and give you a real-time view.
The firm is also adding a screen to its Halo fitness band.
The Halo View has an OLED screen, is swim proof and lasts up to seven days between charges.
Amazon is launching a paid-for Fitness service, with studio workouts similar to Apple Fitness+ and Peloton, as well as a meal and nutrition planning service.
Amazon has partnered with Sesame Street, Nickelodeon, Mattel and Disney for interactive experiences, while extensive parental controls and privacy shutters are built in.

Ring Alarm Pro adds a much-requested feature of local video storage to the firm’s security cameras, plus a Eero wifi6 hub with cellular data backup to keep cameras and devices online if the internet drops out.

Astro can map your home’s layout, recognise objects and check on loved ones and pets remotely using a series of cameras and a display on its front, featuring a set of expressive animated eyes. The robot can handle video calls, recognising you and coming to find you when someone calls, and provides all the features of Alexa on wheels. But Dave Limp, head of Amazon’s devices and services, said “customers don’t just want Alexa on wheels so we’ve embodied it with a unique persona that’s all its own”. Moving at up to one metre a second, Astro can also act as a security robot. It is linked with the doorbell firm Ring’s Protect Pro service, and can patrol your home, investigate disturbances and send an alert if it detects an unrecognised person. It can stop immediately if something suddenly moves in front of it, such as a pet, or when encountering stairs. Owners can set up out-of-bounds areas and turn off cameras and mics, while LED lights and the screen show when someone is viewing the robot’s cameras. Astro also processes images and sensor data on the device to help preserve privacy. It will be available in the US to invited customers as part of Amazon’s Day 1 Editions early device programme costing $999.99 (£749) and will be one of the first domestic robots available, joining robotic vacuum cleaners and mowers. Amazon also launched a super-sized version of its smart display with a 15.6in screen designed to be wall-mounted. It has on-device facial recognition, similar to Google’s Nest Hub Max , and is designed to be a shared digital centre of the home, with calendars, sticky notes, smart home controls and camera feeds all accessible as widgets, alongside the popular digital photo-frame features. The display can act as a TV with Prime Video, Netflix and other services, or a video call screen. It can be taught to recognise custom sounds, such as the fridge beeping when left open or the washing machine finishing, so it can send you an alert. The Echo Show 15 will cost £239.99 ($249.99), shipping later this year. Designed to be an extension of Amazon’s child-friendly Alexa products in the US, the Glow combines a video calling camera and 8in screen with a 19in projected touch-sensitive display. Relatives and friends can call into the Glow and play with children as they interact with the projected display on the floor, and with digital and physical objects such as finishing puzzles. Amazon has partnered with Sesame Street, Nickelodeon, Mattel and Disney for interactive experiences, while extensive parental controls and privacy shutters are built in. The firm is also adding a screen to its Halo fitness band. The Halo View has an OLED screen, is swim proof and lasts up to seven days between charges. It plugs into Amazon’s Halo subscription health service and will cost $79.99 in the US. Amazon is launching a paid-for Fitness service, with studio workouts similar to Apple Fitness+ and Peloton, as well as a meal and nutrition planning service. The security camera can fly about your home along set patrol routes, or move to disturbances detected by other sensors and give you a real-time view. Ring Alarm Pro adds a much-requested feature of local video storage to the firm’s security cameras, plus a Eero wifi6 hub with cellular data backup to keep cameras and devices online if the internet drops out. Device bundles start at $249.99 in the US. Ring also launched a professional remote monitoring subscription to view your camera feeds when you are away or asleep, and warn off burglars or sound an alert. It announced that package detection and custom event alerts would be introduced to some existing security cameras, allowing customers to teach the cameras to recognise things such as a car being parked in the drive.

sources.title: Ring, known for its doorbell cameras, launches a home security drone and an enterprise security robot
passages: Automated security is one space the tech industry has never quite cracked.
In 2021, Amazon launched its own home security robot, known as Astro.

Astro, which resembles Ring’s new robot (the company says that it was inspired to create the bot because of “feedback from Amazon Astro customers”), was first announced as a kind of nebulous domestic helper before being repurposed as an enterprise security product.
Ring calls the device a “flying indoor security camera” — which should give you a pretty good idea of what it’s supposed to do and how it’s supposed to work.
Ring Drone Cam is designed to fly from room to room, inspecting what is happening in a user’s house and, if there’s trouble, to alert them.
The first new device is a home security drone that users will be able to deploy to patrol their domiciles when they’re out.

It also comes with a periscope camera, which can be adjusted to see over specific obstacles, and it also includes two-way audio — meaning that, should the remote user need to communicate with a person at the store (be that an employee or a burglar), they can speak to them through the robot.
The company announced Ring Robotics on Tuesday, debuting two new devices that are sure to stir more than a little bit of controversy.
Ring says that both robots are powered by the same proprietary AI system, known as AI Pilot.

The company says this system leverages “specialized vision models, sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” Both devices, using this software, are designed to develop a detailed schematic of your house or office purely by exploring the space for themselves, the company says.
However, Ring claims that both devices have been built with “privacy and security” baked into them.
Ring cameras generally record their videos to the cloud.

extraction.body: Ring, the Amazon-owned home security company, is launching its own robotics division, with an eye toward automating security at both the home and the office. The company announced Ring Robotics on Tuesday, debuting two new devices that are sure to stir more than a little bit of controversy. The first new device is a home security drone that users will be able to deploy to patrol their domiciles when they’re out. The other item that the company is launching is a roving enterprise security robot, designed for businesses. First, the drone. Ring calls the device a “flying indoor security camera” — which should give you a pretty good idea of what it’s supposed to do and how it’s supposed to work. Ring Drone Cam is designed to fly from room to room, inspecting what is happening in a user’s house and, if there’s trouble, to alert them. It has been built to integrate with Ring’s other home security devices so, for instance, if a Ring alarm goes off in a particular part of the home (say, the backdoor), the bot will supposedly fly to that location and investigate. When it’s not in use, the drone stays inactive in a docking bay. The drone shoots video in 2K and it also comes equipped with LED lights so that it can keep watch at night and record video in low light. It can be controlled via Amazon’s Alexa Home Map , and the bot can also be scheduled to patrol the house at specific times — so, if you know you’re going to be out for the night or even on vacation, the drone can keep you apprised of what’s happening while you’re away. Now, let’s turn to Ring Rover Cam. Like the drone, this roving robot can be set to patrol specific routes, at specific times, within the user’s business. The robot streams video in continuous 4K, which is viewable via Ring’s mobile app, and a trigger can be set to automatically record if it detects a human. It also comes with a periscope camera, which can be adjusted to see over specific obstacles, and it also includes two-way audio — meaning that, should the remote user need to communicate with a person at the store (be that an employee or a burglar), they can speak to them through the robot. Ring says that both robots are powered by the same proprietary AI system, known as AI Pilot. The company says this system leverages “specialized vision models, sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” Both devices, using this software, are designed to develop a detailed schematic of your house or office purely by exploring the space for themselves, the company says. “Together, it’s like having a guard on patrol who never clocks out,” the company claims, of its new devices. “Ring Rover can do a sweep of the floor after close and investigate when sensor trips at 2 a.m. — streaming it all to your phone, wherever you are.” Automated security is one space the tech industry has never quite cracked. In 2021, Amazon launched its own home security robot, known as Astro. Astro, which resembles Ring’s new robot (the company says that it was inspired to create the bot because of “feedback from Amazon Astro customers”), was first announced as a kind of nebulous domestic helper before being repurposed as an enterprise security product. The device never took off, however, and seven months into the robot’s glow-up as a small business security guard, Amazon put the device out to pasture . Privacy concerns have long dogged Ring — with critics frequently alleging that the company’s cameras have created unofficial surveillance networks that police departments can (and routinely do) tap into. It seems natural to assume that similar complaints will be lodged about the company’s newest products, given the invasive potential of both. However, Ring claims that both devices have been built with “privacy and security” baked into them. The company notes that the videos recorded by both devices are protected by TAKE (Throw Away the Key Encryption), which the company calls its “strongest default encryption yet.” It’s unclear whether there will be an option for local video storage. Ring cameras generally record their videos to the cloud. The Rover is being made available starting on December 16 and it will retail at a whopping $1,000. The drone, meanwhile, won’t launch until next year, on January 27, and will be made available for $270. sources.title: Ring launches drone to fly around, monitor your home while you're away
passages: Ring, the security-camera company owned by Amazon, on Thursday announced a new indoor security camera that can fly around the house to keep an eye on your home while you're away.
Amazon acquired Ring for $1 billion in early 2018, providing the e-commerce giant's growing hardware and smart-home divisions with home-surveillance capabilities.
The device, called the Ring Always Home Cam, will cost $250 when it launches in 2021, the company said.
The device can record only while in flight, Ring said.
In the past year, however, Ring has run into some controversy over privacy and security.
Two couples alleging that intruders had compromised their Ring devices filed a class-action lawsuit in January.
Ring's partnerships with hundreds of police departments across the United States have caused concern among privacy advocates, civil-rights groups, and lawmakers, for example.
The home-security company also came under scrutiny after reports of hacking.
Google's Nest smart home cameras have suffered similar attacks.

Ring, the security-camera company owned by Amazon, on Thursday announced a new indoor security camera that can fly around the house to keep an eye on your home while you're away. The device, called the Ring Always Home Cam, will cost $250 when it launches in 2021, the company said. The Ring Always Home Cam is intended to help people keep tabs on their home without having to install multiple cameras, the company said. Users can set a path for the camera by carrying it around the house, and it can check for disturbances if a Ring Alarm is triggered. (A Ring Alarm triggers if it senses something that might be an intruder, a fire, or another emergency, such as a stove being left on.) The camera has a battery life of about five minutes; it's designed to make short trips of about one minute each. The device can record only while in flight, Ring said. When it's not zipping around the house, the Always Home Cam sits in its dock, where the camera is blocked. It will also make a sound in flight to alert that it's recording, Ring said. It said that later this year it would launch end-to-end encryption for certain devices, though it did not say which products would be compatible.

extraction.body: Ring, the Amazon-owned home security company, is launching its own robotics division, with an eye toward automating security at both the home and the office. The company announced Ring Robotics on Tuesday, debuting two new devices that are sure to stir more than a little bit of controversy. The first new device is a home security drone that users will be able to deploy to patrol their domiciles when they’re out. The other item that the company is launching is a roving enterprise security robot, designed for businesses. First, the drone. Ring calls the device a “flying indoor security camera” — which should give you a pretty good idea of what it’s supposed to do and how it’s supposed to work. Ring Drone Cam is designed to fly from room to room, inspecting what is happening in a user’s house and, if there’s trouble, to alert them. It has been built to integrate with Ring’s other home security devices so, for instance, if a Ring alarm goes off in a particular part of the home (say, the backdoor), the bot will supposedly fly to that location and investigate. When it’s not in use, the drone stays inactive in a docking bay. The drone shoots video in 2K and it also comes equipped with LED lights so that it can keep watch at night and record video in low light. It can be controlled via Amazon’s Alexa Home Map , and the bot can also be scheduled to patrol the house at specific times — so, if you know you’re going to be out for the night or even on vacation, the drone can keep you apprised of what’s happening while you’re away. Now, let’s turn to Ring Rover Cam. Like the drone, this roving robot can be set to patrol specific routes, at specific times, within the user’s business. The robot streams video in continuous 4K, which is viewable via Ring’s mobile app, and a trigger can be set to automatically record if it detects a human. It also comes with a periscope camera, which can be adjusted to see over specific obstacles, and it also includes two-way audio — meaning that, should the remote user need to communicate with a person at the store (be that an employee or a burglar), they can speak to them through the robot. Ring says that both robots are powered by the same proprietary AI system, known as AI Pilot. The company says this system leverages “specialized vision models, sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” Both devices, using this software, are designed to develop a detailed schematic of your house or office purely by exploring the space for themselves, the company says. “Together, it’s like having a guard on patrol who never clocks out,” the company claims, of its new devices. “Ring Rover can do a sweep of the floor after close and investigate when sensor trips at 2 a.m. — streaming it all to your phone, wherever you are.” Automated security is one space the tech industry has never quite cracked. In 2021, Amazon launched its own home security robot, known as Astro. Astro, which resembles Ring’s new robot (the company says that it was inspired to create the bot because of “feedback from Amazon Astro customers”), was first announced as a kind of nebulous domestic helper before being repurposed as an enterprise security product. The device never took off, however, and seven months into the robot’s glow-up as a small business security guard, Amazon put the device out to pasture . Privacy concerns have long dogged Ring — with critics frequently alleging that the company’s cameras have created unofficial surveillance networks that police departments can (and routinely do) tap into. It seems natural to assume that similar complaints will be lodged about the company’s newest products, given the invasive potential of both. However, Ring claims that both devices have been built with “privacy and security” baked into them. The company notes that the videos recorded by both devices are protected by TAKE (Throw Away the Key Encryption), which the company calls its “strongest default encryption yet.” It’s unclear whether there will be an option for local video storage. Ring cameras generally record their videos to the cloud. The Rover is being made available starting on December 16 and it will retail at a whopping $1,000. The drone, meanwhile, won’t launch until next year, on January 27, and will be made available for $270. sources.title: Ring launches drone to fly around, monitor your home while you're away
passages: Ring, the security-camera company owned by Amazon, on Thursday announced a new indoor security camera that can fly around the house to keep an eye on your home while you're away.
Amazon acquired Ring for $1 billion in early 2018, providing the e-commerce giant's growing hardware and smart-home divisions with home-surveillance capabilities.
The device, called the Ring Always Home Cam, will cost $250 when it launches in 2021, the company said.
The device can record only while in flight, Ring said.
In the past year, however, Ring has run into some controversy over privacy and security.
Two couples alleging that intruders had compromised their Ring devices filed a class-action lawsuit in January.
Ring's partnerships with hundreds of police departments across the United States have caused concern among privacy advocates, civil-rights groups, and lawmakers, for example.
The home-security company also came under scrutiny after reports of hacking.
Google's Nest smart home cameras have suffered similar attacks.

extraction.body: Delivery isn't the only area Amazon has been exploring when it comes to autonomous flying cameras. Ring, the security-camera company owned by Amazon, on Thursday announced a new indoor security camera that can fly around the house to keep an eye on your home while you're away. The device, called the Ring Always Home Cam, will cost $250 when it launches in 2021, the company said. The Ring Always Home Cam is intended to help people keep tabs on their home without having to install multiple cameras, the company said. Users can set a path for the camera by carrying it around the house, and it can check for disturbances if a Ring Alarm is triggered. (A Ring Alarm triggers if it senses something that might be an intruder, a fire, or another emergency, such as a stove being left on.) The camera has a battery life of about five minutes; it's designed to make short trips of about one minute each. The device can record only while in flight, Ring said. When it's not zipping around the house, the Always Home Cam sits in its dock, where the camera is blocked. It will also make a sound in flight to alert that it's recording, Ring said. Amazon acquired Ring for $1 billion in early 2018, providing the e-commerce giant's growing hardware and smart-home divisions with home-surveillance capabilities. In the past year, however, Ring has run into some controversy over privacy and security. Ring's partnerships with hundreds of police departments across the United States have caused concern among privacy advocates, civil-rights groups, and lawmakers, for example. The home-security company also came under scrutiny after reports of hacking. Two couples alleging that intruders had compromised their Ring devices filed a class-action lawsuit in January. Google's Nest smart home cameras have suffered similar attacks. In addition to announcing new devices, Ring said on Thursday that it planned to improve the security of its products. It said that later this year it would launch end-to-end encryption for certain devices, though it did not say which products would be compatible.

sources.title: Spirit Airlines Wants to Sell Its Data to Google. Former Flight Attendants Are Freaked Out
passages: Just days after the court announced Google’s winning bid, the labor union representing 5,500 former Spirit Airlines flight attendants filed an objection to the sale.
“We feel it's another slap in the face that we're waiting for our missing wages while Spirit is going to profit $10 million off our private information,” says the former flight attendant.

“If this goes forward with no limitation, there is no protection for any employee.” The fact that flight attendants are at the forefront of this labor question, rather than workers who sit at desks and type all day, is a reminder that all employees can create data with market value.

The law has not caught up,” says Seema Patel, a law professor at the University of California, College of the Law, San Francisco, who studies labor issues and technology. (California is one of the few states to have explicit worker data protection laws.) "Companies are having a field day with this.” In the past few months, startups specializing in selling defunct companies’ data—including old Slack messages, GitHub content, and Google Drives—to those training AI have reportedly made millions.

The flight attendant says his and other employees’ email accounts and Microsoft files included deeply sensitive personal and medical information shared with the airline as part of their employment and insurance agreements, detailing everything from miscarriages to incidents of domestic violence to union contract negotiations.
The union argues the bankruptcy court should either exclude all flight-attendant-related data from the sale or guarantee that employee data receives the same protections as consumer information.

extraction.body: In a statement, a Google spokesperson said the data “can be helpful in improving our products and AI models.” The sale would not include customer data, and Google “will not receive any personal information from this dataset,” the spokesperson said. The winning offer, chosen over a competing $7.5 million proposal from AI data and training company Mercor, has to be approved by a judge. If former Spirit Airlines attendants have their way, that won’t happen easily. Just days after the court announced Google’s winning bid, the labor union representing 5,500 former Spirit Airlines flight attendants filed an objection to the sale. Lawyers for the 55,000-member Association of Flight Attendants (AFA) argue the sale would include an enormous amount of sensitive employee information, and that even Google’s promised safeguards wouldn’t prevent privacy violations of decades of flight attendants who never could have guessed that their data would be sold to train AI systems. The employee data “has no business being sold,” Sara Nelson, the president of the AFA, said in a written statement to WIRED. “This is outrageous!” The legal objection opens a potential new front in the AI data wars, as major frontier labs including Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mercor scramble to find new sources of data to help train their products. US laws have contemplated how best to protect consumer data, even after companies go bankrupt and are sold off for parts—laws that have taken on new salience and value in the age of AI. But the Spirit Airlines’ flight attendants’ legal objection highlights the gap between data protections for consumers and for workers. It also marks the first public tangle between labor unions and corporations over the sale and use of employee data for AI training purposes, legal experts say. “There is no boundary between the information and data that the employee is producing and their own personal information. The law has not caught up,” says Seema Patel, a law professor at the University of California, College of the Law, San Francisco, who studies labor issues and technology. (California is one of the few states to have explicit worker data protection laws.) "Companies are having a field day with this.” In the past few months, startups specializing in selling defunct companies’ data—including old Slack messages, GitHub content, and Google Drives—to those training AI have reportedly made millions. Meanwhile, so-called egocentric data collection efforts are on the rise, as companies race to record humans performing work like cooking meals, cleaning kitchens, and operating factory lines, and use that data to train machines to aid and eventually replace them. The Spirit data sale would, according to a court filing, include more than 1 million time-card records, over 175,000 employee records, nearly 150,000 employee tax forms, employment contracts and litigation files, 80,000 email accounts, 17 million individually owned Microsoft OneDrive items, 20.6 million shared Microsoft SharePoint files, and 500 million Microsoft Teams records. The court filing describes a process through which the data buyer—Google—would select or OK a third party to strip the data of elements that could be used to link the information with a particular consumer. A hearing related to the data sale has been delayed to September 9. One former Spirit Airlines flight attendant called the potential data sale “troubling.” “I knew they were going to sell every single part of consumer data. It never crossed my mind that they would be so bold as to sell our private data for AI,” says the flight attendant, who spoke to WIRED under condition of anonymity because they’re still looking for new employment. The flight attendant says his and other employees’ email accounts and Microsoft files included deeply sensitive personal and medical information shared with the airline as part of their employment and insurance agreements, detailing everything from miscarriages to incidents of domestic violence to union contract negotiations. “There’s this huge consensus of feeling extremely violated by this,” he says. In its legal objection, AFA argues that “deidentifying” employee data isn’t the same as providing confidentiality, because AI itself makes it much easier to relink private information across datasets, even without specific names. “The privacy architecture of this transaction is consumer-facing; its payload is disproportionately employee-facing,” the union's lawyers wrote. The union argues the bankruptcy court should either exclude all flight-attendant-related data from the sale or guarantee that employee data receives the same protections as consumer information. Though the flight attendants’ objections are just a small part of the larger Spirit Airlines bankruptcy proceeding, the outcome could have a major effect on how labor unions and companies think about employee data going forward, says Ari Ezra Waldman, a professor of law at the University of California, Irvine, who studies privacy and technology. “In a world where billions and trillions are being spent on [large language models], anything where words are used is subject to its own profit-making purpose,” he says. “If this goes forward with no limitation, there is no protection for any employee.” The fact that flight attendants are at the forefront of this labor question, rather than workers who sit at desks and type all day, is a reminder that all employees can create data with market value. “All workers bring an immense amount of knowledge,” Patel says. “Now artificial intelligence has given us the ability to process all different kinds of data.” More value, meanwhile, is one of the former Spirit Airlines’ flight attendants’ goals. Separately, the union has also intervened in the bankruptcy to demand roughly $68 million in unpaid vacation, health care, and back pay. “We feel it's another slap in the face that we're waiting for our missing wages while Spirit is going to profit $10 million off our private information,” says the former flight attendant.

extraction.body: In an unusual case, Google bid $10 million on the corporate data from Spirit Airlines , which stopped flying in May this year. One could ask: what could Google want from this data that includes things like emails, messages, and lines of code? The purpose of the acquisition has been questioned, and the specific information they have is unknown at this stage. Google beat out AI training data startups, such as Mercor, proving how valuable private corporate data has become. It is controversial due to privacy laws and the potential for confidential information to be released, so it's understandable that Spirit Airlines ex-employees such as flight attendants are unhappy about the move. In this guide, we will explore what this could mean and what the outcome might be. Google won a bankruptcy auction on August 14 with a $10 million bid for Spirit Airlines' internal enterprise dataset, outbidding AI data firm Mercor's $7.5 million bid. Another AI data company, Micro1, submitted a higher bid of $12.5 million after the auction closed. But why is there such a bidding war for the data of a failed airline? AI companies have been competing to build the best AI coding agent and to use publicly available code from the internet to train these models. Teaching agents to perform other kinds of white-collar work may require data that is largely private and buried in corporate emails and chats, according to Time . AI companies are moving quickly to acquire bankrupt companies' data to improve their AI models in areas such as customer service and financial services. These companies are willing to pay for this new valuable source of training material. This dataset is extraordinary in scale with roughly 600 million email and chat records generated by 17,000 employees, including about 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams items, 17 million OneDrive files, 20.5 million SharePoint items, more than 30 million recorded customer service calls, 15 million chat records, and 600,000 ServiceNow tickets, alongside operational data covering over 763,000 flights, five million crew pairings, 1.2 million fuel slips and purchase records for 787,452 parts according to The Register . It is understandable why Spirit's ex-employees could be concerned. The Association of Flight Attendants-CWA , which still represents Spirit Airlines flight attendants, filed a limited objection in the US Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York. They argue that the tranche includes sensitive, decades-old employee and workplace records. Union president Sara Nelson said the AFA is objecting to the sale of data that, in its view, should not be sold at all. The union is seeking specific restrictions on flight attendant employee data and additional contractual protections in any approved version. They say that all personal data should be removed, but the dataset would maintain “referential integrity,” meaning that links between data types would be preserved. This is what makes the data useful to train AI systems. The union also said it may allow the use of anonymous information. They are asking for additional privacy protection. “This is outrageous! We are filing a court objection to Google’s attempt to buy data that has no business being sold,” Sara Nelson, international president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, which continues to represent more than 5,500 of Spirit’s flight attendants, told Forbes . Nelson also publicly criticized Spirit Airlines for attempting to monetize its workforce after the airline collapsed. She pointed out that former flight attendants still have not been paid their accrued vacation time, sick leave, and outstanding compensation . Using their private conversations to train AI models without their consent was blasted by the union as corporate exploitation and "adding insult to injury," according to Fortune . The ultra-low-cost carrier has been the subject of many viral TikTok videos. Google wants Spirit’s internal corporate files to teach AI how actual businesses operate behind closed doors. This could include things like handling disputes and customer complaints, writing code, and managing logistics. AI models can be trained on publicly available information, but AI developers struggle to find new data, making this kind of business data invaluable. Operational records are useful for developing AI agents that perform real workplace tasks. In addition, they have a 34-year operating history of the airline from start to finish. Therefore, Google can use AI assistants to solve travel issues in the complex world of aviation, including flight disruptions, dynamic pricing, and customer refunds. AI companies’ long-term goal is to automate large sectors of the economy; that's more likely why they wanted the data from Spirit. They can gain insight into how the aviation industry operates and use it to improve their products and AI models. It is thought that the data would be 'scrubbed' by a third party to remove all personal data before delivery to Google. A court-appointed third-party ombudsman will oversee a process known as “deidentification,” which requires “reasonable measures” to anonymize data so it cannot be linked to individuals. “The privacy architecture of this transaction is consumer-facing; its payload is disproportionately employee-facing,” the AFA argued. “Hence, the employee data is far more confidential than the customer data, yet receives far less protection than the customer data.” Understandably, there are privacy concerns. Indeed, the AFA says the agreement’s language does not address confidential records. “With a group the size of the Spirit flight attendant population, our union has significant concerns that it may be possible that information about identifiable individuals or small identifiable groups can still be reconstructed and determined,” the union said in a statement. The AFA is concerned about the underlying confidentiality of disciplinary records, payroll history, and internal communications, saying the deal’s privacy provisions are designed to protect consumers, specifically passengers, but not employee data. The union argued that even when de-identified, disciplinary records, training deficiencies, and medical or accommodation requests are still sensitive. In smaller data batches, such as crew bases, it’s possible to infer who is being discussed from communication and operations datasets, the union said. The AFA asked the court to reject the sale unless changes are made to exclude all flight attendant information, including training records, time cards, and payroll, as well as any Microsoft 365 content containing flight attendant data. To protect workers, the AFA asked the court to deny approval of the sale until Google agrees to exclude all flight attendant information from the purchase and to notify workers when Google allows a third party to access the data. Google says it acquired part of an enterprise dataset that may help improve its products and AI models, and told CNN it will not receive personal information. It has been said that Google is not interested in acquiring customers’ personal information, including loyalty membership or credit card details, according to a Forbes article. Florida-based Spirit shut down on May 2 amid its second Chapter 11 Bankruptcy Protection in two years due to surging fuel prices and failed financing talks. The airline filed for bankruptcy with about $8.1 billion in debt and eventually laid off roughly 17,000 employees. Issues included surging jet fuel prices linked to the Middle East conflict, ongoing liquidity shortages, and the failure to secure a $500 million federal rescue deal. The carrier had previously navigated two bankruptcy filings starting in late 2024. The sale of data is unusual because Spirit was the first significant US airline in 25 years to halt operations entirely rather than be absorbed by another carrier. In contrast, normally an acquiring airline takes the data along with the business. US bankruptcy Judge Sean Lane's hearing, originally set for August 19, has been pushed to September 9 to review the labor and privacy challenges. Spirit Airlines has been selling off its remaining assets through the bankruptcy process ever since its closure. While most of that is aircraft, equipment, and real estate, there’s now something else to consider: an airline's data. In the era of artificial intelligence, data is being used to train new AI models to perform more operational tasks than ever before. The data has been stripped of anything that could identify individuals, according to the court filing. AFA-CWA is urging the court to exclude all flight attendant data from the transaction and has stated it will continue to oppose the sale until stronger safeguards are adopted. extraction.body: They lost their paychecks, livelihoods, and health insurance this spring. Now, they may lose their privacy. As out-of-business Spirit Airlines liquidates, the planes and the landing rights aren’t the only leftovers for sale. The people overseeing the remaining assets also want to sell employee data to Google to train artificial intelligence. At first, workers put up a big “No” when told about the plan. But over the past month, opposition has softened. A bankruptcy court hearing on the issue, after several postponements, is now set for Nov. 6. Why does Silicon Valley want Spirit’s worker info? Because AI machines grow more useful when fed lots of real-world data on humans. Spirit’s efforts to sell tranches of data to Google for $10 million hit several speed bumps after getting public attention in August. Criticism immediately poured from unions and businesses. Data on passengers aren’t part of the proposed sale. “Our data simply is not for sale. We did not and do not consent,” Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, AFL-CIO, told the Miami Herald in August. But since then, several conversations have softened the opposition, including from the flight attendants union. Spirit has excluded more data from the sale and offered more privacy protections. “The parties have made progress,” the union said in a filing on Sept. 24 with the New York federal court overseeing the Broward-based airline’s bankruptcy. On Oct. 5, a consumer privacy ombudsman, appointed by the court to review the case, recommended that the sale go forward. The conclusions are non-binding and face criticism, and the ultimate approval is up to the judge. The case is unusual in that public controversies over data usually involve consumers, Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, an attorney with the Electronic Privacy Information Center, told the Miami Herald. But in this case, former employees are the focus, not Spirit’s old customers, at least for now. Known as EPIC, the nonpartisan, nonprofit focused on protecting the right to privacy in the digital age filed a request on Oct. 1 to serve as a friend of the court, on the side of the flight attendants union. In a court filing, EPIC said “no employer has attempted to sell its employees’ data as an asset in bankruptcy prior to the instant case.” On Aug. 14, Spirit and its representatives held an auction for large amounts of data the airline maintained. Google won with a bid of $10 million. San Francisco-based AI company Mercor was chosen as the runner-up with a $7.5 million offer. Google agreed that the data chest would first go to a third-party firm that acts as a “deidentification agent.” That’s a company that can scrape off personally identifying characteristics. And the data awarded didn’t include the personal information of customers, both Google and Spirit said. “We’re acquiring part of an enterprise dataset from Spirit Airlines, which can be helpful in improving our products and AI models,” Google spokesperson Gareth Evans said in an email to the Miami Herald at that time. “We will not receive any personal information from this dataset. Any data we receive will be rigorously scrubbed of any personally identifiable information by a third party before receipt.” Still, the amount of data awarded in the auction was massive, and the move caught many by surprise. It even possibly included software and information developed by another company that was a Spirit vendor. Google obtained access to productivity and collaboration data, “including, without limitation, email data, calendar data, chat, collaboration and messaging data, documents, presentations, spreadsheets, knowledge repositories and wikis,” according to court documents. It encompassed potentially “the entire employment and workplace record of Spirit Airlines, including decades of payroll, timekeeping, training, travel, and recruiting files,” the flight attendant union’s initial objection said. That’s “together with approximately 100 million emails, 80,000 email accounts, 17,082,644 OneDrive items, 20,577,677 SharePoint items, and 500,000,000 Teams items.” Other information Google would get access to comes from over 1 million time cards, 148,000 employee tax forms and over 3 million payroll records, according to court documents. Yet, in a nod to compromise, the union over the past month has been in discussions with Spirit, and the airline has reduced the amount of data it seeks to sell. In response to the flight attendants’ initial objection, Spirit sent out a revised proposal on Aug. 31, identifying each category of data the union was concerned about. The airline agreed to exclude “several of the most sensitive categories,” including data on health, disabilities, drug and alcohol testing, and collective bargaining, according to a court filing. Spirit continues to work with the unions and is open to excluding even more data, a person familiar with the process told the Herald. Spirit hopes to win the support of the unions by Nov. 6. The tech company developed a software platform that analyzes and synthesizes tons of sources of operational data. It organized that information in ways that allow employees to know what tasks to complete and when, and make quicker real-time decisions. That ultimately helps reduce flight delays. In the filing, the company requested that the court consider “Springshot’s ownership of substantial intellectual property utilized by Spirit Aviation for its operations and which appear to be among the categories of data Google is seeking to acquire,” and block the sale. Yet the two companies have also shown signs of coming together. Others have also voiced concerns, including several other unions that support the flight attendants union n court filings. They include the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers and the Transport Workers Union of America Local 570, Air Line Pilots Association International, and the Professional Airline Flight Control Association. And on Sept. 29, the Allied Pilots Association, which represents American Airlines pilots, including over 700 who used to work for Spirit, objected to the data sale, saying in a court filing that it “threatens to have a chilling effect across all commercial airlines.” The flight attendants union still has objections, too. In its latest court filing, AFA acknowledged that Spirit agreed that employees’ identification numbers won’t be part of what’s sold, for example, because they’ll be replaced by randomized identifiers. And those will be different in each dataset. The union sees that as progress. But Spirit has yet to agree to exclude flight attendants’ tax forms from the data sale, AFA said, a big concern. Another worry all unions share is whether removing an individual’s identity from data is enough to protect privacy. “We’re worried about the bigger picture,” said EPIC’s Tobin-Miyaji in an interview. “There are so few protections on workers’ data,” the digital rights lawyer said. “We hope we encourage the judge to consider the privacy issues at stake.” That’s one of the disadvantages the former employees face: lack of laws safeguarding their privacy in the workplace. Employees generally have few rights, if any, when it comes to their personal information. They are dictated by employer policy. HIPPA, or the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, is the exception. “There are no clear rules in the bankruptcy code to protect employee privacy,” Tobin-Miyaji said. That’s in contrast to consumers who have protections in several states. For example, Spirit and Google said they’ll follow the deidentification standard adopted within the California Consumer Privacy Act in the initial auction in August. And the ombudsman appointed by the court focused on impact on the consumer and had little to say about former employees or the union’s concerns.

“We’re acquiring part of an enterprise dataset from Spirit Airlines, which can be helpful in improving our products and AI models,” Google spokesperson Gareth Evans said in an email to the Miami Herald at that time. “We will not receive any personal information from this dataset. Google obtained access to productivity and collaboration data, “including, without limitation, email data, calendar data, chat, collaboration and messaging data, documents, presentations, spreadsheets, knowledge repositories and wikis,” according to court documents.

It encompassed potentially “the entire employment and workplace record of Spirit Airlines, including decades of payroll, timekeeping, training, travel, and recruiting files,” the flight attendant union’s initial objection said. That’s “together with approximately 100 million emails, 80,000 email accounts, 17,082,644 OneDrive items, 20,577,677 SharePoint items, and 500,000,000 Teams items.”
Other information Google would get access to comes from over 1 million time cards, 148,000 employee tax forms and over 3 million payroll records, according to court documents.
Yet, in a nod to compromise, the union over the past month has been in discussions with Spirit, and the airline has reduced the amount of data it seeks to sell.

In response to the flight attendants’ initial objection, Spirit sent out a revised proposal on Aug. 31, identifying each category of data the union was concerned about. The airline agreed to exclude “several of the most sensitive categories,” including data on health, disabilities, drug and alcohol testing, and collective bargaining, according to a court filing.
Spirit continues to work with the unions and is open to excluding even more data, a person familiar with the process told the Herald. Spirit hopes to win the support of the unions by Nov. 6.

The tech company developed a software platform that analyzes and synthesizes tons of sources of operational data. It organized that information in ways that allow employees to know what tasks to complete and when, and make quicker real-time decisions. That ultimately helps reduce flight delays.

In the filing, the company requested that the court consider “Springshot’s ownership of substantial intellectual property utilized by Spirit Aviation for its operations and which appear to be among the categories of data Google is seeking to acquire,” and block the sale.
Yet the two companies have also shown signs of coming together.

Others have also voiced concerns, including several other unions that support the flight attendants union n court filings. They include the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers and the Transport Workers Union of America Local 570, Air Line Pilots Association International, and the Professional Airline Flight Control Association.

And on Sept. 29, the Allied Pilots Association, which represents American Airlines pilots, including over 700 who used to work for Spirit, objected to the data sale, saying in a court filing that it “threatens to have a chilling effect across all commercial airlines.”
The flight attendants union still has objections, too.

In its latest court filing, AFA acknowledged that Spirit agreed that employees’ identification numbers won’t be part of what’s sold, for example, because they’ll be replaced by randomized identifiers. And those will be different in each dataset. The union sees that as progress.
But Spirit has yet to agree to exclude flight attendants’ tax forms from the data sale, AFA said, a big concern.
Another worry all unions share is whether removing an individual’s identity from data is enough to protect privacy.
“We’re worried about the bigger picture,” said EPIC’s Tobin-Miyaji in an interview.
“There are so few protections on workers’ data,” the digital rights lawyer said. “We hope we encourage the judge to consider the privacy issues at stake.”

That’s one of the disadvantages the former employees face: lack of laws safeguarding their privacy in the workplace. Employees generally have few rights, if any, when it comes to their personal information. They are dictated by employer policy. HIPPA, or the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, is the exception.
“There are no clear rules in the bankruptcy code to protect employee privacy,” Tobin-Miyaji said.

That’s in contrast to consumers who have protections in several states. For example, Spirit and Google said they’ll follow the deidentification standard adopted within the California Consumer Privacy Act in the initial auction in August. extraction.body: In a statement, a Google spokesperson said the data “can be helpful in improving our products and AI models.” The sale would not include customer data, and Google “will not receive any personal information from this dataset,” the spokesperson said. The winning offer, chosen over a competing $7.5 million proposal from AI data and training company Mercor, has to be approved by a judge. If former Spirit Airlines attendants have their way, that won’t happen easily. Just days after the court announced Google’s winning bid, the labor union representing 5,500 former Spirit Airlines flight attendants filed an objection to the sale. Lawyers for the 55,000-member Association of Flight Attendants (AFA) argue the sale would include an enormous amount of sensitive employee information, and that even Google’s promised safeguards wouldn’t prevent privacy violations of decades of flight attendants who never could have guessed that their data would be sold to train AI systems. The employee data “has no business being sold,” Sara Nelson, the president of the AFA, said in a written statement to WIRED. “This is outrageous!” The legal objection opens a potential new front in the AI data wars, as major frontier labs including Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mercor scramble to find new sources of data to help train their products. US laws have contemplated how best to protect consumer data, even after companies go bankrupt and are sold off for parts—laws that have taken on new salience and value in the age of AI. But the Spirit Airlines’ flight attendants’ legal objection highlights the gap between data protections for consumers and for workers. It also marks the first public tangle between labor unions and corporations over the sale and use of employee data for AI training purposes, legal experts say. “There is no boundary between the information and data that the employee is producing and their own personal information. The law has not caught up,” says Seema Patel, a law professor at the University of California, College of the Law, San Francisco, who studies labor issues and technology. (California is one of the few states to have explicit worker data protection laws.) "Companies are having a field day with this.” In the past few months, startups specializing in selling defunct companies’ data—including old Slack messages, GitHub content, and Google Drives—to those training AI have reportedly made millions. Meanwhile, so-called egocentric data collection efforts are on the rise, as companies race to record humans performing work like cooking meals, cleaning kitchens, and operating factory lines, and use that data to train machines to aid and eventually replace them. The Spirit data sale would, according to a court filing, include more than 1 million time-card records, over 175,000 employee records, nearly 150,000 employee tax forms, employment contracts and litigation files, 80,000 email accounts, 17 million individually owned Microsoft OneDrive items, 20.6 million shared Microsoft SharePoint files, and 500 million Microsoft Teams records. The court filing describes a process through which the data buyer—Google—would select or OK a third party to strip the data of elements that could be used to link the information with a particular consumer. A hearing related to the data sale has been delayed to September 9. One former Spirit Airlines flight attendant called the potential data sale “troubling.” “I knew they were going to sell every single part of consumer data. It never crossed my mind that they would be so bold as to sell our private data for AI,” says the flight attendant, who spoke to WIRED under condition of anonymity because they’re still looking for new employment. The flight attendant says his and other employees’ email accounts and Microsoft files included deeply sensitive personal and medical information shared with the airline as part of their employment and insurance agreements, detailing everything from miscarriages to incidents of domestic violence to union contract negotiations. “There’s this huge consensus of feeling extremely violated by this,” he says. In its legal objection, AFA argues that “deidentifying” employee data isn’t the same as providing confidentiality, because AI itself makes it much easier to relink private information across datasets, even without specific names. “The privacy architecture of this transaction is consumer-facing; its payload is disproportionately employee-facing,” the union's lawyers wrote. The union argues the bankruptcy court should either exclude all flight-attendant-related data from the sale or guarantee that employee data receives the same protections as consumer information. sources.title: Flight Attendants' Union Objects to Google's Purchase of Spirit Airlines' Employee Data Over Privacy Concerns
passages: A flight attendants' union has formally objected to Google's proposed $10m purchase of Spirit Airlines' internal data, arguing the deal fails to adequately protect the privacy of former employees.The Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, AFL-CIO raised concerns over disciplinary records, payroll history and internal communications tied to Spirit's roughly 17,000 former staff in a filing to the US Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York.Why Google Wants Spirit's 100 Million EmailsSpirit ceased flying in May 2026 after rescue talks collapsed, marking the airline's second Chapter 11 filing in two years.

Mercor has since been named backup buyer should Google's purchase fail to close.Union Fights To Block Employee Data TransferThe AFA argues the sale's privacy provisions were built to protect passengers, not employees.

Google has said any material it receives will first be scrubbed of personal identifiers by an independent third party, though the union's objection centres specifically on whether that process is sufficient for internal staff data rather than customer records.The union's filing puts a specific, named legal challenge behind concerns that had so far mostly circulated online as general unease about AI firms buying corporate data in bankruptcy sales.

It shifts the debate from an abstract question about the ethics of the practice to a concrete legal test of whether de-identification standards, largely designed around consumer privacy law, hold up when applied to employees' own workplace records.If the court sides with the union, it could set a precedent requiring stronger worker-specific privacy conditions in future bankruptcy data sales, a question likely to resurface as more struggling companies treat their internal archives as saleable assets.

extraction.body: In an unusual case, Google bid $10 million on the corporate data from Spirit Airlines , which stopped flying in May this year. One could ask: what could Google want from this data that includes things like emails, messages, and lines of code? The purpose of the acquisition has been questioned, and the specific information they have is unknown at this stage. Google beat out AI training data startups, such as Mercor, proving how valuable private corporate data has become. It is controversial due to privacy laws and the potential for confidential information to be released, so it's understandable that Spirit Airlines ex-employees such as flight attendants are unhappy about the move. In this guide, we will explore what this could mean and what the outcome might be. Google won a bankruptcy auction on August 14 with a $10 million bid for Spirit Airlines' internal enterprise dataset, outbidding AI data firm Mercor's $7.5 million bid. Another AI data company, Micro1, submitted a higher bid of $12.5 million after the auction closed. But why is there such a bidding war for the data of a failed airline? AI companies have been competing to build the best AI coding agent and to use publicly available code from the internet to train these models. Teaching agents to perform other kinds of white-collar work may require data that is largely private and buried in corporate emails and chats, according to Time . AI companies are moving quickly to acquire bankrupt companies' data to improve their AI models in areas such as customer service and financial services. These companies are willing to pay for this new valuable source of training material. This dataset is extraordinary in scale with roughly 600 million email and chat records generated by 17,000 employees, including about 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams items, 17 million OneDrive files, 20.5 million SharePoint items, more than 30 million recorded customer service calls, 15 million chat records, and 600,000 ServiceNow tickets, alongside operational data covering over 763,000 flights, five million crew pairings, 1.2 million fuel slips and purchase records for 787,452 parts according to The Register . It is understandable why Spirit's ex-employees could be concerned. The Association of Flight Attendants-CWA , which still represents Spirit Airlines flight attendants, filed a limited objection in the US Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York. They argue that the tranche includes sensitive, decades-old employee and workplace records. Union president Sara Nelson said the AFA is objecting to the sale of data that, in its view, should not be sold at all. The union is seeking specific restrictions on flight attendant employee data and additional contractual protections in any approved version. They say that all personal data should be removed, but the dataset would maintain “referential integrity,” meaning that links between data types would be preserved. This is what makes the data useful to train AI systems. The union also said it may allow the use of anonymous information. They are asking for additional privacy protection. “This is outrageous! We are filing a court objection to Google’s attempt to buy data that has no business being sold,” Sara Nelson, international president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, which continues to represent more than 5,500 of Spirit’s flight attendants, told Forbes . Nelson also publicly criticized Spirit Airlines for attempting to monetize its workforce after the airline collapsed. She pointed out that former flight attendants still have not been paid their accrued vacation time, sick leave, and outstanding compensation . Using their private conversations to train AI models without their consent was blasted by the union as corporate exploitation and "adding insult to injury," according to Fortune . The ultra-low-cost carrier has been the subject of many viral TikTok videos. Google wants Spirit’s internal corporate files to teach AI how actual businesses operate behind closed doors. This could include things like handling disputes and customer complaints, writing code, and managing logistics. AI models can be trained on publicly available information, but AI developers struggle to find new data, making this kind of business data invaluable. Operational records are useful for developing AI agents that perform real workplace tasks. In addition, they have a 34-year operating history of the airline from start to finish. Therefore, Google can use AI assistants to solve travel issues in the complex world of aviation, including flight disruptions, dynamic pricing, and customer refunds. AI companies’ long-term goal is to automate large sectors of the economy; that's more likely why they wanted the data from Spirit. They can gain insight into how the aviation industry operates and use it to improve their products and AI models. It is thought that the data would be 'scrubbed' by a third party to remove all personal data before delivery to Google. A court-appointed third-party ombudsman will oversee a process known as “deidentification,” which requires “reasonable measures” to anonymize data so it cannot be linked to individuals. “The privacy architecture of this transaction is consumer-facing; its payload is disproportionately employee-facing,” the AFA argued. “Hence, the employee data is far more confidential than the customer data, yet receives far less protection than the customer data.” Understandably, there are privacy concerns. Indeed, the AFA says the agreement’s language does not address confidential records. “With a group the size of the Spirit flight attendant population, our union has significant concerns that it may be possible that information about identifiable individuals or small identifiable groups can still be reconstructed and determined,” the union said in a statement. The AFA is concerned about the underlying confidentiality of disciplinary records, payroll history, and internal communications, saying the deal’s privacy provisions are designed to protect consumers, specifically passengers, but not employee data. The union argued that even when de-identified, disciplinary records, training deficiencies, and medical or accommodation requests are still sensitive. In smaller data batches, such as crew bases, it’s possible to infer who is being discussed from communication and operations datasets, the union said. The AFA asked the court to reject the sale unless changes are made to exclude all flight attendant information, including training records, time cards, and payroll, as well as any Microsoft 365 content containing flight attendant data. To protect workers, the AFA asked the court to deny approval of the sale until Google agrees to exclude all flight attendant information from the purchase and to notify workers when Google allows a third party to access the data. Google says it acquired part of an enterprise dataset that may help improve its products and AI models, and told CNN it will not receive personal information. It has been said that Google is not interested in acquiring customers’ personal information, including loyalty membership or credit card details, according to a Forbes article. Florida-based Spirit shut down on May 2 amid its second Chapter 11 Bankruptcy Protection in two years due to surging fuel prices and failed financing talks. The airline filed for bankruptcy with about $8.1 billion in debt and eventually laid off roughly 17,000 employees. Issues included surging jet fuel prices linked to the Middle East conflict, ongoing liquidity shortages, and the failure to secure a $500 million federal rescue deal. The carrier had previously navigated two bankruptcy filings starting in late 2024. The sale of data is unusual because Spirit was the first significant US airline in 25 years to halt operations entirely rather than be absorbed by another carrier. In contrast, normally an acquiring airline takes the data along with the business. US bankruptcy Judge Sean Lane's hearing, originally set for August 19, has been pushed to September 9 to review the labor and privacy challenges. Spirit Airlines has been selling off its remaining assets through the bankruptcy process ever since its closure. While most of that is aircraft, equipment, and real estate, there’s now something else to consider: an airline's data. In the era of artificial intelligence, data is being used to train new AI models to perform more operational tasks than ever before. The Association of Flight Attendants-CWA (AFA-CWA) has formally challenged the proposed sale of Spirit Airlines’ data to Google and says that the agreement provides stronger protections for customer data than for employee records, leaving flight attendants and other staff potentially exposed to privacy risks. AFA-CWA is urging the court to exclude all flight attendant data from the transaction and has stated it will continue to oppose the sale until stronger safeguards are adopted.
