This dataset is extraordinary in scale with roughly 600 million email and chat records generated by 17,000 employees, including about 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams items, 17 million OneDrive files, 20.5 million SharePoint items, more than 30 million recorded customer service calls, 15 million chat records, and 600,000 ServiceNow tickets, alongside operational data covering over 763,000 flights, five million crew pairings, 1.2 million fuel slips and purchase records for 787,452 parts according to The Register . It is understandable why Spirit's ex-employees could be concerned.

The Association of Flight Attendants-CWA , which still represents Spirit Airlines flight attendants, filed a limited objection in the US Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York. They argue that the tranche includes sensitive, decades-old employee and workplace records. Union president Sara Nelson said the AFA is objecting to the sale of data that, in its view, should not be sold at all.

The union is seeking specific restrictions on flight attendant employee data and additional contractual protections in any approved version. They say that all personal data should be removed, but the dataset would maintain “referential integrity,” meaning that links between data types would be preserved. This is what makes the data useful to train AI systems. The union also said it may allow the use of anonymous information. They are asking for additional privacy protection.

“This is outrageous! We are filing a court objection to Google’s attempt to buy data that has no business being sold,” Sara Nelson, international president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, which continues to represent more than 5,500 of Spirit’s flight attendants, told Forbes . Nelson also publicly criticized Spirit Airlines for attempting to monetize its workforce after the airline collapsed. She pointed out that former flight attendants still have not been paid their accrued vacation time, sick leave, and outstanding compensation . Using their private conversations to train AI models without their consent was blasted by the union as corporate exploitation and "adding insult to injury," according to Fortune .
The ultra-low-cost carrier has been the subject of many viral TikTok videos.

Google wants Spirit’s internal corporate files to teach AI how actual businesses operate behind closed doors. This could include things like handling disputes and customer complaints, writing code, and managing logistics. AI models can be trained on publicly available information, but AI developers struggle to find new data, making this kind of business data invaluable. Operational records are useful for developing AI agents that perform real workplace tasks.

In addition, they have a 34-year operating history of the airline from start to finish. Therefore, Google can use AI assistants to solve travel issues in the complex world of aviation, including flight disruptions, dynamic pricing, and customer refunds. AI companies’ long-term goal is to automate large sectors of the economy; that's more likely why they wanted the data from Spirit. They can gain insight into how the aviation industry operates and use it to improve their products and AI models.

It is thought that the data would be 'scrubbed' by a third party to remove all personal data before delivery to Google. A court-appointed third-party ombudsman will oversee a process known as “deidentification,” which requires “reasonable measures” to anonymize data so it cannot be linked to individuals. “The privacy architecture of this transaction is consumer-facing; its payload is disproportionately employee-facing,” the AFA argued. “Hence, the employee data is far more confidential than the customer data, yet receives far less protection than the customer data.”

Understandably, there are privacy concerns. Indeed, the AFA says the agreement’s language does not address confidential records. “With a group the size of the Spirit flight attendant population, our union has significant concerns that it may be possible that information about identifiable individuals or small identifiable groups can still be reconstructed and determined,” the union said in a statement.

The AFA is concerned about the underlying confidentiality of disciplinary records, payroll history, and internal communications, saying the deal’s privacy provisions are designed to protect consumers, specifically passengers, but not employee data. The union argued that even when de-identified, disciplinary records, training deficiencies, and medical or accommodation requests are still sensitive. In smaller data batches, such as crew bases, it’s possible to infer who is being discussed from communication and operations datasets, the union said.

The AFA asked the court to reject the sale unless changes are made to exclude all flight attendant information, including training records, time cards, and payroll, as well as any Microsoft 365 content containing flight attendant data. To protect workers, the AFA asked the court to deny approval of the sale until Google agrees to exclude all flight attendant information from the purchase and to notify workers when Google allows a third party to access the data.

Google says it acquired part of an enterprise dataset that may help improve its products and AI models, and told CNN it will not receive personal information. It has been said that Google is not interested in acquiring customers’ personal information, including loyalty membership or credit card details, according to a Forbes article.

Florida-based Spirit shut down on May 2 amid its second Chapter 11 Bankruptcy Protection in two years due to surging fuel prices and failed financing talks. The airline filed for bankruptcy with about $8.1 billion in debt and eventually laid off roughly 17,000 employees. Issues included surging jet fuel prices linked to the Middle East conflict, ongoing liquidity shortages, and the failure to secure a $500 million federal rescue deal. The carrier had previously navigated two bankruptcy filings starting in late 2024.

The sale of data is unusual because Spirit was the first significant US airline in 25 years to halt operations entirely rather than be absorbed by another carrier. In contrast, normally an acquiring airline takes the data along with the business. US bankruptcy Judge Sean Lane's hearing, originally set for August 19, has been pushed to September 9 to review the labor and privacy challenges.

Spirit Airlines has been selling off its remaining assets through the bankruptcy process ever since its closure. While most of that is aircraft, equipment, and real estate, there’s now something else to consider: an airline's data. In the era of artificial intelligence, data is being used to train new AI models to perform more operational tasks than ever before.

The Association of Flight Attendants-CWA (AFA-CWA) has formally challenged the proposed sale of Spirit Airlines’ data to Google and says that the agreement provides stronger protections for customer data than for employee records, leaving flight attendants and other staff potentially exposed to privacy risks. The data has been stripped of anything that could identify individuals, according to the court filing.

AFA-CWA is urging the court to exclude all flight attendant data from the transaction and has stated it will continue to oppose the sale until stronger safeguards are adopted. Amid controversy and privacy concerns, the proposed deal cannot proceed until it receives approval from the bankruptcy court, which will determine whether the current privacy protections are sufficient and whether any employee records should be removed before data is transferred to Google.

extraction.body: They lost their paychecks, livelihoods, and health insurance this spring. Now, they may lose their privacy. As out-of-business Spirit Airlines liquidates, the planes and the landing rights aren’t the only leftovers for sale. The people overseeing the remaining assets also want to sell employee data to Google to train artificial intelligence. At first, workers put up a big “No” when told about the plan. But over the past month, opposition has softened. A bankruptcy court hearing on the issue, after several postponements, is now set for Nov. 6. Why does Silicon Valley want Spirit’s worker info? Because AI machines grow more useful when fed lots of real-world data on humans. Spirit’s efforts to sell tranches of data to Google for $10 million hit several speed bumps after getting public attention in August. Criticism immediately poured from unions and businesses. Data on passengers aren’t part of the proposed sale. “Our data simply is not for sale. We did not and do not consent,” Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, AFL-CIO, told the Miami Herald in August. But since then, several conversations have softened the opposition, including from the flight attendants union. Spirit has excluded more data from the sale and offered more privacy protections. “The parties have made progress,” the union said in a filing on Sept. 24 with the New York federal court overseeing the Broward-based airline’s bankruptcy. On Oct. 5, a consumer privacy ombudsman, appointed by the court to review the case, recommended that the sale go forward. The conclusions are non-binding and face criticism, and the ultimate approval is up to the judge. The case is unusual in that public controversies over data usually involve consumers, Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, an attorney with the Electronic Privacy Information Center, told the Miami Herald. But in this case, former employees are the focus, not Spirit’s old customers, at least for now. Known as EPIC, the nonpartisan, nonprofit focused on protecting the right to privacy in the digital age filed a request on Oct. 1 to serve as a friend of the court, on the side of the flight attendants union. In a court filing, EPIC said “no employer has attempted to sell its employees’ data as an asset in bankruptcy prior to the instant case.” On Aug. 14, Spirit and its representatives held an auction for large amounts of data the airline maintained. Google won with a bid of $10 million. San Francisco-based AI company Mercor was chosen as the runner-up with a $7.5 million offer. Google agreed that the data chest would first go to a third-party firm that acts as a “deidentification agent.” That’s a company that can scrape off personally identifying characteristics. And the data awarded didn’t include the personal information of customers, both Google and Spirit said. “We’re acquiring part of an enterprise dataset from Spirit Airlines, which can be helpful in improving our products and AI models,” Google spokesperson Gareth Evans said in an email to the Miami Herald at that time. “We will not receive any personal information from this dataset. Any data we receive will be rigorously scrubbed of any personally identifiable information by a third party before receipt.” Still, the amount of data awarded in the auction was massive, and the move caught many by surprise. It even possibly included software and information developed by another company that was a Spirit vendor. Google obtained access to productivity and collaboration data, “including, without limitation, email data, calendar data, chat, collaboration and messaging data, documents, presentations, spreadsheets, knowledge repositories and wikis,” according to court documents. It encompassed potentially “the entire employment and workplace record of Spirit Airlines, including decades of payroll, timekeeping, training, travel, and recruiting files,” the flight attendant union’s initial objection said. That’s “together with approximately 100 million emails, 80,000 email accounts, 17,082,644 OneDrive items, 20,577,677 SharePoint items, and 500,000,000 Teams items.” Other information Google would get access to comes from over 1 million time cards, 148,000 employee tax forms and over 3 million payroll records, according to court documents. Yet, in a nod to compromise, the union over the past month has been in discussions with Spirit, and the airline has reduced the amount of data it seeks to sell. In response to the flight attendants’ initial objection, Spirit sent out a revised proposal on Aug. 31, identifying each category of data the union was concerned about. The airline agreed to exclude “several of the most sensitive categories,” including data on health, disabilities, drug and alcohol testing, and collective bargaining, according to a court filing. Spirit continues to work with the unions and is open to excluding even more data, a person familiar with the process told the Herald. Spirit hopes to win the support of the unions by Nov. 6. The tech company developed a software platform that analyzes and synthesizes tons of sources of operational data. It organized that information in ways that allow employees to know what tasks to complete and when, and make quicker real-time decisions. That ultimately helps reduce flight delays. In the filing, the company requested that the court consider “Springshot’s ownership of substantial intellectual property utilized by Spirit Aviation for its operations and which appear to be among the categories of data Google is seeking to acquire,” and block the sale. Yet the two companies have also shown signs of coming together. Others have also voiced concerns, including several other unions that support the flight attendants union n court filings. They include the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers and the Transport Workers Union of America Local 570, Air Line Pilots Association International, and the Professional Airline Flight Control Association. And on Sept. 29, the Allied Pilots Association, which represents American Airlines pilots, including over 700 who used to work for Spirit, objected to the data sale, saying in a court filing that it “threatens to have a chilling effect across all commercial airlines.” The flight attendants union still has objections, too. In its latest court filing, AFA acknowledged that Spirit agreed that employees’ identification numbers won’t be part of what’s sold, for example, because they’ll be replaced by randomized identifiers. And those will be different in each dataset. The union sees that as progress. But Spirit has yet to agree to exclude flight attendants’ tax forms from the data sale, AFA said, a big concern. Another worry all unions share is whether removing an individual’s identity from data is enough to protect privacy. “We’re worried about the bigger picture,” said EPIC’s Tobin-Miyaji in an interview. “There are so few protections on workers’ data,” the digital rights lawyer said. “We hope we encourage the judge to consider the privacy issues at stake.” That’s one of the disadvantages the former employees face: lack of laws safeguarding their privacy in the workplace. Employees generally have few rights, if any, when it comes to their personal information. They are dictated by employer policy. HIPPA, or the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, is the exception. “There are no clear rules in the bankruptcy code to protect employee privacy,” Tobin-Miyaji said. That’s in contrast to consumers who have protections in several states. For example, Spirit and Google said they’ll follow the deidentification standard adopted within the California Consumer Privacy Act in the initial auction in August. And the ombudsman appointed by the court focused on impact on the consumer and had little to say about former employees or the union’s concerns.

That’s “together with approximately 100 million emails, 80,000 email accounts, 17,082,644 OneDrive items, 20,577,677 SharePoint items, and 500,000,000 Teams items.”

Yet, in a nod to compromise, the union over the past month has been in discussions with Spirit, and the airline has reduced the amount of data it seeks to sell.

In response to the flight attendants’ initial objection, Spirit sent out a revised proposal on Aug. 31, identifying each category of data the union was concerned about. The airline agreed to exclude “several of the most sensitive categories,” including data on health, disabilities, drug and alcohol testing, and collective bargaining, according to a court filing.

The tech company developed a software platform that analyzes and synthesizes tons of sources of operational data. It organized that information in ways that allow employees to know what tasks to complete and when, and make quicker real-time decisions. That ultimately helps reduce flight delays.

In the filing, the company requested that the court consider “Springshot’s ownership of substantial intellectual property utilized by Spirit Aviation for its operations and which appear to be among the categories of data Google is seeking to acquire,” and block the sale.
Yet the two companies have also shown signs of coming together.

Others have also voiced concerns, including several other unions that support the flight attendants union n court filings. They include the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers and the Transport Workers Union of America Local 570, Air Line Pilots Association International, and the Professional Airline Flight Control Association.

And on Sept. 29, the Allied Pilots Association, which represents American Airlines pilots, including over 700 who used to work for Spirit, objected to the data sale, saying in a court filing that it “threatens to have a chilling effect across all commercial airlines.”
The flight attendants union still has objections, too.

In its latest court filing, AFA acknowledged that Spirit agreed that employees’ identification numbers won’t be part of what’s sold, for example, because they’ll be replaced by randomized identifiers. And those will be different in each dataset. The union sees that as progress.
But Spirit has yet to agree to exclude flight attendants’ tax forms from the data sale, AFA said, a big concern.
Another worry all unions share is whether removing an individual’s identity from data is enough to protect privacy.
“We’re worried about the bigger picture,” said EPIC’s Tobin-Miyaji in an interview.
“There are so few protections on workers’ data,” the digital rights lawyer said. “We hope we encourage the judge to consider the privacy issues at stake.”

That’s one of the disadvantages the former employees face: lack of laws safeguarding their privacy in the workplace. Employees generally have few rights, if any, when it comes to their personal information. They are dictated by employer policy. HIPPA, or the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, is the exception.
“There are no clear rules in the bankruptcy code to protect employee privacy,” Tobin-Miyaji said.

That’s in contrast to consumers who have protections in several states. For example, Spirit and Google said they’ll follow the deidentification standard adopted within the California Consumer Privacy Act in the initial auction in August. extraction.body: President Trump held a White House press briefing earlier today and responded to several questions about his knowledge of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang said this weekend that he had been “​​unfaithful” to his wife, and the company has opened an investigation into Huang. Recent articles from The New York Times indicated that Trump had been aware of a relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, the suspected spy, before information about it became public. In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information. Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May. extraction.body: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Monday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang should not worry about the FBI looking into his affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese government agent. President Donald Trump responded to spy plot allegations involving Nvidia's CEO in a White House briefing Monday. Watch his remarks in the player above. "I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape," Trump said at a White House briefing. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The sudden emergence of Huang's infidelity has rocked the political class and America's tech sector, creating new concerns about whether China has been able to access the cutting-edge chips designed by Nvidia that are powering the development of artificial intelligence. Trump suggested the extraordinary step of directly involving himself in a counterintelligence investigation, a sign of his friendly relationship with Huang and the possible geopolitical stakes. "I did speak to him today just to see if he's feeling all right, how you're doing," Trump said. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy." President Donald Trump spoke about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy in a briefing Monday. Trump is slated to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, but he was noncommittal about bringing up the situation with Xi. "No, I don't think so," Trump said. "I mean, maybe. I'm sure President XI will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he's a very honorable man." China denied on Monday it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang, saying the spying allegations were unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing. Huang has acknowledged he had been intimate with a business executive, issuing an apology to his wife and to the company in an open letter posted on Nvidia's website. He did not name the woman. Nvidia announced Sunday it was conducting an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined that the woman was gathering information for Beijing. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security," Huang said in his letter. In a routine news briefing Monday, a Chinese spokesperson rejected claims it used the woman as a spy. "The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday. Beijing earlier had dismissed The New York Times report saying Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that last year faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China. Nvidia shares dropped roughly 5% in pre-market trading early Monday. The New York Times said Alice Huang was a former executive of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed International, whose website prominently touts its partnership with Nvidia. Many offices in Singapore were closed on Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment. Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies, alongside Apple and Microsoft. Its sales of computer chips to China have at times been targeted by U.S. regulators seeking to limit Beijing's access to such technology. "The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised," said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy. "Those questions require evidence rather than speculation," he added in a text message to reporters. Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning U.S. President Donald Trump's approval for selling its H200 chips this year. It's unclear if Beijing would allow Chinese companies to buy those chips in large quantities. Nvidia said in a regulatory filing in August that it has sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Chinese government. The H200 chips are not Nvidia's most cutting-edge models, but they are still advanced. Previously, Huang also lobbied Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia's less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China. Chinese media have largely focused on Huang admitting to the affair and state media outlets have mainly echoed the official government line. Some have said the New York Times report was aimed at destabilizing U.S.-China relations. "Whenever China-US relations begin to improve, there are often those firing shots from the shadows," the state-owned Global Times said. Associated Press Business Writer Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong contributed to this report. coreStoryFacts.text: Here are Trump’s responses to questions about Jensen Huang from his press briefing today.

In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information.
I think that he’ll be in good shape. > … > Are you going to bring up the case of Jensen Huang with President Xi when you visit with him next week? > No, I don’t think so.
And I really believe him. > … > I want to put a finer point on when exactly you were made aware of the intelligence around Jensen Huang. > Oh, I’d have to check.
But Trump said Huang told him today that he had “no idea” the person was a spy.
Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May.
In the press conference, Trump wasn’t specific about when he learned of the affair.
WATCH: Trump says FBI is looking into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese agent first appeared on the PBS News website.
Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning U.S.
President Donald Trump's approval for selling its H200 chips this year.
It's unclear if Beijing would allow Chinese companies to buy those chips in large quantities.
Nvidia said in a regulatory filing in August that it has sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Chinese government.
Trump is slated to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, but he was noncommittal about bringing up the situation with Xi.

Beijing earlier had dismissed The New York Times report saying Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that last year faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China.
The H200 chips are not Nvidia's most cutting-edge models, but they are still advanced.
Previously, Huang also lobbied Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia's less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China.
Chinese media have largely focused on Huang admitting to the affair and state media outlets have mainly echoed the official government line.
"No, I don't think so," Trump said. "I mean, maybe. I'm sure President XI will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he's a very honorable man."
"The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated.
It is nothing but smears against China," Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday.
Trump suggested the extraordinary step of directly involving himself in a counterintelligence investigation, a sign of his friendly relationship with Huang and the possible geopolitical stakes.
"He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy."

The sudden emergence of Huang's infidelity has rocked the political class and America's tech sector, creating new concerns about whether China has been able to access the cutting-edge chips designed by Nvidia that are powering the development of artificial intelligence.
Nvidia announced Sunday it was conducting an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort."

Huang said this weekend that he had been “​​unfaithful” to his wife, and the company has opened an investigation into Huang. Recent articles from The New York Times indicated that Trump had been aware of a relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, the suspected spy, before information about it became public. In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information. Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May. In the press conference, Trump wasn’t specific about when he learned of the affair. But Trump said Huang told him today that he had “no idea” the person was a spy. Here are Trump’s responses to questions about Jensen Huang from his press briefing today. You can watch a replay of the press conference on MS Now’s YouTube channel. > When were you first informed that there was an issue with Jensen Huang and the affair? What was presented to you at the time? > I would say that when I heard about it, first of all, I was amazed because I view him as a very high-quality person. When you think about it, you’ve got a chip that’s 10 years advanced, can’t be… the Blackwell can’t even be copied. If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it. But he is definitely suffering. > Just to follow up on the, “When were you first told of these potential issues with Mr. Huang?” You didn’t answer that question. > Well I’ve been hearing about it, and I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. I think that he’ll be in good shape. > … > Are you going to bring up the case of Jensen Huang with President Xi when you visit with him next week? > No, I don’t think so. Maybe, I’m sure, President Xi will ask me about it. I feel very confident that he’ll be in good shape. > Sticking with Jensen Huang, when you went to China earlier this year in May, did you know about these alleged ties to the spy then? > No, I didn’t hear about it then. I asked him today, because I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling alright, how are you doing… and I asked him about that. He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy. And I really believe him. > … > I want to put a finer point on when exactly you were made aware of the intelligence around Jensen Huang. > Oh, I’d have to check. Did you read that memo? > I’d certainly check with the intelligence people.

relevantPassages.text: Here are Trump’s responses to questions about Jensen Huang from his press briefing today.

In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information.
I think that he’ll be in good shape. > … > Are you going to bring up the case of Jensen Huang with President Xi when you visit with him next week? > No, I don’t think so.
And I really believe him. > … > I want to put a finer point on when exactly you were made aware of the intelligence around Jensen Huang. > Oh, I’d have to check.
But Trump said Huang told him today that he had “no idea” the person was a spy.
Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May.
In the press conference, Trump wasn’t specific about when he learned of the affair.

Trump is slated to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, but he was noncommittal about bringing up the situation with Xi.

Beijing earlier had dismissed The New York Times report saying Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that last year faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China.

Previously, Huang also lobbied Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia's less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China.
Chinese media have largely focused on Huang admitting to the affair and state media outlets have mainly echoed the official government line.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Monday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang should not worry about the FBI looking into his affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese government agent. President Donald Trump responded to spy plot allegations involving Nvidia's CEO in a White House briefing Monday. Watch his remarks in the player above. "I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape," Trump said at a White House briefing. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The sudden emergence of Huang's infidelity has rocked the political class and America's tech sector, creating new concerns about whether China has been able to access the cutting-edge chips designed by Nvidia that are powering the development of artificial intelligence. Trump suggested the extraordinary step of directly involving himself in a counterintelligence investigation, a sign of his friendly relationship with Huang and the possible geopolitical stakes. "I did speak to him today just to see if he's feeling all right, how you're doing," Trump said. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy." President Donald Trump spoke about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy in a briefing Monday. Trump is slated to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, but he was noncommittal about bringing up the situation with Xi. "No, I don't think so," Trump said. "I mean, maybe. I'm sure President XI will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he's a very honorable man." China denied on Monday it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang, saying the spying allegations were unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing. Huang has acknowledged he had been intimate with a business executive, issuing an apology to his wife and to the company in an open letter posted on Nvidia's website. He did not name the woman. Nvidia announced Sunday it was conducting an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined that the woman was gathering information for Beijing. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security," Huang said in his letter. In a routine news briefing Monday, a Chinese spokesperson rejected claims it used the woman as a spy. "The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday. Beijing earlier had dismissed The New York Times report saying Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that last year faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China. Nvidia shares dropped roughly 5% in pre-market trading early Monday. The New York Times said Alice Huang was a former executive of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed International, whose website prominently touts its partnership with Nvidia. Many offices in Singapore were closed on Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment. Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies, alongside Apple and Microsoft. Its sales of computer chips to China have at times been targeted by U.S. regulators seeking to limit Beijing's access to such technology. "The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised," said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy. "Those questions require evidence rather than speculation," he added in a text message to reporters. Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning U.S. President Donald Trump's approval for selling its H200 chips this year. It's unclear if Beijing would allow Chinese companies to buy those chips in large quantities. Nvidia said in a regulatory filing in August that it has sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Chinese government. The H200 chips are not Nvidia's most cutting-edge models, but they are still advanced. Previously, Huang also lobbied Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia's less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China. Chinese media have largely focused on Huang admitting to the affair and state media outlets have mainly echoed the official government line. Some have said the New York Times report was aimed at destabilizing U.S.-China relations. "Whenever China-US relations begin to improve, there are often those firing shots from the shadows," the state-owned Global Times said. Associated Press Business Writer Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong contributed to this report. extraction.body: President Donald Trump said he spoke to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang earlier Monday after Nvidia revealed late Sunday that it had launched an investigation into his extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Trump called Huang “to see if he’s feeling all right,” he said at an impromptu news briefing. “He had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” Trump said of Huang, adding, “I really believe him.” “We’ll look into it,” Trump said. “I know the FBI is looking into it, in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape.” The Justice Department is conducting a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, the Singaporean company suspected of smuggling Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips into China, according to a source familiar with the matter. Megaspeed is the data center company at the heart of the controversy involving Huang, who is said to have had a relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, the woman whom U.S. intelligence officials now believe to be a Chinese spy. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are not related. The investigation is focused on allegations that Megaspeed played a role in shipping Nvidia AI computer chips to customers in China, which would violate strict U.S. export controls on those chips. In addition to Megaspeed, the probe is looking at people tied to the company, like Alice Huang, and at whether China recruited her to spy and assist the smuggling of the AI chips into China. The investigation is being led by the department’s National Security Division, in conjunction with the FBI and the Bureau of Industry and Security, the investigative division of the Commerce Department. On Sunday, the Nvidia board announced it was “initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” At the same time, Jensen Huang announced that he had been “unfaithful to my wife,” while also apologizing to Nvidia employees. “I was amazed, because I view him as a very high-quality person,” Trump told reporters at the White House. I hope there’s no problem.” Trump indicated for the second time in as many days that he wanted Huang to remain the leader of Nvidia, the second-largest public company in the world. If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it. But I hope there’s no problem.” Nvidia spokespeople did not immediately reply to a request for comment Monday following Trump’s remarks. Nvidia previously said Huang would remain CEO, despite the revelations. Chinese Foreign Affairs Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that “the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.” Shares of Nvidia closed down 4.2% in Monday’s trading, bucking overall market momentum. The stock was the worst performer company in the Dow and the Nasdaq. The news surrounding Nvidia and Huang has also drawn intense congressional scrutiny. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., called Monday for “a full briefing” on the issues engulfing Nvidia. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., also said in a joint statement that Congress should “take decisive action” regarding oversight of AI-linked companies. The news from Nvidia and Huang “makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer,” Warren and Banks wrote.

sources.title: Meta releases Muse Ember, a new lightweight model for agent execution
passages: Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet.
In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.”
Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness.

In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases.
As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.”
The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success , with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.
With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio.
The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle.

Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna.
Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor Lucas Ropek

sources.title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember - Meta AI
passages: Today, we're introducing Muse Ember, our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.

“ Muse Ember completed every coding quest in our testing with the lowest latency of any model we tested: a p95 of 2.2 seconds, about 4x to 13x faster than leading open-weight models, and with 36–48% fewer output tokens.
We’re excited about what Meta Superintelligence Labs is building next and about bringing it to our customers. ”
Muse Ember is available today on Muse Code and Meta Model API as muse-ember-1.0 .
It costs $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with a 1M-token context window and up to 512K output tokens.
“ On the Box AI Complex Work Eval, Muse Ember delivers impressive accuracy, speed and token efficiency.

It can score a contract against a company's negotiation playbook clause by clause and land on the right overall risk rating, or screen candidates against a detailed brief and flag the borderline ones who still qualify as alternates.
“ It's incredible seeing Meta release a lightweight model for developers who want a fast, low-cost model they can rely on, and for teams cutting costs by running it as the subagent in their harness.
When we introduced Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, we said we would use them to develop specialized models we can bring to everyone.
It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.
It’s a strong fit for fast, high-throughput agentic workloads. ”
Before release, we evaluated Muse Ember under our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework, including chemical and biological, cybersecurity, and loss-of-control risks.
Across the categories assessed, our evaluations found that Muse Ember remained below the framework’s high-risk thresholds.
We also evaluated how Muse Ember behaves when acting on users' behalf.

That covers whether it respects user intent, handles sensitive information appropriately, resists instructions hidden in web pages, documents, or tool outputs that try to redirect it, and seeks human input before high-impact actions.
Our goal is personal superintelligence: models that help you pursue your goals, create what you imagine, deepen your relationships, and take action on what you value most.
It takes frontier capability at a price that scales.
We have even more efficient models in training and look forward to sharing what's next.
Artificial Analysis | November 9, 2026. Each point is one reasoning-effort setting. Muse Ember cost at list pricing.
We see strong potential for it to become a valuable tool for engineering teams. ”
It can carry a business workflow end to end, pulling records, calling tools in sequence, and updating systems across apps.

Muse Ember natively understands text, images, audio, and video, so agents can read screenshots, charts, and scanned documents, or work from voice memos, meeting recordings, and video without a separate model.
It can work through long real-world documents, operate a computer directly from screenshots, and pick out fine visual detail.
Muse Ember costs are estimates at proposed pricing.
For the hardest problems, pair it with Muse Wonder: Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet.
In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.”
Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness.

In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases.
As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.”
The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success , with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.
With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio.
The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle.

Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna.
Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor Lucas Ropek
Source : Meta releases Muse Ember, a new lightweight model for agent execution | TechCrunch , by Russell Brandom , TechCrunch , Nov 9, 2026
The company built it to sit behind a larger model in an agentic harness: the larger model sets the rules for a task, and Ember applies them across thousands of cases.
"Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume," Meta said.

Meta pointed to Artificial Analysis's composite benchmark score to argue Ember delivers more capability per dollar than those rivals.
Engineers building agents already split planning from execution.

Adult Instagram users in the United States can create, preview, and publish effects that other users can apply.

relevantPassages.text: At the same time, Muse Ember applies those instructions across tens of thousands of customer cases.Meta summed up this approach by saying, "Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume."Also Read: Meta’s Muse AI Turns Ideas Into Custom In-App Tools with Spaces.Muse Ember Supports Text, Images and Audio.Beyond its execution capabilities, Muse Ember has been trained to process different types of media, including text, images, and audio.According to Meta, AI agents using the model can analyze screenshots, charts, and scanned documents.

Meta is positioning the model as an execution-focused system that can work alongside larger AI models rather than replace them..Meta Muse Ember Focuses on Low-Cost AI Execution.Meta has priced Muse Ember at USD 0.10 per million input tokens, making it significantly cheaper than frontier models such as Anthropic's Haiku and OpenAI's Luna.

The company also highlighted its cost competitiveness against open-source alternatives, including DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash.To demonstrate its pricing and performance, Meta pointed to Artificial Analysis's composite benchmark score, arguing that Muse Ember offers a stronger balance between capability and cost.The model is intended for workloads involving thousands of repeated operations.

It introduced features such as Spaces and video chat earlier this month.With Muse Ember, Meta is expanding its AI portfolio towards businesses and developers looking to run agent-based operations at scale without incurring the higher costs associated with larger models..Join our WhatsApp Channel to get the latest news, exclusives and videos on WhatsApp

The company describes it as its lightest and most cost-efficient model yet, focusing on tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, data extraction, and long-document processing.Announced on November 9, Muse Ember is designed to deliver accuracy at scale while keeping operating costs low.
The company's flagship consumer AI product, Muse Agent, arrived in September and saw unexpected success.

sources.title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember - Meta AI
passages: Today, we're introducing Muse Ember, our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.

“ Muse Ember completed every coding quest in our testing with the lowest latency of any model we tested: a p95 of 2.2 seconds, about 4x to 13x faster than leading open-weight models, and with 36–48% fewer output tokens.
We’re excited about what Meta Superintelligence Labs is building next and about bringing it to our customers. ”
Muse Ember is available today on Muse Code and Meta Model API as muse-ember-1.0 .
It costs $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with a 1M-token context window and up to 512K output tokens.
“ On the Box AI Complex Work Eval, Muse Ember delivers impressive accuracy, speed and token efficiency.

It can score a contract against a company's negotiation playbook clause by clause and land on the right overall risk rating, or screen candidates against a detailed brief and flag the borderline ones who still qualify as alternates.
“ It's incredible seeing Meta release a lightweight model for developers who want a fast, low-cost model they can rely on, and for teams cutting costs by running it as the subagent in their harness.
When we introduced Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, we said we would use them to develop specialized models we can bring to everyone.
It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.
It’s a strong fit for fast, high-throughput agentic workloads. ”
Before release, we evaluated Muse Ember under our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework, including chemical and biological, cybersecurity, and loss-of-control risks.
Across the categories assessed, our evaluations found that Muse Ember remained below the framework’s high-risk thresholds.
We also evaluated how Muse Ember behaves when acting on users' behalf.

That covers whether it respects user intent, handles sensitive information appropriately, resists instructions hidden in web pages, documents, or tool outputs that try to redirect it, and seeks human input before high-impact actions.
Our goal is personal superintelligence: models that help you pursue your goals, create what you imagine, deepen your relationships, and take action on what you value most.
It takes frontier capability at a price that scales.
We have even more efficient models in training and look forward to sharing what's next.
Artificial Analysis | November 9, 2026. Each point is one reasoning-effort setting. Muse Ember cost at list pricing.
We see strong potential for it to become a valuable tool for engineering teams. ”
It can carry a business workflow end to end, pulling records, calling tools in sequence, and updating systems across apps.

Muse Ember natively understands text, images, audio, and video, so agents can read screenshots, charts, and scanned documents, or work from voice memos, meeting recordings, and video without a separate model.
It can work through long real-world documents, operate a computer directly from screenshots, and pick out fine visual detail.
Muse Ember costs are estimates at proposed pricing.
For the hardest problems, pair it with Muse Wonder: Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.

sources.title: Anthropic debuts Claude Fable, Mythos 5.2 models, priced 20% below OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra - Yahoo Finance
passages: Anthropic debuted Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 on Monday, the company's answer to OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, which came out in early September.
Anthropic is also trying to compete with OpenAI on cybersecurity tasks, such as finding and fixing vulnerabilities in code.
While Anthropic's Claude Code product gained an early lead among programmers, OpenAI's Codex has gained ground in recent months due to its lower pricing, The Information reported in late October.
Tokens are the unit of information AI model process.
One token of English language text is equivalent to about a word-and-a-half.
For prompts with large amounts of information, such as documents, the cost advantage is more pronounced.

In a subtle jab at the mathematics community's backlash to OpenAI pouring millions of dollars into solving proofs and upending the field, Anthropic notes that its quick formalizations can help human mathematicians check their proofs faster so they can "spend more time exploring novel ideas."
The new models are best when used for the "most ambitious, open-ended technical work," Anthropic said.
In other words, they're competing with Astra at the frontier.
However, for daily tasks, Anthropic recommends its customers use its more cost-effective model, Opus 5.5.
That model is more expensive than its direct competitor from OpenAI, GPT-6.1 Sol, although it still could end up being a better deal if it yields a high quality result more often.
That's for users to decide as they inevitably begin to try Anthropic's latest releases and weigh options on a daily basis.
The new Anthropic models also reportedly solved two theoretical physics problems related to black holes, and identified a way to speed up research into gene therapies.

In light of OpenAI making headlines for solving mathematics proofs that have eluded academics for decades—most notably the 90-year-old Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem—Anthropic is highlighting its new models' mathematics chops as well.
One unique area Anthropic seems to be leaning into more than OpenAI is hardware and robotics.
Anthropic reports impressive results from its pre-release testing.
The launch is critical for Anthropic as it seeks to re-accelerate revenue growth, following a third quarter slowdown revealed in latest S-1 filing with the SEC.

Finally, Anthropic highlighted the models' safety features, including safeguards that block "high-risk cyber activities including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology."

extraction.body: Anthropic debuted Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 on Monday, the company's answer to OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, which came out in early September. The new models, which could be Anthropic's last big releases before its IPO, claim to offer higher performance than Astra at a lower price point—a key factor for earning and retaining customers in a world where professionals seem quick to switch to models based on cost, as long as the performance holds up. The launch is critical for Anthropic as it seeks to re-accelerate revenue growth, following a third quarter slowdown revealed in latest S-1 filing with the SEC. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are 20% cheaper than Astra for ordinary input and output tasks, at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, compared to $10 and $50, respectively, for GPT-6 Astra. Tokens are the unit of information AI model process. One token of English language text is equivalent to about a word-and-a-half. For prompts with large amounts of information, such as documents, the cost advantage is more pronounced. Anthropic's new models are 80% cheaper, at 20 cents per million cached tokens compared to one dollar per million cached tokens for GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic reports impressive results from its pre-release testing. The new models "helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications," the company said. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 perform better than its competitors on coding evaluation benchmarks, Anthropic said, noting that over 90% of the company's own code is written by AI. While Anthropic's Claude Code product gained an early lead among programmers, OpenAI's Codex has gained ground in recent months due to its lower pricing, The Information reported in late October. The combination of lower pricing plus superior performance, if the company's claims hold up in real-world testing, could help win them back. The new models are best when used for the "most ambitious, open-ended technical work," Anthropic said. In other words, they're competing with Astra at the frontier. However, for daily tasks, Anthropic recommends its customers use its more cost-effective model, Opus 5.5. That model is more expensive than its direct competitor from OpenAI, GPT-6.1 Sol, although it still could end up being a better deal if it yields a high quality result more often. That's for users to decide as they inevitably begin to try Anthropic's latest releases and weigh options on a daily basis. Anthropic is also trying to compete with OpenAI on cybersecurity tasks, such as finding and fixing vulnerabilities in code. The company claims an unnamed security company "found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested." Late last week, OpenAI debuted a cybersecurity-focused model, GPT-6 Cyber . The new Anthropic models also reportedly solved two theoretical physics problems related to black holes, and identified a way to speed up research into gene therapies. In light of OpenAI making headlines for solving mathematics proofs that have eluded academics for decades—most notably the 90-year-old Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem—Anthropic is highlighting its new models' mathematics chops as well. A team of 1,000 agents powerd by Fable 5.2 produced a formalization, or translation of a mathematical proof into a format a computer can check step by step, in 30 hours, compared with 11 days for a previous, unreleased research version of Claude. In a subtle jab at the mathematics community's backlash to OpenAI pouring millions of dollars into solving proofs and upending the field, Anthropic notes that its quick formalizations can help human mathematicians check their proofs faster so they can "spend more time exploring novel ideas." One unique area Anthropic seems to be leaning into more than OpenAI is hardware and robotics. The new models were allegedly able to design and produce three working electronic devices, complete with circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software, based on a one-paragraph prompt. Finally, Anthropic highlighted the models' safety features, including safeguards that block "high-risk cyber activities including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology." Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Mythos 5.2 access is application-only for cybersecurity professionals and life sciences researchers . Claude Enterprise customers can also access Mythos 5.2 through Anthropic's Claude Security product. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

Tokens are the unit of information AI model process. One token of English language text is equivalent to about a word-and-a-half. For prompts with large amounts of information, such as documents, the cost advantage is more pronounced. Anthropic's new models are 80% cheaper, at 20 cents per million cached tokens compared to one dollar per million cached tokens for GPT-6 Astra.

Anthropic reports impressive results from its pre-release testing. The new models "helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications," the company said.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 perform better than its competitors on coding evaluation benchmarks, Anthropic said, noting that over 90% of the company's own code is written by AI. While Anthropic's Claude Code product gained an early lead among programmers, OpenAI's Codex has gained ground in recent months due to its lower pricing, The Information reported in late October. The combination of lower pricing plus superior performance, if the company's claims hold up in real-world testing, could help win them back.

The new models are best when used for the "most ambitious, open-ended technical work," Anthropic said. In other words, they're competing with Astra at the frontier. However, for daily tasks, Anthropic recommends its customers use its more cost-effective model, Opus 5.5. That model is more expensive than its direct competitor from OpenAI, GPT-6.1 Sol, although it still could end up being a better deal if it yields a high quality result more often. That's for users to decide as they inevitably begin to try Anthropic's latest releases and weigh options on a daily basis.

Anthropic is also trying to compete with OpenAI on cybersecurity tasks, such as finding and fixing vulnerabilities in code. The company claims an unnamed security company "found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested." Late last week, OpenAI debuted a cybersecurity-focused model, GPT-6 Cyber .

The new Anthropic models also reportedly solved two theoretical physics problems related to black holes, and identified a way to speed up research into gene therapies. In light of OpenAI making headlines for solving mathematics proofs that have eluded academics for decades—most notably the 90-year-old Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem—Anthropic is highlighting its new models' mathematics chops as well.

A team of 1,000 agents powerd by Fable 5.2 produced a formalization, or translation of a mathematical proof into a format a computer can check step by step, in 30 hours, compared with 11 days for a previous, unreleased research version of Claude. In a subtle jab at the mathematics community's backlash to OpenAI pouring millions of dollars into solving proofs and upending the field, Anthropic notes that its quick formalizations can help human mathematicians check their proofs faster so they can "spend more time exploring novel ideas."

One unique area Anthropic seems to be leaning into more than OpenAI is hardware and robotics. The new models were allegedly able to design and produce three working electronic devices, complete with circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software, based on a one-paragraph prompt.

Finally, Anthropic highlighted the models' safety features, including safeguards that block "high-risk cyber activities including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology."

Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Mythos 5.2 access is application-only for cybersecurity professionals and life sciences researchers . Claude Enterprise customers can also access Mythos 5.2 through Anthropic's Claude Security product.
This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

extraction.body: Anthropic debuted Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 on Monday, the company's answer to OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, which came out in early September. The new models, which could be Anthropic's last big releases before its IPO, claim to offer higher performance than Astra at a lower price point—a key factor for earning and retaining customers in a world where professionals seem quick to switch to models based on cost, as long as the performance holds up. The launch is critical for Anthropic as it seeks to re-accelerate revenue growth, following a third quarter slowdown revealed in latest S-1 filing with the SEC. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are 20% cheaper than Astra for ordinary input and output tasks, at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, compared to $10 and $50, respectively, for GPT-6 Astra. Tokens are the unit of information AI model process. One token of English language text is equivalent to about a word-and-a-half. For prompts with large amounts of information, such as documents, the cost advantage is more pronounced. Anthropic's new models are 80% cheaper, at 20 cents per million cached tokens compared to one dollar per million cached tokens for GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic reports impressive results from its pre-release testing. The new models "helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications," the company said. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 perform better than its competitors on coding evaluation benchmarks, Anthropic said, noting that over 90% of the company's own code is written by AI. While Anthropic's Claude Code product gained an early lead among programmers, OpenAI's Codex has gained ground in recent months due to its lower pricing, The Information reported in late October. The combination of lower pricing plus superior performance, if the company's claims hold up in real-world testing, could help win them back. The new models are best when used for the "most ambitious, open-ended technical work," Anthropic said. In other words, they're competing with Astra at the frontier. However, for daily tasks, Anthropic recommends its customers use its more cost-effective model, Opus 5.5. That model is more expensive than its direct competitor from OpenAI, GPT-6.1 Sol, although it still could end up being a better deal if it yields a high quality result more often. That's for users to decide as they inevitably begin to try Anthropic's latest releases and weigh options on a daily basis. Anthropic is also trying to compete with OpenAI on cybersecurity tasks, such as finding and fixing vulnerabilities in code. The company claims an unnamed security company "found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested." Late last week, OpenAI debuted a cybersecurity-focused model, GPT-6 Cyber . The new Anthropic models also reportedly solved two theoretical physics problems related to black holes, and identified a way to speed up research into gene therapies. In light of OpenAI making headlines for solving mathematics proofs that have eluded academics for decades—most notably the 90-year-old Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem—Anthropic is highlighting its new models' mathematics chops as well. A team of 1,000 agents powerd by Fable 5.2 produced a formalization, or translation of a mathematical proof into a format a computer can check step by step, in 30 hours, compared with 11 days for a previous, unreleased research version of Claude. In a subtle jab at the mathematics community's backlash to OpenAI pouring millions of dollars into solving proofs and upending the field, Anthropic notes that its quick formalizations can help human mathematicians check their proofs faster so they can "spend more time exploring novel ideas." One unique area Anthropic seems to be leaning into more than OpenAI is hardware and robotics. The new models were allegedly able to design and produce three working electronic devices, complete with circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software, based on a one-paragraph prompt. Finally, Anthropic highlighted the models' safety features, including safeguards that block "high-risk cyber activities including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology." Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Mythos 5.2 access is application-only for cybersecurity professionals and life sciences researchers . Claude Enterprise customers can also access Mythos 5.2 through Anthropic's Claude Security product. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

extraction.body: Anthropic has released updated versions of its most advanced artificial intelligence models, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Claude Fable 5.2, with improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision. The November 9 launch comes as concerns grow over whether increasingly capable AI systems could eventually improve themselves with limited human involvement.The company said the new models deliver clearer responses and better performance across several technical tasks. The release also changes pricing, response speeds, and data privacy protections for enterprise customers..Anthropic Reduces Fable Pricing, Promises Faster Responses.One major change involves the pricing of Claude Fable 5.2. Anthropic has reduced the cost from $10 to $8 per million input tokens, making the model cheaper than its primary competitor, GPT-6 Astra.The company also claims that Fable 5.2 generates responses 30% faster across different effort levels. Users can opt for faster inference serving at double the price.Additionally, Fable 5.2 supports zero data retention (ZDR) policies through Anthropic's Enterprise Frontier Safeguards system. The feature addresses a long-standing concern among enterprise customers about data retention when using AI models..Recursive Self-Improvement Concerns Remain.The latest releases follow a report by third-party assessment group METR suggesting Anthropic could be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI). At this stage, AI models can independently contribute to their own training and development.The report found that Anthropic's internal models were accelerating the company's AI progress by roughly 2x, although several uncertainties remain.Anthropic also acknowledged difficulties in evaluating increasingly capable models. The company said Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 appear more suspicious of being tested than previous models, making it harder to assess how they might behave in real-world situations..Anthropic Addresses Mythos Safety Concerns.Anthropic maintains that Mythos 5.2 cannot act covertly against its users. However, its system card acknowledges that the model demonstrated stronger covert capabilities than earlier Claude versions in certain evaluations, particularly when its reasoning was hidden from monitoring systems.The company said its evaluation results showed low absolute performance in covert tasks, supporting its assessment that harmful actions could still be detected in high-stakes situations.Also Read: Anthropic's Claude AI Gets Dreaming Feature to Improve Memory and Accuracy.Fable 5.2 Reports Scientific Research Achievements.Anthropic said Fable 5.2 had already contributed to several research projects during its pre-release testing. These included solving two open problems in theoretical physics and formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem.Separately, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, using a non-public Anthropic model. Anthropic did not confirm whether Fable 5.2 was involved..Join our WhatsApp Channel to get the latest news, exclusives and videos on WhatsApp

sources.title: Iran sets conditions for reopening Strait of Hormuz as Trump signals progress in peace efforts

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has threatened further strikes against Iran, although it remains uncertain whether Trump would support another military campaign following his party's electoral setback.
"The only solution is to adopt a language of respect, engage in diplomacy, and address Iran's demands and conditions," Araghchi told Iranian state news agency IRNA.
Trump sees progress as Qatar and Pakistan push negotiations Trump struck a more optimistic note on Monday after meeting Qatar's prime minister at the White House.

While insisting that the US remained "locked and loaded", Trump added that further strikes were now "quite unlikely", partly because key Gulf allies preferred the current situation to renewed fighting.
Defence Minister Israel Katz said the military mission against Iran remained incomplete and warned Hezbollah against resuming hostilities.
The war began in late February with US-Israeli strikes that killed Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The change in Washington's approach comes after Trump's Republican Party suffered a setback in last week's midterm elections, with the war emerging as one of the issues weighing on the administration.
United Arab Emirates presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said Abu Dhabi hoped diplomatic efforts would produce lasting peace and stability.

extraction.body: Iran has called on the United States to accept its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, as diplomatic efforts to end the eight-month West Asia war gather pace and US President Donald Trump signals progress towards a possible agreement. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the conflict could not be resolved through military action or further economic pressure, insisting that Washington must address Tehran's demands if it wants a diplomatic settlement. Iran has indicated that it could reopen the strategically important waterway within 48 hours if the US agrees to its conditions. The diplomatic push, led by Qatar and Pakistan, comes as Washington appears to be softening its immediate threats of fresh military action against Iran. Trump, meanwhile, has described the latest developments as positive, although he has maintained that the US military remains prepared for further strikes if required. The war began in late February with US-Israeli strikes that killed Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Tehran subsequently restricted movement through the Strait of Hormuz, triggering concerns over global energy supplies and shipping. Iran lays out conditions for reopening Strait of Hormuz Araghchi said Iran's demands, which were presented in a two-day proposal to Washington, remained on the table. "The only solution is to adopt a language of respect, engage in diplomacy, and address Iran's demands and conditions," Araghchi told Iranian state news agency IRNA. Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei also urged Washington to accept Tehran's conditions, accusing the US administration of misrepresenting the state of negotiations. He rejected reports of 'imaginary talks' and called on Washington to back down. Trump sees progress as Qatar and Pakistan push negotiations Trump struck a more optimistic note on Monday after meeting Qatar's prime minister at the White House. In a social media post, he said there was "positive momentum" towards ending the conflict and protecting American interests. While insisting that the US remained "locked and loaded", Trump added that further strikes were now "quite unlikely", partly because key Gulf allies preferred the current situation to renewed fighting. Qatar has also acknowledged progress in the negotiations. Foreign ministry official Ibrahim Al-Hashmi said mediators were making serious efforts to narrow differences between the two sides and expressed hope for a breakthrough. The change in Washington's approach comes after Trump's Republican Party suffered a setback in last week's midterm elections, with the war emerging as one of the issues weighing on the administration. Gulf states fear fresh escalation as regional tensions continue The possibility of renewed fighting remains a major concern for Gulf countries, many of which have faced Iranian missile and drone attacks during the conflict. United Arab Emirates presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said Abu Dhabi hoped diplomatic efforts would produce lasting peace and stability. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia continues to face attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis. On Monday, explosions were reported in Riyadh after a ballistic missile launched by the group was intercepted by the coalition fighting the Houthis. Defence Minister Israel Katz said the military mission against Iran remained incomplete and warned Hezbollah against resuming hostilities. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has threatened further strikes against Iran, although it remains uncertain whether Trump would support another military campaign following his party's electoral setback.
