Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif travelled to Doha on Thursday for talks with Qatar’s leadership as momentum builds for a possible new round of negotiations between the US and Iran to end the ongoing war. The meeting comes as the fragile ceasefire continues to hold and diplomatic contacts between Washington and Tehran show signs of picking up again. US President Donald Trump suggested that talks could take place within days, potentially in Pakistan, while UN Secretary-General António Guterres said it is “highly probable” that discussions will restart. Sharif’s visit to Qatar follows a stop in Saudi Arabia and comes ahead of meetings in Turkey, as Islamabad pushes on with its mediation efforts to secure a second round of talks between the two sides. Pakistan’s mediation effort is unfolding across several channels. In parallel with Sharif’s visit, the country’s army chief Asim Munir travelled to Tehran for talks officials described as part of ongoing efforts to sustain dialogue. Munir met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, with both sides stressing the need to avoid further escalation. Islamabad has already hosted direct talks between US and Iranian officials, which ended without an agreement, and is now seeking to secure a second round of negotiations before the current ceasefire expires, in what officials see as a narrowing window for diplomacy. In Doha, Sharif held talks that also touched on regional coordination, with Qatar remaining a key, if cautious, player in mediation efforts. During the meeting, Qatar’s Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and Sharif discussed de-escalation, with Doha signalling support for Pakistan’s role in sustaining dialogue between Washington and Tehran. The talks also pointed to growing concern among Gulf states over energy flows and maritime security. The discussions follow a call between Emir Al Thani and Trump on the impact of the conflict on global energy markets and supply chains. Earlier in the tour, Sharif met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Jeddah, and is also due to attend the Antalya Diplomacy Forum in Turkey, where he is expected to meet Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. The push for talks comes as pressure on Tehran continues, including a US naval blockade of Iranian ports. Both sides have signalled that communication channels remain open, raising the prospect that talks could resume even as key differences remain unresolved.

Reviewed by Codex validator (AI) · 10 Nov 2026 Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it continues Doha-led mediation efforts between the United States and Iran and that it has received positive reactions from both sides to find a way out of the current crisis. Ibrahim Sultan al-Hoshemi, Director of Information and Communications at the Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said a meeting held by Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani with U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House was characterized as 'positive,' reflecting progress in the negotiation process. Qatar warned that approaching winter, alongside the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz, doubles the high cost of the ongoing crisis between Washington and Tehran and its impact on energy supplies and navigation. Qatar’s mediation message also came as Iranian Foreign Minister عباس عراقجي denied the authenticity of reports about a possible meeting between U.S. Vice President جيه دي فانس and Iranian Supreme National Security Council Secretary محسن رضائي, calling them unfounded rumors and baseless media fabrications. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry also condemned attacks targeting Saudi Arabia and confirmed Doha’s full solidarity with Riyadh and its absolute support for measures the Kingdom is taking to safeguard its security and stability. Iran’s position on negotiations remained tied to its seven conditions, with an Iranian security official saying Tehran would not negotiate with Washington until practical steps are taken to meet those conditions. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said, “We can negotiate with dignity and end the matter with dignity,” while also stressing that “Iran will not submit to force or bullying.” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Ismail Baghaei said, “Iran controls the Hormuz Strait and ships that travel on ‘unsafe’ routes,” and he added that ships that want to pass must coordinate with Iranian authorities. Baghaei also said the two-day plan presented by Iran was proof of goodwill, and he argued that “All that America has agreed upon in the Islamabad meeting is in this plan.” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said negotiations with Iran have made only limited progress and described Iran’s demands as “unacceptable,” and at times “inflammatory, ridiculous, and utterly unrealistic.” The crisis around the Strait of Hormuz continued alongside diplomacy, as the IRGC Navy announced the stoppage of two oil tankers after colliding with mines while crossing what it described as a prohibited path in the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC Navy said the first tanker struck a sea mine, causing an explosion, and it said both tankers had shut down all navigation systems and remain on fire off the southern shores of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran International reported that Trump said it was “highly unlikely” that another attack would be necessary if Iran agreed to a strong deal, while also warning that the United States had identified potential infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges that he said could be destroyed within an hour if fighting resumed. Iran International also said Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reiterated Tehran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if its conditions were met, including an end to hostilities on all fronts. Mehr News Agency said the U.S. president would meet Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani behind closed doors at the White House later today, with an unnamed U.S. official telling Reuters that Vice President JD Vance was also scheduled to hold talks. sources.title: Pakistan, Qatar discuss regional stability as mediators push to revive US-Iran talks - Arab News PK
passages: ISLAMABAD: Pakistan and Qatar discussed regional peace and stability on Monday after their interior ministers met in Doha, as mediators from the two countries sought to bring the United States and Iran back to negotiations following a pause in hostilities.

Two regional officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the talks, told the Associated Press that mediators led by Qatar and Pakistan were trying to revive the Islamabad MoU to help the two sides reach the end of the war.

Pakistan’s Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and his Qatari counterpart Sheikh Khalifa bin Hamad bin Khalifa Al-Thani also focused on bilateral cooperation during the meeting, according to an official statement circulated in Islamabad.

The 14-point Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was prepared after months of efforts, allowing both the US and Iran a 60-day period to hold negotiations over a range of outstanding issues and reach a final settlement to the conflict.
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that Iran had sought further discussions after weeks of military exchanges.

coreStoryFacts.text: Iran has called on the United States to accept its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, as diplomatic efforts to end the eight-month West Asia war gather pace and US President Donald Trump signals progress towards a possible agreement.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has threatened further strikes against Iran, although it remains uncertain whether Trump would support another military campaign following his party's electoral setback.
"The only solution is to adopt a language of respect, engage in diplomacy, and address Iran's demands and conditions," Araghchi told Iranian state news agency IRNA.
Trump sees progress as Qatar and Pakistan push negotiations Trump struck a more optimistic note on Monday after meeting Qatar's prime minister at the White House.

While insisting that the US remained "locked and loaded", Trump added that further strikes were now "quite unlikely", partly because key Gulf allies preferred the current situation to renewed fighting.
Defence Minister Israel Katz said the military mission against Iran remained incomplete and warned Hezbollah against resuming hostilities.
The war began in late February with US-Israeli strikes that killed Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The change in Washington's approach comes after Trump's Republican Party suffered a setback in last week's midterm elections, with the war emerging as one of the issues weighing on the administration.
United Arab Emirates presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said Abu Dhabi hoped diplomatic efforts would produce lasting peace and stability.

Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif travelled to Doha on Thursday for talks with Qatar’s leadership as momentum builds for a possible new round of negotiations between the US and Iran to end the ongoing war.
Pakistan’s mediation effort is unfolding across several channels.
In Doha, Sharif held talks that also touched on regional coordination, with Qatar remaining a key, if cautious, player in mediation efforts.

US President Donald Trump suggested that talks could take place within days, potentially in Pakistan, while UN Secretary-General António Guterres said it is “highly probable” that discussions will restart.
Doha-led mediation reports positive reactions from both the United States and Iran.
Qatar says mediation ongoing and tireless efforts to end the crisis.

Pakistan’s Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and his Qatari counterpart Sheikh Khalifa bin Hamad bin Khalifa Al-Thani also focused on bilateral cooperation during the meeting, according to an official statement circulated in Islamabad.

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that Iran had sought further discussions after weeks of military exchanges.

Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif travelled to Doha on Thursday for talks with Qatar’s leadership as momentum builds for a possible new round of negotiations between the US and Iran to end the ongoing war. The meeting comes as the fragile ceasefire continues to hold and diplomatic contacts between Washington and Tehran show signs of picking up again. US President Donald Trump suggested that talks could take place within days, potentially in Pakistan, while UN Secretary-General António Guterres said it is “highly probable” that discussions will restart. Sharif’s visit to Qatar follows a stop in Saudi Arabia and comes ahead of meetings in Turkey, as Islamabad pushes on with its mediation efforts to secure a second round of talks between the two sides. Pakistan’s mediation effort is unfolding across several channels. In parallel with Sharif’s visit, the country’s army chief Asim Munir travelled to Tehran for talks officials described as part of ongoing efforts to sustain dialogue. Munir met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, with both sides stressing the need to avoid further escalation. Islamabad has already hosted direct talks between US and Iranian officials, which ended without an agreement, and is now seeking to secure a second round of negotiations before the current ceasefire expires, in what officials see as a narrowing window for diplomacy. In Doha, Sharif held talks that also touched on regional coordination, with Qatar remaining a key, if cautious, player in mediation efforts. During the meeting, Qatar’s Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and Sharif discussed de-escalation, with Doha signalling support for Pakistan’s role in sustaining dialogue between Washington and Tehran. The talks also pointed to growing concern among Gulf states over energy flows and maritime security. The discussions follow a call between Emir Al Thani and Trump on the impact of the conflict on global energy markets and supply chains. Earlier in the tour, Sharif met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Jeddah, and is also due to attend the Antalya Diplomacy Forum in Turkey, where he is expected to meet Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. The push for talks comes as pressure on Tehran continues, including a US naval blockade of Iranian ports. Both sides have signalled that communication channels remain open, raising the prospect that talks could resume even as key differences remain unresolved.

The Ann Francis vessel was caught in a ferocious storm and blown off course on 28 December 1583 while returning from Spain . Francis Shaxton of Kings Lynn, the ship’s owner, had sent a valuable cargo of grain to Spain and had now lost both ship and payment. The ship was wrecked on Margam beach off the coast of Wales and the majority of its incredible hoard was uncovered by metal detectorist Peter Hughes over a 21-year period of 21 years. Among the treasures was a 400-year-old brass combination lock that is believed to have once secured a “small chest containing items of significant value”. Found near a collection of Spanish silver coins and close to two coin weights recovered from the wreck site, the lock may have protected these objects or secured a chest containing valuable items that have not survived, such as documents or textiles. Researchers from Amgueddfa Cymru and Cardiff University used CT scanning technology to examine the lock's internal mechanism without causing any damage. These scans allowed researchers to identify the correct letter combination – ANCE – and successfully unlock the historic artefact. “By creating a detailed 3D image of the internal mechanism, I could see how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination,” said Dr David Williams, a research associate based at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility at Cardiff University's School of Engineering. “We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us.” Mr Hughs said he was “immediately astonied” by the workmanship and the condition of the lock when he found it. “When I moved the ring dials of the combination they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands and I was left in disbelief,” he said. “I also remember being left excited at the prospect of finding wonderful things from the treasure chest it once locked.” The combination lock, alongside a number of artefacts from the Ann Francis hoard, is currently on display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea until September 2027.

extraction.body: Experts have used cutting-edge technology to open a centuries-old combination lock from one of the most “remarkable” shipwrecks found in the UK . The Ann Francis vessel was caught in a ferocious storm and blown off course on 28 December 1583 while returning from Spain . Francis Shaxton of Kings Lynn, the ship’s owner, had sent a valuable cargo of grain to Spain and had now lost both ship and payment. The ship was wrecked on Margam beach off the coast of Wales and the majority of its incredible hoard was uncovered by metal detectorist Peter Hughes over a 21-year period of 21 years. Among the treasures was a 400-year-old brass combination lock that is believed to have once secured a “small chest containing items of significant value”. Found near a collection of Spanish silver coins and close to two coin weights recovered from the wreck site, the lock may have protected these objects or secured a chest containing valuable items that have not survived, such as documents or textiles. Researchers from Amgueddfa Cymru and Cardiff University used CT scanning technology to examine the lock's internal mechanism without causing any damage. These scans allowed researchers to identify the correct letter combination – ANCE – and successfully unlock the historic artefact. “By creating a detailed 3D image of the internal mechanism, I could see how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination,” said Dr David Williams, a research associate based at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility at Cardiff University's School of Engineering. “We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us.” Mr Hughs said he was “immediately astonied” by the workmanship and the condition of the lock when he found it. “When I moved the ring dials of the combination they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands and I was left in disbelief,” he said. “I also remember being left excited at the prospect of finding wonderful things from the treasure chest it once locked.” The combination lock, alongside a number of artefacts from the Ann Francis hoard, is currently on display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea until September 2027.

Scientists have used cutting-edge technology to crack the four-letter code of a brass combination lock from that lay buried on a beach in Wales for more than four centuries. The 16th-century padlock, recovered from the wreckage of the Ann Francis , had remained firmly sealed since the vessel was wrecked off the South Wales coast in 1583. Now, a collaborative team from Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales and Cardiff University has used modern-day technology to reveal the historic combination that once secured the cargo: ANCE. Researchers believe the intricate device guarded a captain's chest containing Spanish silver, high-value textiles, or sensitive maritime correspondence before the ship ran aground in the Bristol Channel. The breakthrough comes after museum conservators enlisted engineers at Cardiff University's School of Engineering to use micro-computed tomography (CT), a scanning technique normally used to examine bones and other body tissues. The scans produced 3D images of the lock, which were then used to crack the code. Dr David Williams, a research associate at Cardiff University's Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility, explained: “By creating a detailed 3D image of the internal mechanism, I could see how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination.” He added: “We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us.” After waiting for the museum team to test the code, Dr Williams described receiving confirmation that they had done so was “incredibly satisfying”. “It's not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery.” The Ann Francis was returning from a trading voyage to Spain when it was engulfed by a ferocious storm on the evening of 28 December 1583. Driven off course by high winds, the ship grounded and broke apart on Margam Beach, near Port Talbot . While Elizabethan combination locks have been recovered in Britain before, experts described this example as uniquely significant because it can be tied directly to a securely dated shipwreck. The padlock was discovered near a stash of Spanish silver coins and a pair of brass coin-checking weights. Alastair Willis, Senior Curator for Numismatics and the Welsh Economy at Amgueddfa Cymru, said: “Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalising mystery to solve. “Of course, now we’ve solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner.” The padlock forms part of the wider Ann Francis treasure hoard, which was recovered over a 21-year period between 1996 and 2017 by metal detectorist Peter Hughes. The cracked padlock is now on public display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea alongside other recovered treasures, including rare gold coins from the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, and an Elizabethan boatswain's whistle.

extraction.body: The U.S.-Iran ceasefire is on the verge of collapse, and with it any prospect of restoring normal traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Even if the agreement holds, transit fees, sea mines, billions in infrastructure damage, and deep regional mistrust pose significant obstacles to a genuine recovery. The fragile U.S.-Iran cease-fire appeared to be in danger on Wednesday as the two sides exchanged fresh strikes and President Donald Trump threatened to end the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). U.S. forces attacked targets in Iran and the White House reimposed sanctions on Iranian oil sales on Tuesday. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responded by firing at U.S. military sites in Bahrain and Kuwait. “To me, I think it’s over,” Trump said about the agreement during the NATO summit in Ankara on Wednesday. He later claimed that further strikes were imminent. “We hit them [Iran] very hard last night,” he told reporters, “and we’re going to hit them hard again tonight.” The collapse of the sixty-day MOU—signed just over three weeks ago to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and lay the groundwork for a permanent end to the war—would deal a severe blow to efforts to restore normal shipping through the waterway. But reopening the strait, through which roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) transits, is just the first step. Several other formidable roadblocks—continued aggression between the United States and Iran, transit fees, sea mines, infrastructure damage, and deep mistrust in the region—stand between the strait’s nominal reopening and a genuine recovery of global energy markets after one hundred days of disruption. Below, five CFR experts examine the MOU and the obstacles that remain for the Strait of Hormuz—even if the agreement ultimately holds. Edward Fishman is a leading authority on economic statecraft and the author of Chokepoints: American Power in the Age of Economic Warfare . In the opening weeks of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, the White House’s aims shifted by the day, from regime change to denuclearization to demilitarization. But by the time President Donald Trump signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to end the war on June 17, his overriding objective was narrower and more urgent: reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s monthslong closure of the waterway had rapidly depleted oil stockpiles around the world, and analysts warned of a sharp spike in prices unless traffic through the strait resumed. The MOU is thus best understood less as a deal that addresses Iran’s nuclear ambitions or military capabilities than as a Hormuz deal: the United States agreed to provide Iran with sanctions relief in exchange for Iran allowing commercial vessels safe passage through the strait. Yet Iran has no intention of restoring the Strait of Hormuz to the status quo ante, when it functioned as a free and open international waterway. The MOU stipulates that Iran will allow ships to pass “with no charge for 60 days only ” (emphasis added) and that it will work with Oman to “define the future administration and maritime services in the Strait of Hormuz.” Tehran has seized on this language to claim an ongoing role in regulating traffic through the strait. It has already sought to enforce that claim, striking multiple commercial vessels with drones and missiles in recent weeks when they attempted to transit without complying with Iranian protocols. These strikes have been so disruptive that the Trump administration reinstated sanctions on Iran’s oil sales on Tuesday. Controlling Hormuz offers Iran a deterrent and a source of revenue. By closing the strait, Tehran has demonstrated it can ward off the world’s most powerful military. By monetizing it, Iranian officials believe they could generate up to $40 billion a year — roughly the same amount as the country’s annual oil export revenues in recent years. Those are overwhelming incentives to retain control. It’s little wonder that, since the MOU was signed, Iran has moved quickly to institutionalize that control, working with Oman on arrangements for the strait’s future administration. Whether the eventual mechanism comes in the form of a service fee, an insurance requirement, or a charge for maritime safety, Tehran clearly intends to profit. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has rightly rejected this outcome, warning that it would set a dangerous precedent. The best strategy for the United States could be patience, avoiding a return to all-out war and buying time to rally the world to oppose Iran’s claims and invest in assets that weaken Hormuz as a chokepoint. Oil prices have plummeted to near prewar levels, and as commercial stockpiles are replenished, Iran’s leverage will diminish. If Tehran pushes the envelope too far, continually striking commercial vessels and demanding exorbitant fees, it will only accelerate other countries’ efforts to reduce their reliance on the strait by building bypass pipelines, increasing storage capacity and stockpiles, and adopting alternative energy sources. Max Boot is a historian, bestselling author, and foreign policy analyst. His latest book, a biography of Ronald Reagan titled Reagan: His Life and Legend , is his third New York Times bestseller. Why did President Donald Trump agree to such a one-sided MOU with Iran —one that provides tens of billions, and possibly hundreds, of billions of dollars in benefits to Iran without any verifiable limitations on Iran’s nuclear program? In essence, Trump concluded there was no easy, low-cost military option to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway through which 20 percent of the world’s oil flows. As the president said , “If we didn’t do this deal, we could have dropped more bombs for another three weeks, two weeks, four weeks, two years,” but then “you would never have the Hormuz Strait open.” Indeed, since the MOU was signed in mid-June, there have been several instances of Iran attacking merchant ships and U.S. forces responding by bombing Iranian forces. Safe passage through the strait remains tenuous and subject to interruption at Tehran’s whim. How can this be, when the United States assembled such a formidable naval armada just outside the strait? The answer is that this littoral-combat mission—escorting merchant ships safely through a waterway that is only twenty-one miles wide at its narrowest point—negates many of the U.S. Navy’s advantages in blue-water warfare. The collapse of the sixty-day MOU—signed just over three weeks ago to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and lay the groundwork for a permanent end to the war—would deal a severe blow to efforts to restore normal shipping through the waterway. But reopening the strait, through which roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) transits, is just the first step. Several other formidable roadblocks—continued aggression between the United States and Iran, transit fees, sea mines, infrastructure damage, and deep mistrust in the region—stand between the strait’s nominal reopening and a genuine recovery of global energy markets after one hundred days of disruption.
Below, five CFR experts examine the MOU and the obstacles that remain for the Strait of Hormuz—even if the agreement ultimately holds.
Edward Fishman is a leading authority on economic statecraft and the author of Chokepoints: American Power in the Age of Economic Warfare .

Iran’s monthslong closure of the waterway had rapidly depleted oil stockpiles around the world, and analysts warned of a sharp spike in prices unless traffic through the strait resumed. Those are overwhelming incentives to retain control. Whether the eventual mechanism comes in the form of a service fee, an insurance requirement, or a charge for maritime safety, Tehran clearly intends to profit.

Oil prices have plummeted to near prewar levels, and as commercial stockpiles are replenished, Iran’s leverage will diminish. extraction.body: The United States and Iran began face-to-face negotiations Saturday in Pakistan, days after a fragile, two-week ceasefire was announced. The war that has killed thousands of people and shaken global markets entered its seventh week . Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Saturday, Trump claimed military victory against Iran and downplayed the importance of ongoing ceasefire negotiations involving Vice President JD Vance because “regardless what happens we win.” “Let’s see what happens – maybe they make a deal maybe they don’t,” the president said. “It doesn’t matter. From the standpoint of America, we win.” Trump acknowledged “very deep negotiations” with Iran. But he also said the U.S. military was searching for mines in the Strait of Hormuz, which still remained effectively closed to most freighters carrying oil and natural gas out of the Persian Gulf. The country’s Ministry of Transport announced Saturday the full resumption of maritime navigation activities effective Sunday from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., extending the decision to “all categories of marine vessels and transport modes.” It was not immediately clear whether the decision meant that Qatari vessels would be allowed to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which remained effectively closed as of Saturday. A spokesperson for Iran’s joint military command denied an earlier claim by the U.S. that two Navy destroyers transited the waterway, adding that “initiative over the passage of any vessel rests with the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran”, according to Iran’s state media. The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow mouth of the Persian Gulf through which 20% of all oil and natural gas traded once passed, is expected to be one of the most challenging points of negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, currently taking place in the Pakistani capital of Islamabad. Ifat Kalderon, whose cousin Ofer Kalderon was held hostage by Hamas in Gaza and released last year, told the Associated Press she came to the protest to call for Israel to put an end to its wars “in Iran, in Lebanon and in Gaza.” She said the war with Iran had achieved no positive results. “The reality is the same as before, perhaps even worse. We need to translate everything into agreements, we can’t keep living constantly in war.” As of 10:21 p.m. local time in Islamabad, the trilateral in-person talks were ongoing, a senior White House official told reporters traveling with Vice President JD Vance. The destroyers are part of a broader mission to ensure the strait is fully clear of sea mines previously laid by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, CENTCOM stated. Iran’s state media said earlier on Saturday that it had forced a U.S. military ship that was attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz to turn around. The strait has been effectively closed to most oil and gas freighters since the U.S. and Israel began to strike Israel on Feb. 28. Cease-fire talks are now underway in Pakistan. Leo presided over an evening prayer service in St. Peter’s Basilica on the same day the United States and Iran began face-to-face negotiations in Pakistan and as a fragile ceasefire held. History’s first U.S.-born pope didn’t mention the United States or President Donald Trump in his prayer, which was planned before the talks were announced. But Leo’s tone and message appeared directed at Trump and U.S. officials, who have boasted of U.S. military superiority and justified the war in religious terms. “Enough of the idolatry of self and money!” Leo demanded. “Enough of the display of power! Enough of war!” U.S. and Iranian officials resumed a second round of talks Saturday night in Islamabad after a break, with both sides backed by technical experts, two Pakistani officials said. They added that Pakistan’s top political and military leadership is encouraging both sides to resolve their differences to ensure durable peace in the region, and the talks were progressing. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. Trump confirmed in a phone interview with NewsNation that talks among the U.S., Iran and Pakistan had begun, though he does not know how successful they could be. When asked how negotiations would go, Trump said: “I have no idea.” Since the Islamic Revolution in 1979, the highest-level direct contact had been when President Barack Obama, a Democrat, in September 2013 called newly elected Iranian President Hassan Rouhani to discuss Iran’s nuclear program. It’s a high-stakes political task for Vance, who has been a reluctant defender of the U.S. war with Iran, and has little previous diplomatic experience. extraction.body: President Donald Trump’s talks with Qatar’s prime minister come amid a renewed diplomatic push to end the Iran war, but securing terms both Washington and Tehran can present as a victory remains a central obstacle, analysts told Iran International. Trump and Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani met behind closed doors in the Oval Office on Monday, and Axios reported that their discussions focused on Iran. The Qatari prime minister also met Vice President JD Vance earlier in the day. An Iranian official told Al-Monitor on Friday that the country’s nuclear program was “under discussion” with mediators. Tehran has said negotiations depend on Washington meeting its demands, including sanctions relief and the release of billions of dollars in frozen assets. Trump needs a nuclear achievement to justify the war, not just the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, said Aaron David Miller, a former US Middle East negotiator now at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “It’s the nuclear issue. He needs a win to justify this war,” Miller told Iran International. Danny Citrinowicz, a former head of the Iran branch of Israeli military intelligence and now a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv, said an interest in ending the war should not be mistaken for an agreement in sight. “I believe both sides genuinely want to find a way to end this war, but that does not mean they are close to an agreement,” he told Iran International. Iran wants Washington to meet its conditions on Hormuz, the naval blockade, oil exports and other economic restrictions before nuclear talks begin. Washington wants movement on the nuclear issue much earlier, he said. “The problem is not simply what each side wants, but who moves first.” A breakthrough was possible, Citrinowicz said, if Washington accepted a different sequence of reciprocal steps. “Without meaningful American flexibility, however, I see little reason to expect Iran to abandon its red lines.” Miller criticized the interim memorandum of understanding reached in June, which was meant to open the way to nuclear talks but collapsed soon afterward. It committed Washington to a sequence that favored Iran, he said, calling it “one of the worst negotiated documents in the history of US diplomacy.” Even if negotiators settle the order of steps, both governments would have to defend the concessions at home as achievements. Trump could claim victory by reopening Hormuz, lowering energy prices, ending the fighting and securing an Iranian commitment not to build nuclear weapons, Citrinowicz said. Tehran would need an outcome it could present as a success too. “After surviving months of attacks, the Iranian leadership is not going to accept an agreement that looks like surrender,” he said. Iran could reopen Hormuz, stop attacks on shipping and regional infrastructure, return to nuclear talks and possibly accept tighter international monitoring, he said. In return it would expect real steps on sanctions, oil exports, frozen assets and guarantees against further attacks. Miller doubted Trump’s wish to end the war would outweigh his fear of looking beaten. “I think he’d want to be done with this, but I don’t know if he’s prepared to spend the next three years being called a loser,” he said. Eric Mandel, founder of the Middle East Political Information Network, said a deal could let Trump declare victory while leaving the nuclear dispute open. “The president would like to have a diplomatic solution. The president is looking for victories. He may claim victories where there aren’t,” Mandel told Iran International. Tehran was drawing out the talks to wait Trump out, Mandel said, and economic relief in exchange for promises of future nuclear concessions could throw the Islamic Republic a lifeline without securing lasting limits. Turkey’s intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin, said Qatar would host Vance and Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, next week, the Turkish newspaper Türkiye reported. The Tasnim news agency, which is affiliated with the Revolutionary Guards, then quoted a senior Iranian security official as denying any meeting was planned and saying Washington must first act on Iran’s seven conditions. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Tuesday there were no plans for Rezaei to meet Vance. The war, he said, would end neither through military action nor through more sanctions. “The only way to end it is diplomacy and acceptance of the Islamic Republic’s conditions.” Citrinowicz said Rezaei should not be expected to break with the Islamic Republic’s established positions. “He is deeply rooted in the Iranian political and security establishment,” he said. “He is not someone who can simply be persuaded to abandon the regime’s fundamental positions in exchange for an American offer.” The decisive question, Citrinowicz said, is whether Vance has Trump’s authority to offer something substantially different. “A failed meeting could be more dangerous than no meeting at all,” he said. Trump might conclude that diplomacy had run its course and order more strikes to force concessions. Continued economic pressure, indirect talks and a limited interim deal would remain options, he said, but failure to close the gaps could raise the risk of a return to war. His warning comes as Washington continues to combine diplomatic signals with military and economic pressure. On the eve of the midterms, Trump said a deal with Iran “could happen,” and Tehran has since conveyed proposals through Qatari mediators. Meanwhile, the US naval blockade and sanctions remain in place. Reports of preparations for a larger US offensive and the expected arrival of an aircraft carrier group in the region have added to uncertainty. Democrats' sweeping midterm gains have weakened Donald Trump at home. But do they amount to the strategic victory that some in Tehran are claiming? “You lost the war and the election,” Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei declared on X, mocking what he portrayed as turmoil within the Trump administration and questioning who in Washington should receive Tehran's warning against another war. “So who exactly in Washington do we need to get this message across to?” he asked. Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who also serves as Qatar's foreign minister, met Vice President JD Vance separately before his talks with Trump, following a visit to Tehran last week. The Qatari leader sought to persuade Trump to give diplomacy more time, Axios reported, citing sources familiar with the mediation. Vance has been personally involved in indirect negotiations with Iran over the past two weeks, speaking with Al Thani almost daily. Qatar has been mediating a proposed agreement under which Washington would ease its naval blockade and release frozen Iranian funds, while Tehran would allow international nuclear inspections and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Speaking at “The Search for a New Regional Social Contract in the Middle East” conference in Ankara, Kalin said Turkey and other regional mediators were working on a seven-point agreement, with the main disagreement concerning which side should act first. The proposed plan envisages lifting sanctions against Iran and releasing frozen Iranian assets. In return, Tehran would commit not to develop nuclear weapons, begin negotiations with the International Atomic Energy Agency and lift its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, according to Türkiye newspaper. Kalin urged Tehran to show greater flexibility and warned that the next few days could be decisive.

Even if the agreement holds, transit fees, sea mines, billions in infrastructure damage, and deep regional mistrust pose significant obstacles to a genuine recovery. The fragile U.S.-Iran cease-fire appeared to be in danger on Wednesday as the two sides exchanged fresh strikes and President Donald Trump threatened to end the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). U.S. forces attacked targets in Iran and the White House reimposed sanctions on Iranian oil sales on Tuesday. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responded by firing at U.S. military sites in Bahrain and Kuwait. “To me, I think it’s over,” Trump said about the agreement during the NATO summit in Ankara on Wednesday. He later claimed that further strikes were imminent. “We hit them [Iran] very hard last night,” he told reporters, “and we’re going to hit them hard again tonight.” The collapse of the sixty-day MOU—signed just over three weeks ago to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and lay the groundwork for a permanent end to the war—would deal a severe blow to efforts to restore normal shipping through the waterway. But reopening the strait, through which roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) transits, is just the first step. Several other formidable roadblocks—continued aggression between the United States and Iran, transit fees, sea mines, infrastructure damage, and deep mistrust in the region—stand between the strait’s nominal reopening and a genuine recovery of global energy markets after one hundred days of disruption. Below, five CFR experts examine the MOU and the obstacles that remain for the Strait of Hormuz—even if the agreement ultimately holds. Edward Fishman is a leading authority on economic statecraft and the author of Chokepoints: American Power in the Age of Economic Warfare . In the opening weeks of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, the White House’s aims shifted by the day, from regime change to denuclearization to demilitarization. But by the time President Donald Trump signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to end the war on June 17, his overriding objective was narrower and more urgent: reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s monthslong closure of the waterway had rapidly depleted oil stockpiles around the world, and analysts warned of a sharp spike in prices unless traffic through the strait resumed. The MOU is thus best understood less as a deal that addresses Iran’s nuclear ambitions or military capabilities than as a Hormuz deal: the United States agreed to provide Iran with sanctions relief in exchange for Iran allowing commercial vessels safe passage through the strait. Yet Iran has no intention of restoring the Strait of Hormuz to the status quo ante, when it functioned as a free and open international waterway. The MOU stipulates that Iran will allow ships to pass “with no charge for 60 days only ” (emphasis added) and that it will work with Oman to “define the future administration and maritime services in the Strait of Hormuz.” Tehran has seized on this language to claim an ongoing role in regulating traffic through the strait. It has already sought to enforce that claim, striking multiple commercial vessels with drones and missiles in recent weeks when they attempted to transit without complying with Iranian protocols. These strikes have been so disruptive that the Trump administration reinstated sanctions on Iran’s oil sales on Tuesday. Controlling Hormuz offers Iran a deterrent and a source of revenue. By closing the strait, Tehran has demonstrated it can ward off the world’s most powerful military. By monetizing it, Iranian officials believe they could generate up to $40 billion a year — roughly the same amount as the country’s annual oil export revenues in recent years. Those are overwhelming incentives to retain control. It’s little wonder that, since the MOU was signed, Iran has moved quickly to institutionalize that control, working with Oman on arrangements for the strait’s future administration. Whether the eventual mechanism comes in the form of a service fee, an insurance requirement, or a charge for maritime safety, Tehran clearly intends to profit. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has rightly rejected this outcome, warning that it would set a dangerous precedent. The best strategy for the United States could be patience, avoiding a return to all-out war and buying time to rally the world to oppose Iran’s claims and invest in assets that weaken Hormuz as a chokepoint. Oil prices have plummeted to near prewar levels, and as commercial stockpiles are replenished, Iran’s leverage will diminish. If Tehran pushes the envelope too far, continually striking commercial vessels and demanding exorbitant fees, it will only accelerate other countries’ efforts to reduce their reliance on the strait by building bypass pipelines, increasing storage capacity and stockpiles, and adopting alternative energy sources. Max Boot is a historian, bestselling author, and foreign policy analyst. His latest book, a biography of Ronald Reagan titled Reagan: His Life and Legend , is his third New York Times bestseller. Why did President Donald Trump agree to such a one-sided MOU with Iran —one that provides tens of billions, and possibly hundreds, of billions of dollars in benefits to Iran without any verifiable limitations on Iran’s nuclear program? In essence, Trump concluded there was no easy, low-cost military option to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway through which 20 percent of the world’s oil flows. As the president said , “If we didn’t do this deal, we could have dropped more bombs for another three weeks, two weeks, four weeks, two years,” but then “you would never have the Hormuz Strait open.” Indeed, since the MOU was signed in mid-June, there have been several instances of Iran attacking merchant ships and U.S. forces responding by bombing Iranian forces. Safe passage through the strait remains tenuous and subject to interruption at Tehran’s whim. How can this be, when the United States assembled such a formidable naval armada just outside the strait? The answer is that this littoral-combat mission—escorting merchant ships safely through a waterway that is only twenty-one miles wide at its narrowest point—negates many of the U.S. Navy’s advantages in blue-water warfare. Even such an ambitious operation, which would severely tax a navy with fewer than three hundred deployable warships, would not necessarily be successful, because all it would take would be a single Iranian drone striking a single merchant ship for many shipowners to shy away from the risk of sending ships through the strait. In sum, the lack of good military options for reopening the strait forced Trump to rely on diplomacy—and to pay what is in essence a massive bribe to Iran to let merchant traffic flow. But that may offer only a temporary respite—if ships even truly begin to trust the safety of the waterway—because the MOU only commits Iran to allowing traffic without tolls for sixty days. After that Iran could try to impose “user fees” (tolls by another name), and Trump will have to decide whether to accept Iranian interference with freedom of navigation. Optimistic assessments envision that the majority (but not all) of this supply could return to global markets within a few months, even if the U.S.-Iran war could be far from over. The more pessimistic assessments envision that it will be nearly impossible to avoid an uneven regional recovery marred by periodic setbacks, contributing to a weak market case for a full recovery on any timeline. Elisa Ewers’s expertise covers the Middle East and North Africa, security cooperation, Congress, and U.S. national security decision-making. The $58 billion in damages to oil facilities in the Gulf can be repaired and expanded with time and resources. Trust and confidence are harder to rebuild. The region’s recovery from the U.S.-Iran war will be a test between its instincts towards internal competition and mistrust and its need for cooperation to protect the Gulf states’ shared strategic and economic interests. If Trump’s Iran deal holds, the timelines for recovery will vary from country to country. On the short end, some estimates set the clock at six months—others on the longer end set it at several years. Gulf states will continue to mobilize capital quickly , deploying nearly 40 percent of the world’s sovereign wealth to aid in their recovery and hardening, especially in the energy sectors. But the region’s existing pipelines—or even expanded versions—do not facilitate the movement of petroleum products that are vital to the global economy. The building of the infrastructure for those products will require much. In many of these endeavors, cooperation between several Gulf states and neighboring countries could provide more options and better outcomes. Saudi Arabia’s largest undertaking, arguably, is expanding the lines and port terminals associated with its east-west Petroline to allow more product to move to the Red Sea. Still, it might also consider options that expand its overland capability by collaborating with neighbors—using Iraq and Turkey, and at some point even Syria—to expand access to the eastern Mediterranean. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) similarly will need to expand its Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline, which goes west-to-east, and harden its ability to move its product out through the port of Fujairah. It has already begun addressing the damage caused to some of its refineries, ports, and other infrastructure. The UAE, too, could see some benefit by deepening its cooperation with neighbors, whether by tapping into the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor to connect infrastructure across ground, pipelines, and fiber-optic cables. Other states have fewer options. Notably, it will take at least a year , likely longer, for Qatar to repair the damage to its Ras Laffan LNG complex, resulting in a tight market for 5 percent of the world’s natural gas and 20 percent of its LNG supply. Bahrain and Kuwait, as well as Iraq, will have fewer resources and paths to circumvent their reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, but they will use what is available to them. They will likely now have to overcome the political and practical challenges that have plagued the Kirkuk-Ceyhan Oil Pipeline , a potential route for circumventing the Strait for Iraqi oil—and, more surprisingly given the need for new overland infrastructure, perhaps a future option for Kuwaiti oil. Here too, expansion and hardening will be necessary to accommodate flows from the south. Bahrain will need to partner with both Saudi Arabia and UAE to find alternative routes for its products as well. Recovery will require persistent resources and commitment. However, the resulting integrated rail, pipelines, and other infrastructure that run through numerous states to the Red Sea and the Eastern Mediterranean could prove to be a potentially constructive outcome from the war. Just as defense against Iranian attacks proved to be a collaborative effort among Gulf partners, so too could be recovery. It just requires breaking from deep-seated instincts and building political will to do it. Weeks before the U.S. and Iran agreed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the World Food Program issued a blunt warning: even if the conflict were resolved, the hunger fallout would last for months. Disruptions to humanitarian supply chains, energy, and fertilizer markets would not sort themselves out overnight. New numbers confirm the warning. Forty-five million additional people are now facing acute food insecurity because of the war’s cascading effect . This includes surging food and fuel prices in humanitarian settings already reckoning with back-to-back years of donor cuts. Families are now increasingly forced to share one meal across multiple mouths—if there is a meal to share at all. Sudan, South Sudan, and Somalia are at risk of famine in the coming months. The worst outcomes can still be avoided if the United States and Iran prioritize a humanitarian passageway through the strait. To do this, the two countries will have to allow the United Nations to act on the following. First, the UN should be permitted to activate its existing blueprint to prioritize shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to countries most at risk. A UN-run Task Force —led by the UN Office for Project Services, in coordination with UN Trade and Development, the International Maritime Organization (IMO), and the International Chamber of Commerce—developed a technical mechanism to do this back in late March. The objective : move fertilizers, urea, sulphur, and ammonia through the Strait to countries facing humanitarian crisis, particularly those in the northern hemisphere in the middle of planting season. The IMO has a separate role to play: evacuate more than 11,000 stranded seafarers in the Persian Gulf. Working with the Sultanate of Oman, the IMO has established a temporary maritime corridor with two separate routes and a phased departure system to mitigate collision risks. The operation involves coordination with the United States, Iran, and the maritime industry. On June 25, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps attacked a Singapore-flagged ship using an IMO route. Three additional ships were struck by Iran on July 7 in Oman’s territorial waters, according to a U.S. official, exposing the limits of the United Nations’ ability to ensure safe passage. Finally, the UN Secretary-General should offer a unified vision for managing this crisis. The WFP and FAO deserve enormous credit for their timely forecasting, but the broader UN system has fallen short. Historically , the UN performs best when it integrates advocacy, resource mobilization, operations, and political will into a single campaign. A Member State conference should be convened with a single mandate: ensure humanitarian needs are prioritized as maritime traffic resumes. extraction.body: President Donald Trump’s talks with Qatar’s prime minister come amid a renewed diplomatic push to end the Iran war, but securing terms both Washington and Tehran can present as a victory remains a central obstacle, analysts told Iran International. Trump and Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani met behind closed doors in the Oval Office on Monday, and Axios reported that their discussions focused on Iran. The Qatari prime minister also met Vice President JD Vance earlier in the day. An Iranian official told Al-Monitor on Friday that the country’s nuclear program was “under discussion” with mediators. Tehran has said negotiations depend on Washington meeting its demands, including sanctions relief and the release of billions of dollars in frozen assets. Trump needs a nuclear achievement to justify the war, not just the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, said Aaron David Miller, a former US Middle East negotiator now at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “It’s the nuclear issue. He needs a win to justify this war,” Miller told Iran International. Danny Citrinowicz, a former head of the Iran branch of Israeli military intelligence and now a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv, said an interest in ending the war should not be mistaken for an agreement in sight. “I believe both sides genuinely want to find a way to end this war, but that does not mean they are close to an agreement,” he told Iran International. Iran wants Washington to meet its conditions on Hormuz, the naval blockade, oil exports and other economic restrictions before nuclear talks begin. Washington wants movement on the nuclear issue much earlier, he said. “The problem is not simply what each side wants, but who moves first.” A breakthrough was possible, Citrinowicz said, if Washington accepted a different sequence of reciprocal steps. “Without meaningful American flexibility, however, I see little reason to expect Iran to abandon its red lines.” Miller criticized the interim memorandum of understanding reached in June, which was meant to open the way to nuclear talks but collapsed soon afterward. It committed Washington to a sequence that favored Iran, he said, calling it “one of the worst negotiated documents in the history of US diplomacy.” Even if negotiators settle the order of steps, both governments would have to defend the concessions at home as achievements. Trump could claim victory by reopening Hormuz, lowering energy prices, ending the fighting and securing an Iranian commitment not to build nuclear weapons, Citrinowicz said. Tehran would need an outcome it could present as a success too. “After surviving months of attacks, the Iranian leadership is not going to accept an agreement that looks like surrender,” he said. Iran could reopen Hormuz, stop attacks on shipping and regional infrastructure, return to nuclear talks and possibly accept tighter international monitoring, he said. In return it would expect real steps on sanctions, oil exports, frozen assets and guarantees against further attacks. Miller doubted Trump’s wish to end the war would outweigh his fear of looking beaten. “I think he’d want to be done with this, but I don’t know if he’s prepared to spend the next three years being called a loser,” he said. Eric Mandel, founder of the Middle East Political Information Network, said a deal could let Trump declare victory while leaving the nuclear dispute open. “The president would like to have a diplomatic solution. The president is looking for victories. He may claim victories where there aren’t,” Mandel told Iran International. Tehran was drawing out the talks to wait Trump out, Mandel said, and economic relief in exchange for promises of future nuclear concessions could throw the Islamic Republic a lifeline without securing lasting limits. Turkey’s intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin, said Qatar would host Vance and Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, next week, the Turkish newspaper Türkiye reported. The Tasnim news agency, which is affiliated with the Revolutionary Guards, then quoted a senior Iranian security official as denying any meeting was planned and saying Washington must first act on Iran’s seven conditions. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Tuesday there were no plans for Rezaei to meet Vance. The war, he said, would end neither through military action nor through more sanctions. “The only way to end it is diplomacy and acceptance of the Islamic Republic’s conditions.” Citrinowicz said Rezaei should not be expected to break with the Islamic Republic’s established positions. “He is deeply rooted in the Iranian political and security establishment,” he said. “He is not someone who can simply be persuaded to abandon the regime’s fundamental positions in exchange for an American offer.” The decisive question, Citrinowicz said, is whether Vance has Trump’s authority to offer something substantially different. “A failed meeting could be more dangerous than no meeting at all,” he said. Trump might conclude that diplomacy had run its course and order more strikes to force concessions. Continued economic pressure, indirect talks and a limited interim deal would remain options, he said, but failure to close the gaps could raise the risk of a return to war. His warning comes as Washington continues to combine diplomatic signals with military and economic pressure. On the eve of the midterms, Trump said a deal with Iran “could happen,” and Tehran has since conveyed proposals through Qatari mediators. Meanwhile, the US naval blockade and sanctions remain in place. Reports of preparations for a larger US offensive and the expected arrival of an aircraft carrier group in the region have added to uncertainty. Democrats' sweeping midterm gains have weakened Donald Trump at home. But do they amount to the strategic victory that some in Tehran are claiming? “You lost the war and the election,” Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei declared on X, mocking what he portrayed as turmoil within the Trump administration and questioning who in Washington should receive Tehran's warning against another war. “So who exactly in Washington do we need to get this message across to?” he asked. Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who also serves as Qatar's foreign minister, met Vice President JD Vance separately before his talks with Trump, following a visit to Tehran last week. The Qatari leader sought to persuade Trump to give diplomacy more time, Axios reported, citing sources familiar with the mediation. Vance has been personally involved in indirect negotiations with Iran over the past two weeks, speaking with Al Thani almost daily. Qatar has been mediating a proposed agreement under which Washington would ease its naval blockade and release frozen Iranian funds, while Tehran would allow international nuclear inspections and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Speaking at “The Search for a New Regional Social Contract in the Middle East” conference in Ankara, Kalin said Turkey and other regional mediators were working on a seven-point agreement, with the main disagreement concerning which side should act first. The proposed plan envisages lifting sanctions against Iran and releasing frozen Iranian assets. In return, Tehran would commit not to develop nuclear weapons, begin negotiations with the International Atomic Energy Agency and lift its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, according to Türkiye newspaper. Kalin urged Tehran to show greater flexibility and warned that the next few days could be decisive.

extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly hired a crisis communications firm with a history of handling high-profile sex scandals at least a year before admitting to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed suspected by U.S. intelligence officials of being a Chinese spy. The revelation is raising fresh questions as Nvidia faces an independent investigation and its first shareholder lawsuit. According to Wired, Huang engaged Heller Inc., a New York-based crisis communications firm founded by Risa Heller, well before his relationship with Alice Huang became a public controversy. Heller has advised prominent men facing personal scandals and sexual misconduct allegations, according to a 2023 New York Magazine profile. Her reported clients have included former congressman Anthony Weiner, celebrity chef Mario Batali and former New Yorker writer Jeffrey Toobin. The timing of the reported engagement is particularly notable. Nvidia's internal communications team was reportedly instructed to copy Heller Inc. on press inquiries concerning Huang shortly after a New York Times report in October 2025 raised questions about Nvidia chips reaching Chinese companies through Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed. That report highlighted Megaspeed's acquisition of nearly $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips and identified its CEO, Alice Huang, as a prominent figure at an Nvidia customer gathering in Taipei. The controversy also revives allegations made by short-selling firm Culper Research in a report , months before the affair became public. While examining Megaspeed's business ties with Nvidia, Culper also described the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang as "uncomfortably close". The report said the two executives had been spotted partying and socializing together on multiple occasions. It also alleged that some Nvidia employees had questioned whether they had a "special relationship". Culper raised additional concerns about Megaspeed's finances, suggesting that Nvidia's lost China business might have been rerouted through Southeast Asia. It alleged that Chinese technology giant Alibaba secretly financed Megaspeed through shell companies. The report pointed to financial records showing Megaspeed's total liabilities and equity increasing from $33 million at the end of 2023 to approximately $3 billion by the end of 2024, with much of the increase attributed to refundable deposits from an unidentified source. It was also reported that documents showed Alibaba had lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries. However, Culper's allegations of illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. On Nov. 8, Huang publicly acknowledged an extramarital affair with a former Megaspeed executive, although he did not identify Alice Huang by name. Nvidia's board subsequently announced an independent investigation, citing reports that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort". The U.S. intelligence officials reportedly believe Alice Huang was recruited by the Chinese government to gather intelligence on the Nvidia chief and influence his position on U.S. export controls governing advanced AI chips. Nvidia has previously defended its interactions with Megaspeed, stating, "Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." The fallout has now moved into the courts. Rosen Law Firm has filed the first securities class-action lawsuit against Nvidia and Huang, alleging that they failed to disclose or misled investors about the relationship, raising questions about potential securities fraud and reputational damage. Several other law firms, including Schall, Brown & Schwartz, Levi & Korsinsky and the office of Frank R. Cruz, have also announced investigations into potential securities claims. The notices cite Nvidia's share-price decline following the revelations, although the reported figures vary. Some firms pointed to a 5.5% premarket decline, while others cited larger intraday losses. For investors, the central question is no longer limited to Huang's personal relationship. It is whether Nvidia adequately disclosed information that could have exposed the world's most valuable AI chipmaker to reputational, regulatory and financial risks.

extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly hired a crisis communications firm with a history of handling high-profile sex scandals at least a year before admitting to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed suspected by U.S. intelligence officials of being a Chinese spy. The revelation is raising fresh questions as Nvidia faces an independent investigation and its first shareholder lawsuit. According to Wired, Huang engaged Heller Inc., a New York-based crisis communications firm founded by Risa Heller, well before his relationship with Alice Huang became a public controversy. Heller has advised prominent men facing personal scandals and sexual misconduct allegations, according to a 2023 New York Magazine profile. Her reported clients have included former congressman Anthony Weiner, celebrity chef Mario Batali and former New Yorker writer Jeffrey Toobin. The timing of the reported engagement is particularly notable. Nvidia's internal communications team was reportedly instructed to copy Heller Inc. on press inquiries concerning Huang shortly after a New York Times report in October 2025 raised questions about Nvidia chips reaching Chinese companies through Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed. That report highlighted Megaspeed's acquisition of nearly $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips and identified its CEO, Alice Huang, as a prominent figure at an Nvidia customer gathering in Taipei. The controversy also revives allegations made by short-selling firm Culper Research in a report , months before the affair became public. While examining Megaspeed's business ties with Nvidia, Culper also described the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang as "uncomfortably close". The report said the two executives had been spotted partying and socializing together on multiple occasions. It also alleged that some Nvidia employees had questioned whether they had a "special relationship". Culper raised additional concerns about Megaspeed's finances, suggesting that Nvidia's lost China business might have been rerouted through Southeast Asia. It alleged that Chinese technology giant Alibaba secretly financed Megaspeed through shell companies. The report pointed to financial records showing Megaspeed's total liabilities and equity increasing from $33 million at the end of 2023 to approximately $3 billion by the end of 2024, with much of the increase attributed to refundable deposits from an unidentified source. It was also reported that documents showed Alibaba had lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries. However, Culper's allegations of illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. On Nov. 8, Huang publicly acknowledged an extramarital affair with a former Megaspeed executive, although he did not identify Alice Huang by name. Nvidia's board subsequently announced an independent investigation, citing reports that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort". The U.S. intelligence officials reportedly believe Alice Huang was recruited by the Chinese government to gather intelligence on the Nvidia chief and influence his position on U.S. export controls governing advanced AI chips. Nvidia has previously defended its interactions with Megaspeed, stating, "Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." The fallout has now moved into the courts. Rosen Law Firm has filed the first securities class-action lawsuit against Nvidia and Huang, alleging that they failed to disclose or misled investors about the relationship, raising questions about potential securities fraud and reputational damage. Several other law firms, including Schall, Brown & Schwartz, Levi & Korsinsky and the office of Frank R. Cruz, have also announced investigations into potential securities claims. The notices cite Nvidia's share-price decline following the revelations, although the reported figures vary. Some firms pointed to a 5.5% premarket decline, while others cited larger intraday losses. For investors, the central question is no longer limited to Huang's personal relationship. It is whether Nvidia adequately disclosed information that could have exposed the world's most valuable AI chipmaker to reputational, regulatory and financial risks.

extraction.body: Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI Get started with one of these featured services or browse all From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels. Industrial operations present AI challenges that don’t show up in typical enterprise software. In most facilities, plant data and control logic are spread across separate systems from different vendors: programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and distributed control systems (DCS) run the equipment logic, historians record time-series tags under site-specific naming schemes, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems drive operator screens, and standalone optimization tools or alarm loggers sit on the side. Bolting an external AI agent onto that stack rarely works well in practice. Each system uses its own naming conventions. The logic that actually governs how equipment behaves (the control sequences, state machines, and safety interlocks) is locked inside proprietary controller code that an external tool can’t inspect. Giving a bolt-on agent access across multiple operational technology (OT) systems also means distributing credentials across the plant network. CrossnoKaye took a different approach to bring physical AI to heavy industry using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . Its software-defined automation platform, ATLAS, connects live plant data and AI reasoning to closed-loop control of the equipment running food and beverage plants, industrial refrigeration facilities, aggregates quarries, and manufacturing sites. Across more than 100 industrial facilities and 13,000 controlled assets, CrossnoKaye stores over 22 trillion machine data points, ingests more than 50 billion new readings every day, and runs over 1,000 live advanced process control (APC) applications; CrossnoKaye reports that these applications improve production throughput by 11–17 percent while reducing total facility energy costs by an average of 21 percent. Because ATLAS already manages the facility model, the base control software, the historian, and the optimization applications in one platform on AWS, CrossnoKaye’s agentic intelligence system, AURA, has native access to the full operational state of the plant within a single security boundary. Having the plant context is only half the problem, though. Large language models (LLMs) are good at interpreting engineering context and planning an investigation, but they cannot reliably compute statistics or physical balances over millions of sensor readings in a prompt. To back every numerical answer with real math, AURA uses the code interpreter capability in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to write and run Python workloads at runtime inside isolated, AWS managed microVM sandboxes, alongside Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and local edge safety controls. This post covers how CrossnoKaye architected ATLAS and AURA on AWS, how AURA uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore across interactive Chats, repeatable Tasks, and automated Routines, and what the team learned running physical AI in production. ATLAS controls industrial processes across existing PLC and DCS infrastructure, from kilns, crushers, drying rooms, ovens, and spiral freezers to chillers, turbines, valves, and compressors, without requiring customers to rip and replace plant hardware. Figure 1 illustrates how on-premises ATLAS edge clusters, continuous cloud optimization, and AURA work together on AWS. Figure 1: CrossnoKaye AURA and ATLAS physical AI architecture with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore ATLAS and AURA are built around three core layers: First, the plant is defined in software from the edge up. At each facility, an on-premises ATLAS control panel with redundant computers, power supplies, and network switches (so local control continues uninterrupted while a failed hardware component is replaced) runs a local Kubernetes cluster that uses contract-first microservices, extending the ATLAS cloud platform on AWS to the plant floor. In the cloud, ATLAS authors, validates, and versions the facility’s base control narratives (defining equipment state machines, sequences, operating bounds, interlocks, and alarm rules), which are downloaded to the edge appliances and run locally against existing equipment and controllers. CrossnoKaye reports over 9,000 control software deployments per year and more than 1 million run hours with zero safety incidents. Each edge appliance also acts as an outbound-only information technology/operational technology (IT/OT) gateway that opens zero inbound firewall ports inside the plant, streaming high-frequency telemetry to AWS through Amazon VPC Lattice and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) . If cloud connectivity drops, the plant continues running safely on the base control narratives on the local edge cluster. Second, derived engineering signals and closed-loop optimization applications run on top of base control using the same shared plant model. In the cloud, CrossnoKaye’s Scheduling system runs two continuous pipelines from versioned Python packages in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) , operating on configurable per-instance cadences and event-driven triggers when plant settings change. Synthetic reading algorithms compute derived engineering metrics, such as heat-flow distributions, asset health indices, energy intensity, and mass-balance deviations, and write them back to the historian alongside physical I/O. Closed-loop optimization applications run on top of the base control layer, combining those derived synthetic readings with physics models, model predictive control (MPC), reinforcement learning, utility tariffs, and weather forecasts to compute optimal setpoint schedules. Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queues order every schedule and state update by facility before dispatching setpoints to the local base control narrative on the edge cluster, which CrossnoKaye reports runs 650,000 closed-loop control actions per day. Third, AURA runs inside the platform boundary on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) as microservices and durable Temporal workflows. Under the caller’s enterprise permissions, AURA agents query the internal Atlas Data gateway to read the operational state of a facility or fleet in one consistent model: upstream and downstream equipment topology, the deployed base control narratives and interlocks, physical I/O and synthetic readings, setting change and alarm histories, active optimization schedules, and plant documentation indexed in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases . Having the equipment layout, the base control logic, and the sensor data in the same system makes a concrete difference when diagnosing plant issues. At an aggregates quarry running primary, secondary, and tertiary rock crushers, the back half of the plant tripped twice in a single shift. From the control room, operators saw the secondary crusher fault, cleared the alarm, and restarted the line, only for it to trip again hours later. In the historian timestamps alone, the secondary crusher faulted seconds after the tertiary crusher, which made it look like a crusher problem. Because AURA also reads the conveyor layout and the deployed base control interlocks, its investigation followed the actual control logic. A recirculating belt beneath the tertiary crusher was slipping, which tripped the tertiary crusher’s overload interlock.
