Industrial operations present AI challenges that don’t show up in typical enterprise software. In most facilities, plant data and control logic are spread across separate systems from different vendors: programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and distributed control systems (DCS) run the equipment logic, historians record time-series tags under site-specific naming schemes, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems drive operator screens, and standalone optimization tools or alarm loggers sit on the side. Bolting an external AI agent onto that stack rarely works well in practice. Each system uses its own naming conventions. The logic that actually governs how equipment behaves (the control sequences, state machines, and safety interlocks) is locked inside proprietary controller code that an external tool can’t inspect. Giving a bolt-on agent access across multiple operational technology (OT) systems also means distributing credentials across the plant network.

CrossnoKaye took a different approach to bring physical AI to heavy industry using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . Its software-defined automation platform, ATLAS, connects live plant data and AI reasoning to closed-loop control of the equipment running food and beverage plants, industrial refrigeration facilities, aggregates quarries, and manufacturing sites. Across more than 100 industrial facilities and 13,000 controlled assets, CrossnoKaye stores over 22 trillion machine data points, ingests more than 50 billion new readings every day, and runs over 1,000 live advanced process control (APC) applications; CrossnoKaye reports that these applications improve production throughput by 11–17 percent while reducing total facility energy costs by an average of 21 percent. Because ATLAS already manages the facility model, the base control software, the historian, and the optimization applications in one platform on AWS, CrossnoKaye’s agentic intelligence system, AURA, has native access to the full operational state of the plant within a single security boundary.

Having the plant context is only half the problem, though. Large language models (LLMs) are good at interpreting engineering context and planning an investigation, but they cannot reliably compute statistics or physical balances over millions of sensor readings in a prompt. To back every numerical answer with real math, AURA uses the code interpreter capability in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to write and run Python workloads at runtime inside isolated, AWS managed microVM sandboxes, alongside Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and local edge safety controls. This post covers how CrossnoKaye architected ATLAS and AURA on AWS, how AURA uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore across interactive Chats, repeatable Tasks, and automated Routines, and what the team learned running physical AI in production.

ATLAS controls industrial processes across existing PLC and DCS infrastructure, from kilns, crushers, drying rooms, ovens, and spiral freezers to chillers, turbines, valves, and compressors, without requiring customers to rip and replace plant hardware. ATLAS and AURA are built around three core layers:

First, the plant is defined in software from the edge up. At each facility, an on-premises ATLAS control panel with redundant computers, power supplies, and network switches (so local control continues uninterrupted while a failed hardware component is replaced) runs a local Kubernetes cluster that uses contract-first microservices, extending the ATLAS cloud platform on AWS to the plant floor. In the cloud, ATLAS authors, validates, and versions the facility’s base control narratives (defining equipment state machines, sequences, operating bounds, interlocks, and alarm rules), which are downloaded to the edge appliances and run locally against existing equipment and controllers. CrossnoKaye reports over 9,000 control software deployments per year and more than 1 million run hours with zero safety incidents. Each edge appliance also acts as an outbound-only information technology/operational technology (IT/OT) gateway that opens zero inbound firewall ports inside the plant, streaming high-frequency telemetry to AWS through Amazon VPC Lattice and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) . If cloud connectivity drops, the plant continues running safely on the base control narratives on the local edge cluster.

Second, derived engineering signals and closed-loop optimization applications run on top of base control using the same shared plant model. In the cloud, CrossnoKaye’s Scheduling system runs two continuous pipelines from versioned Python packages in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) , operating on configurable per-instance cadences and event-driven triggers when plant settings change. Synthetic reading algorithms compute derived engineering metrics, such as heat-flow distributions, asset health indices, energy intensity, and mass-balance deviations, and write them back to the historian alongside physical I/O. Closed-loop optimization applications run on top of the base control layer, combining those derived synthetic readings with physics models, model predictive control (MPC), reinforcement learning, utility tariffs, and weather forecasts to compute optimal setpoint schedules. Having the equipment layout, the base control logic, and the sensor data in the same system makes a concrete difference when diagnosing plant issues. At an aggregates quarry running primary, secondary, and tertiary rock crushers, the back half of the plant tripped twice in a single shift. Because AURA also reads the conveyor layout and the deployed base control interlocks, its investigation followed the actual control logic. That interlock’s upstream safety interlock immediately halted the secondary crusher to prevent burying a stopped downstream crusher in stone. extraction.body: CrossnoKaye physical AI puts generated engineering answers through Python execution rather than accepting a language model’s arithmetic. A November 9 AWS case study describes AURA, its agentic investigation system, using ATLAS plant context and isolated Amazon Bedrock AgentCore environments. The distinction matters: a convincing explanation and a checkable calculation give engineers different grounds for action. The competitive reference is Siemens, which also connects industrial agents to engineering systems. The central contest, however, concerns approaches: assistants that offer plausible interpretations versus systems that expose enough evidence for engineers to challenge them. Neither a familiar interface nor a fluent diagnosis settles whether an answer fits the equipment. For plant operators, the practical question is how much investigative work an agent removes without weakening review. For developers and enterprise buyers, the case raises a related question: where should model reasoning stop and enforceable software boundaries begin? According to the AWS physical AI architecture , ATLAS supplies operational context while AURA investigates it. The company describes generated Python running inside isolated environments, with output checks before results reach engineers. Automated investigations remain read-only; proposed setting changes require human approval. The meaningful change is the connection between a question, operational evidence, and an inspectable calculation. Treating those as separate product features misses the engineering problem. A useful answer requires their relationship to survive the entire investigation. CrossnoKaye’s public positioning for ATLAS already centers on unified control applications and live facility data. That helps explain the strategic direction. An investigation system attached to an existing operational platform starts with a different integration problem than an assistant assembled from disconnected exports. That distinction does not establish superiority by itself. A unified platform can still contain incomplete records, outdated descriptions, or inconsistent measurements. Its potential advantage is that developers have a shared place to reconcile those problems and attach meaning to the data. Consider an illustrative investigation into a refrigeration problem. An engineer needs more than a pressure chart. Equipment relationships, operating mode, maintenance activity, and recent changes all affect which explanation deserves attention. A model supplied only with measurements might identify a correlation and write a reasonable narrative. An investigation supplied with equipment context has more opportunities to test that narrative against how the system actually operates. The opportunity matters even when the final answer remains uncertain. This is why grounding, meaning connecting an answer to relevant evidence, needs a broader definition in industrial applications. Document retrieval supplies text. Operational grounding also requires knowing which equipment, measurements, and conditions the question concerns. That framing keeps attention on the right question. Can a reviewer follow the route from plant condition to calculation to recommendation? If the route disappears behind a polished answer, the interface has concealed the most consequential part of the work. The pressure falls on vendors that promise engineering answers without making the supporting work accessible. Plant buyers need a basis for deciding whether an answer deserves investigation, approval, or rejection. Fluency alone provides little help with that decision. The pressure is immediate during product evaluation. A demonstration can make an assistant look useful by selecting a clear incident with complete records. A procurement decision needs evidence about ambiguous incidents, missing inputs, and cases where several explanations remain plausible. Siemens provides relevant competitive context. Its April 20 announcement describes the Eigen Engineering Agent , an automation engineering product connected to TIA Portal, its engineering platform. Siemens says the agent uses project context and validates outputs before presenting them for review. The products address overlapping industrial needs, but their described workflows are different. Siemens emphasizes executing engineering tasks within project environments. CrossnoKaye’s case emphasizes investigations connected to operating plant context. That difference prevents a fair ranking from announcement language alone. The common commercial signal is more useful than an invented winner. Both accounts treat access to the relevant environment as essential. General model capability is only part of the proposition; the surrounding engineering system supplies constraints and context. The same distinction applies to workload. More automated reports can increase review demand if each report requires manual reconstruction. The useful unit of productivity is a completed, defensible investigation, rather than the volume of generated material. Plant engineers also face pressure to define acceptance criteria. Vendors cannot demonstrate relevance against an unspecified standard. Buyers need to identify what a correct investigation must preserve and what would make a result unusable. For example, a comparison across operating periods should disclose whether the equipment was performing comparable work. Otherwise, a numerical difference can be real while the implied explanation remains misleading. That is an analytical concern, not merely a presentation defect. Versioning matters for the same reason. If the calculation or input selection changes, a later result needs to remain distinguishable from the earlier one. Otherwise, disagreement becomes difficult to investigate after the underlying analysis has moved. This is the useful reading of CrossnoKaye AURA explained: model reasoning proposes an investigative path, while software and engineers assess the resulting evidence. The architecture’s value depends on how well those responsibilities remain visible. The mechanism is consequential without implying infallibility. It can turn an answer into something another person can examine. Whether that examination is easy, complete, and routinely performed remains an operational question. A sandbox, meaning a restricted execution environment, describes only part of that boundary. Buyers still need to understand network access, credentials, data exposure, and available interfaces. The label alone leaves those questions unanswered. Amazon’s network settings documentation makes this distinction explicit. AgentCore Code Interpreter supports different connectivity configurations, including public and private network access. Its sandbox mode also permits specified AWS service access. Consequently, isolated execution should not be interpreted as universal disconnection. The relevant security property depends on the deployed configuration. A buyer needs evidence about the particular environment rather than assumptions derived from a product name. A transparent answer can still be wrong. A secure execution environment can still process unsuitable inputs. A reproducible result can still rely on an invalid assumption. These properties support each other without becoming interchangeable. The AWS case study offers a quarry example: CrossnoKaye says AURA traced crusher shutdowns to a slipping recirculating belt using equipment relationships and control logic. That is a company-reported account, not an independent comparative evaluation. Its analytical significance is the relationship between a visible symptom and an initiating fault. To evaluate broader reliability, buyers would need cases where similar symptoms had different causes. They would also need to see investigations that remained unresolved. Failure reporting would strengthen the evidence. Useful categories include unsupported conclusions, missed conditions, unnecessary escalations, and investigations stopped because inputs were inadequate. Combining them into a single accuracy figure would conceal practical differences. Uncertainty handling deserves equal attention. A system should be able to identify what additional observation would distinguish competing explanations. An investigation that requests a physical inspection can be more useful than one that prematurely commits to a cause. Economic evaluation has its own attribution problem. If a deployment combines new controls, improved data access, optimization, and an assistant, the overall benefit cannot automatically be assigned to conversational AI. Each component contributes differently. That makes maintenance part of product quality. Buyers should ask how the system detects outdated context and how corrections affect existing reports. A convincing initial deployment does not settle how reliably the application adapts. CrossnoKaye physical AI is therefore best understood as an architecture worth examining, with deployment effectiveness requiring broader evidence. That judgment recognizes the technical direction while preserving the distinction between a detailed account and an independent assessment. The next useful evidence should show how the system performs across ordinary work, how much integration it requires, and how engineers use its outputs. These are observation priorities, not announced milestones. For engineering organizations, a searchable knowledge base addresses a related documentation need. Preserving technical records helps teams revisit assumptions and decisions. That is a separate function from validating plant calculations or authorizing equipment changes. CrossnoKaye physical AI gives buyers a concrete architecture to question. Compare the total review effort with the existing workflow, then inspect what happens when evidence is missing. Developers should apply the same scrutiny to their own agent designs. Does the application help a qualified person make a defensible decision, and can another person later understand why that decision was made?

extraction.body: Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI Get started with one of these featured services or browse all From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels. Industrial operations present AI challenges that don’t show up in typical enterprise software. In most facilities, plant data and control logic are spread across separate systems from different vendors: programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and distributed control systems (DCS) run the equipment logic, historians record time-series tags under site-specific naming schemes, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems drive operator screens, and standalone optimization tools or alarm loggers sit on the side. Bolting an external AI agent onto that stack rarely works well in practice. Each system uses its own naming conventions. The logic that actually governs how equipment behaves (the control sequences, state machines, and safety interlocks) is locked inside proprietary controller code that an external tool can’t inspect. Giving a bolt-on agent access across multiple operational technology (OT) systems also means distributing credentials across the plant network. CrossnoKaye took a different approach to bring physical AI to heavy industry using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . Its software-defined automation platform, ATLAS, connects live plant data and AI reasoning to closed-loop control of the equipment running food and beverage plants, industrial refrigeration facilities, aggregates quarries, and manufacturing sites. Across more than 100 industrial facilities and 13,000 controlled assets, CrossnoKaye stores over 22 trillion machine data points, ingests more than 50 billion new readings every day, and runs over 1,000 live advanced process control (APC) applications; CrossnoKaye reports that these applications improve production throughput by 11–17 percent while reducing total facility energy costs by an average of 21 percent. Because ATLAS already manages the facility model, the base control software, the historian, and the optimization applications in one platform on AWS, CrossnoKaye’s agentic intelligence system, AURA, has native access to the full operational state of the plant within a single security boundary. Having the plant context is only half the problem, though. Large language models (LLMs) are good at interpreting engineering context and planning an investigation, but they cannot reliably compute statistics or physical balances over millions of sensor readings in a prompt. To back every numerical answer with real math, AURA uses the code interpreter capability in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to write and run Python workloads at runtime inside isolated, AWS managed microVM sandboxes, alongside Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and local edge safety controls. This post covers how CrossnoKaye architected ATLAS and AURA on AWS, how AURA uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore across interactive Chats, repeatable Tasks, and automated Routines, and what the team learned running physical AI in production. ATLAS controls industrial processes across existing PLC and DCS infrastructure, from kilns, crushers, drying rooms, ovens, and spiral freezers to chillers, turbines, valves, and compressors, without requiring customers to rip and replace plant hardware. Figure 1 illustrates how on-premises ATLAS edge clusters, continuous cloud optimization, and AURA work together on AWS. Figure 1: CrossnoKaye AURA and ATLAS physical AI architecture with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore ATLAS and AURA are built around three core layers: First, the plant is defined in software from the edge up. At each facility, an on-premises ATLAS control panel with redundant computers, power supplies, and network switches (so local control continues uninterrupted while a failed hardware component is replaced) runs a local Kubernetes cluster that uses contract-first microservices, extending the ATLAS cloud platform on AWS to the plant floor. In the cloud, ATLAS authors, validates, and versions the facility’s base control narratives (defining equipment state machines, sequences, operating bounds, interlocks, and alarm rules), which are downloaded to the edge appliances and run locally against existing equipment and controllers. CrossnoKaye reports over 9,000 control software deployments per year and more than 1 million run hours with zero safety incidents. Each edge appliance also acts as an outbound-only information technology/operational technology (IT/OT) gateway that opens zero inbound firewall ports inside the plant, streaming high-frequency telemetry to AWS through Amazon VPC Lattice and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) . If cloud connectivity drops, the plant continues running safely on the base control narratives on the local edge cluster. Second, derived engineering signals and closed-loop optimization applications run on top of base control using the same shared plant model. In the cloud, CrossnoKaye’s Scheduling system runs two continuous pipelines from versioned Python packages in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) , operating on configurable per-instance cadences and event-driven triggers when plant settings change. Synthetic reading algorithms compute derived engineering metrics, such as heat-flow distributions, asset health indices, energy intensity, and mass-balance deviations, and write them back to the historian alongside physical I/O. Industrial operations present AI challenges that don’t show up in typical enterprise software. In most facilities, plant data and control logic are spread across separate systems from different vendors: programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and distributed control systems (DCS) run the equipment logic, historians record time-series tags under site-specific naming schemes, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems drive operator screens, and standalone optimization tools or alarm loggers sit on the side. Bolting an external AI agent onto that stack rarely works well in practice. Each system uses its own naming conventions. The logic that actually governs how equipment behaves (the control sequences, state machines, and safety interlocks) is locked inside proprietary controller code that an external tool can’t inspect. Giving a bolt-on agent access across multiple operational technology (OT) systems also means distributing credentials across the plant network.

CrossnoKaye took a different approach to bring physical AI to heavy industry using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . Its software-defined automation platform, ATLAS, connects live plant data and AI reasoning to closed-loop control of the equipment running food and beverage plants, industrial refrigeration facilities, aggregates quarries, and manufacturing sites. Across more than 100 industrial facilities and 13,000 controlled assets, CrossnoKaye stores over 22 trillion machine data points, ingests more than 50 billion new readings every day, and runs over 1,000 live advanced process control (APC) applications; CrossnoKaye reports that these applications improve production throughput by 11–17 percent while reducing total facility energy costs by an average of 21 percent. extraction.body: CrossnoKaye physical AI puts generated engineering answers through Python execution rather than accepting a language model’s arithmetic. A November 9 AWS case study describes AURA, its agentic investigation system, using ATLAS plant context and isolated Amazon Bedrock AgentCore environments. The distinction matters: a convincing explanation and a checkable calculation give engineers different grounds for action. The competitive reference is Siemens, which also connects industrial agents to engineering systems. The central contest, however, concerns approaches: assistants that offer plausible interpretations versus systems that expose enough evidence for engineers to challenge them. Neither a familiar interface nor a fluent diagnosis settles whether an answer fits the equipment. For plant operators, the practical question is how much investigative work an agent removes without weakening review. For developers and enterprise buyers, the case raises a related question: where should model reasoning stop and enforceable software boundaries begin? According to the AWS physical AI architecture , ATLAS supplies operational context while AURA investigates it. The company describes generated Python running inside isolated environments, with output checks before results reach engineers. Automated investigations remain read-only; proposed setting changes require human approval. The meaningful change is the connection between a question, operational evidence, and an inspectable calculation. Treating those as separate product features misses the engineering problem. A useful answer requires their relationship to survive the entire investigation. CrossnoKaye’s public positioning for ATLAS already centers on unified control applications and live facility data. That helps explain the strategic direction. An investigation system attached to an existing operational platform starts with a different integration problem than an assistant assembled from disconnected exports. That distinction does not establish superiority by itself. A unified platform can still contain incomplete records, outdated descriptions, or inconsistent measurements. Its potential advantage is that developers have a shared place to reconcile those problems and attach meaning to the data. Consider an illustrative investigation into a refrigeration problem. An engineer needs more than a pressure chart. Equipment relationships, operating mode, maintenance activity, and recent changes all affect which explanation deserves attention. A model supplied only with measurements might identify a correlation and write a reasonable narrative. An investigation supplied with equipment context has more opportunities to test that narrative against how the system actually operates. The opportunity matters even when the final answer remains uncertain. This is why grounding, meaning connecting an answer to relevant evidence, needs a broader definition in industrial applications. Document retrieval supplies text. Operational grounding also requires knowing which equipment, measurements, and conditions the question concerns. That framing keeps attention on the right question. Can a reviewer follow the route from plant condition to calculation to recommendation? If the route disappears behind a polished answer, the interface has concealed the most consequential part of the work. The pressure falls on vendors that promise engineering answers without making the supporting work accessible. Plant buyers need a basis for deciding whether an answer deserves investigation, approval, or rejection. Fluency alone provides little help with that decision. The pressure is immediate during product evaluation. A demonstration can make an assistant look useful by selecting a clear incident with complete records. A procurement decision needs evidence about ambiguous incidents, missing inputs, and cases where several explanations remain plausible. Siemens provides relevant competitive context. Its April 20 announcement describes the Eigen Engineering Agent , an automation engineering product connected to TIA Portal, its engineering platform. Siemens says the agent uses project context and validates outputs before presenting them for review. The products address overlapping industrial needs, but their described workflows are different. Siemens emphasizes executing engineering tasks within project environments. CrossnoKaye’s case emphasizes investigations connected to operating plant context. That difference prevents a fair ranking from announcement language alone. The common commercial signal is more useful than an invented winner. Both accounts treat access to the relevant environment as essential. General model capability is only part of the proposition; the surrounding engineering system supplies constraints and context. The same distinction applies to workload. More automated reports can increase review demand if each report requires manual reconstruction. The useful unit of productivity is a completed, defensible investigation, rather than the volume of generated material. Plant engineers also face pressure to define acceptance criteria. Vendors cannot demonstrate relevance against an unspecified standard. Buyers need to identify what a correct investigation must preserve and what would make a result unusable. For example, a comparison across operating periods should disclose whether the equipment was performing comparable work. Otherwise, a numerical difference can be real while the implied explanation remains misleading. That is an analytical concern, not merely a presentation defect. Versioning matters for the same reason. If the calculation or input selection changes, a later result needs to remain distinguishable from the earlier one. Otherwise, disagreement becomes difficult to investigate after the underlying analysis has moved. This is the useful reading of CrossnoKaye AURA explained: model reasoning proposes an investigative path, while software and engineers assess the resulting evidence. The architecture’s value depends on how well those responsibilities remain visible. The mechanism is consequential without implying infallibility. It can turn an answer into something another person can examine. Whether that examination is easy, complete, and routinely performed remains an operational question. A sandbox, meaning a restricted execution environment, describes only part of that boundary. Buyers still need to understand network access, credentials, data exposure, and available interfaces. The label alone leaves those questions unanswered. Amazon’s network settings documentation makes this distinction explicit. AgentCore Code Interpreter supports different connectivity configurations, including public and private network access. Its sandbox mode also permits specified AWS service access. Consequently, isolated execution should not be interpreted as universal disconnection. The relevant security property depends on the deployed configuration. A buyer needs evidence about the particular environment rather than assumptions derived from a product name. A transparent answer can still be wrong. A secure execution environment can still process unsuitable inputs. A reproducible result can still rely on an invalid assumption. These properties support each other without becoming interchangeable. The AWS case study offers a quarry example: CrossnoKaye says AURA traced crusher shutdowns to a slipping recirculating belt using equipment relationships and control logic. That is a company-reported account, not an independent comparative evaluation. Its analytical significance is the relationship between a visible symptom and an initiating fault. To evaluate broader reliability, buyers would need cases where similar symptoms had different causes. They would also need to see investigations that remained unresolved. Failure reporting would strengthen the evidence. Useful categories include unsupported conclusions, missed conditions, unnecessary escalations, and investigations stopped because inputs were inadequate. Combining them into a single accuracy figure would conceal practical differences. Uncertainty handling deserves equal attention. A system should be able to identify what additional observation would distinguish competing explanations. An investigation that requests a physical inspection can be more useful than one that prematurely commits to a cause. Economic evaluation has its own attribution problem. If a deployment combines new controls, improved data access, optimization, and an assistant, the overall benefit cannot automatically be assigned to conversational AI. Each component contributes differently. That makes maintenance part of product quality. Buyers should ask how the system detects outdated context and how corrections affect existing reports. A convincing initial deployment does not settle how reliably the application adapts. CrossnoKaye physical AI is therefore best understood as an architecture worth examining, with deployment effectiveness requiring broader evidence. That judgment recognizes the technical direction while preserving the distinction between a detailed account and an independent assessment. The next useful evidence should show how the system performs across ordinary work, how much integration it requires, and how engineers use its outputs. These are observation priorities, not announced milestones. For engineering organizations, a searchable knowledge base addresses a related documentation need. Preserving technical records helps teams revisit assumptions and decisions. That is a separate function from validating plant calculations or authorizing equipment changes. Compare the total review effort with the existing workflow, then inspect what happens when evidence is missing. Developers should apply the same scrutiny to their own agent designs. Siemens provides relevant competitive context. Its April 20 announcement describes the Eigen Engineering Agent , an automation engineering product connected to TIA Portal, its engineering platform. Siemens says the agent uses project context and validates outputs before presenting them for review.

The products address overlapping industrial needs, but their described workflows are different. Siemens emphasizes executing engineering tasks within project environments. CrossnoKaye’s case emphasizes investigations connected to operating plant context. That difference prevents a fair ranking from announcement language alone.

The common commercial signal is more useful than an invented winner. Both accounts treat access to the relevant environment as essential. General model capability is only part of the proposition; the surrounding engineering system supplies constraints and context.

The same distinction applies to workload. More automated reports can increase review demand if each report requires manual reconstruction. The useful unit of productivity is a completed, defensible investigation, rather than the volume of generated material.

Plant engineers also face pressure to define acceptance criteria. Vendors cannot demonstrate relevance against an unspecified standard. Buyers need to identify what a correct investigation must preserve and what would make a result unusable.

For example, a comparison across operating periods should disclose whether the equipment was performing comparable work. Otherwise, a numerical difference can be real while the implied explanation remains misleading. That is an analytical concern, not merely a presentation defect.

Versioning matters for the same reason. If the calculation or input selection changes, a later result needs to remain distinguishable from the earlier one. Otherwise, disagreement becomes difficult to investigate after the underlying analysis has moved.

This is the useful reading of CrossnoKaye AURA explained: model reasoning proposes an investigative path, while software and engineers assess the resulting evidence. The architecture’s value depends on how well those responsibilities remain visible.

The mechanism is consequential without implying infallibility. It can turn an answer into something another person can examine. Whether that examination is easy, complete, and routinely performed remains an operational question.

A sandbox, meaning a restricted execution environment, describes only part of that boundary. Buyers still need to understand network access, credentials, data exposure, and available interfaces. The label alone leaves those questions unanswered.

Amazon’s network settings documentation makes this distinction explicit. AgentCore Code Interpreter supports different connectivity configurations, including public and private network access. Its sandbox mode also permits specified AWS service access.

Consequently, isolated execution should not be interpreted as universal disconnection. The relevant security property depends on the deployed configuration. A buyer needs evidence about the particular environment rather than assumptions derived from a product name.

A transparent answer can still be wrong. A secure execution environment can still process unsuitable inputs. A reproducible result can still rely on an invalid assumption. These properties support each other without becoming interchangeable.

The AWS case study offers a quarry example: CrossnoKaye says AURA traced crusher shutdowns to a slipping recirculating belt using equipment relationships and control logic. That is a company-reported account, not an independent comparative evaluation.

That makes maintenance part of product quality. Buyers should ask how the system detects outdated context and how corrections affect existing reports. A convincing initial deployment does not settle how reliably the application adapts.

sources.title: Apple Patches iMessage Flaws That Could Let Strangers Read Your Group Chats Without an Invite
passages: Apple has fixed two iMessage flaws that could let unauthorised users join group chats and read messages, including some sent before they were added.The vulnerabilities were addressed in security updates released on 9 November 2026, alongside fixes for separate Bluetooth and AirPlay pairing issues.One flaw could allow a remote attacker to join a group without authorisation and receive its messages.

Another, CVE-2026-113964, could let an attacker within Bluetooth range bypass limits on pairing-code attempts and pair with a device without the owner interacting with it.Apple also documented CVE-2026-113968, which could allow an attacker within Bluetooth range to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing-code attempts.

It also does not identify any affected conversations or users.The two Messages vulnerabilities were listed separately in Apple's security documentation, with CVE-2026-113961 covering unauthorised group-chat access and CVE-2026-113960 covering access to messages sent before a user joined.

The company fixed this by removing the vulnerable code.Neither description establishes that an attacker successfully accessed anyone's conversations.Apple has not said whether either vulnerability was exploited in real-world attacks, how frequently they could be triggered or whether specific users were affected.Both Messages flaws are credited to an anonymous researcher.

That issue concerns AirPlay pairing rather than the same direct Bluetooth pairing impact described in the other two entries.The advisory also does not say that every nearby device could automatically connect to an iPhone, nor does it establish that these weaknesses were used to access personal data.

extraction.body: An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it. The updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined. As of today, other updates released yesterday for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, the iPad (7th generation) and some Apple Watch models do not list either fix. The company's notes also do not say whether either flaw has been exploited, what an attacker would need, whether group members would see someone who joined this way, or whether every member must update to be protected. The updates that fix the iMessage flaws also fix a flaw in Google's Brotli compression library. The notes do not mention any attacks using that flaw. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27. The flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat is tracked as CVE-2026-113961. It is an authorization issue that the updates fix through improved validation. The flaw involving earlier messages is CVE-2026-113960. Each operating system version got its own update. The security advisory for iOS and iPadOS 27.2.1 describes all three flaws. The security releases list links to the notes for every update. The iOS 18.7.12 notes and the watchOS 26.6.1 notes list other security fixes but not the iMessage or Brotli fixes. The company does not say whether devices on those versions are affected by the three flaws. Its notes also offer no workaround for anyone who cannot update right away. The Brotli flaw, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the library's decoder that could let malicious input corrupt memory. CISA's catalog entry for the Brotli decoder flaw names Google's Brotli as the affected product and says different products could use the component. All nine updates fix Bluetooth and AirPlay flaws. Two could allow a malicious Bluetooth device, or an attacker within Bluetooth range, to pair with a device without user interaction. The notes do not say what a paired device could then do. Two others could let an attacker bypass the limit on pairing code attempts, one from Bluetooth range and one from the same network. Another could let an attacker in Bluetooth range corrupt process memory. extraction.body: An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it. The updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined. As of today, other updates released yesterday for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, the iPad (7th generation) and some Apple Watch models do not list either fix. The company's notes also do not say whether either flaw has been exploited, what an attacker would need, whether group members would see someone who joined this way, or whether every member must update to be protected. The updates that fix the iMessage flaws also fix a flaw in Google's Brotli compression library. The notes do not mention any attacks using that flaw. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27. The flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat is tracked as CVE-2026-113961. It is an authorization issue that the updates fix through improved validation. The flaw involving earlier messages is CVE-2026-113960. Each operating system version got its own update. The security advisory for iOS and iPadOS 27.2.1 describes all three flaws. The security releases list links to the notes for every update. The iOS 18.7.12 notes and the watchOS 26.6.1 notes list other security fixes but not the iMessage or Brotli fixes. The company does not say whether devices on those versions are affected by the three flaws. Its notes also offer no workaround for anyone who cannot update right away. The Brotli flaw, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the library's decoder that could let malicious input corrupt memory. CISA's catalog entry for the Brotli decoder flaw names Google's Brotli as the affected product and says different products could use the component. All nine updates fix Bluetooth and AirPlay flaws. Two could allow a malicious Bluetooth device, or an attacker within Bluetooth range, to pair with a device without user interaction. The notes do not say what a paired device could then do. Two others could let an attacker bypass the limit on pairing code attempts, one from Bluetooth range and one from the same network. Another could let an attacker in Bluetooth range corrupt process memory. The General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania , United States , has enacted ‘Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act’, after receiving assent from the Pennsylvania Governor, Josh Shapiro, to become an act enforceable under the court of law. The act defines ‘artificial intelligence’ or ‘AI’ as a machine‑based system that, for a given set of human‑defined objectives, can make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments, and includes generative artificial intelligence. Further, the term ‘Generative artificial intelligence’ is defined as the class of models that emulate the structure and characteristics of input data in order to generate synthetic content. As per the provisions of the act , any advertisement – whether a still image, video, audio or text – that ‘has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence’ include a label in the same format as the ad itself. The requirement applies to advertisements broadcast or displayed in Pennsylvania, regardless of where the ad was created, meaning disclosures may appear in commercials aired in other states if they are also intended for Pennsylvania audiences. The legislation is among the first in the United States to mandate the labelling of AI-generated advertising content, setting a precedent as to how AI‑derived content may be disclosed to consumers. In a related development, Congresswoman Shontel Brown has also introduced the Securing Elections from AI Deception Act, which seeks to prohibit the use of artificial intelligence to deprive or defraud individuals of their right to vote and require disclaimers on AI-generated campaign content. The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania enacted AI Deceptive Advertising Act, requiring clear and conspicuous disclosure of AI‑generated synthetic content in advertisements.

The General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania , United States , has enacted ‘Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act’, after receiving assent from the Pennsylvania Governor, Josh Shapiro, to become an act enforceable under the court of law. The act defines ‘artificial intelligence’ or ‘AI’ as a machine‑based system that, for a given set of human‑defined objectives, can make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments, and includes generative artificial intelligence. Further, the term ‘Generative artificial intelligence’ is defined as the class of models that emulate the structure and characteristics of input data in order to generate synthetic content.

As per the provisions of the act , any advertisement – whether a still image, video, audio or text – that ‘has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence’ include a label in the same format as the ad itself. The requirement applies to advertisements broadcast or displayed in Pennsylvania, regardless of where the ad was created, meaning disclosures may appear in commercials aired in other states if they are also intended for Pennsylvania audiences.

The legislation is among the first in the United States to mandate the labelling of AI-generated advertising content, setting a precedent as to how AI‑derived content may be disclosed to consumers. In a related development, Congresswoman Shontel Brown has also introduced the Securing Elections from AI Deception Act, which seeks to prohibit the use of artificial intelligence to deprive or defraud individuals of their right to vote and require disclaimers on AI-generated campaign content.

He is currently working with the National Internet Exchange of India, a not-for-profit organisation under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Government of India.
The Digital Watch is an initiative of the Geneva Internet Platform, supported by the Swiss Confederation and the Republic and Canton of Geneva. The GIP is operated by DiploFoundation.

The GIP Digital Watch observatory reflects on a wide variety of themes and actors involved in global digital policy, curated by a dedicated team of experts from around the world. extraction.body: Insights on Tech Law, Regulation & Policy, AI, IoT and More On October 22, 2026, the Governor of Pennsylvania signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act ( Senate Bill 806 ) (“Act”) into law. The Act joins a growing number of state laws focused on the use of AI in advertising. However, unlike the laws in New York and California, Pennsylvania’s disclosure requirement is not limited to AI-generated advertisements using a synthetic performer. The law takes effect 60 days after enactment, on December 21, 2026. As chair of Covington’s Advertising & Consumer Protection Investigations practice group, Laura represents corporate and individual clients in investigations before the FTC and State Attorneys General. She also provides pragmatic compliance advice on a wide range of consumer protection issues, including substantiating claims involving generative artificial intelligence, environmental benefits, and “Made in USA.” She counsels brands on emerging issues involving influencers, consumer reviews, AI-generated content, and subscription autorenewals. Laura regularly represents both challengers and advertisers before the NAD, achieving favorable outcomes in matters involving artificial intelligence, influencers, and claim substantiation. During her twelve-year tenure at the FTC, Laura served as Assistant Director in two divisions of the Bureau of Consumer Protection, Attorney Advisor to Chairman William E. Kovacic, and Chief of Staff to Bureau Director Jessica Rich. She oversaw major rulemakings—including the Green Guides and the Telemarketing Sales Rule—and supervised dozens of investigations and enforcement actions. As Assistant Director in the Division of Enforcement, Laura also supervised compliance monitoring and enforcement proceedings for companies under federal court or Commission order. Jayne counsels clients across industries to launch and enhance products, services, and governance programs involving their collection and use of data and emerging technologies. Her experience spans U.S. comprehensive privacy, automated decisionmaking, AI governance, biometric privacy, surveillance and algorithmic pricing, and AI transparency, disclosure, and safety frameworks. She partners with clients to design products and governance programs that keep pace with the dynamic regulatory environment, including in connection with digital and online advertising, social media, AI-powered and agentic services, connected devices, and robotics. In addition, she advises companies on engagement with federal and state regulators, including through enforcement and rulemaking. Jayne analyzes privacy and security risks in complex corporate transactions. Jayne maintains an active pro bono practice, focusing on assisting nonprofits with their privacy programs and elder estate planning. The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania enacted AI Deceptive Advertising Act, requiring clear and conspicuous disclosure of AI‑generated synthetic content in advertisements.

The General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania , United States , has enacted ‘Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act’, after receiving assent from the Pennsylvania Governor, Josh Shapiro, to become an act enforceable under the court of law. The act defines ‘artificial intelligence’ or ‘AI’ as a machine‑based system that, for a given set of human‑defined objectives, can make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments, and includes generative artificial intelligence. Further, the term ‘Generative artificial intelligence’ is defined as the class of models that emulate the structure and characteristics of input data in order to generate synthetic content.

As per the provisions of the act , any advertisement – whether a still image, video, audio or text – that ‘has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence’ include a label in the same format as the ad itself. The requirement applies to advertisements broadcast or displayed in Pennsylvania, regardless of where the ad was created, meaning disclosures may appear in commercials aired in other states if they are also intended for Pennsylvania audiences.

The legislation is among the first in the United States to mandate the labelling of AI-generated advertising content, setting a precedent as to how AI‑derived content may be disclosed to consumers. In a related development, Congresswoman Shontel Brown has also introduced the Securing Elections from AI Deception Act, which seeks to prohibit the use of artificial intelligence to deprive or defraud individuals of their right to vote and require disclaimers on AI-generated campaign content.

extraction.body: Google on Monday released updates to patch nine security vulnerabilities, including one that has come under active exploitation in the wild. The high-severity vulnerability, assigned the CVE identifier CVE-2026-125350 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a use-after-free bug in the XML component. Use-after-free bugs typically occur when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has already been freed. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to achieve data corruption, program crashes, or arbitrary code execution. An anonymous security researcher has been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw on November 6, 2026. Google acknowledged it is "aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," but has not revealed any additional specific information related to how it's being abused in real-world attacks or who is behind them. "Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix," the tech giant added. "We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third-party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven't yet fixed." sources.title: Hotel giant Wyndham exposed customer data after app security lapse - TechCrunch
passages: Hotel and resort giant Wyndham has acknowledged a cybersecurity incident after a good-faith security researcher discovered a bug that allowed anyone to access customers’ personal information.
TechCrunch also asked Wyndham whether it planned to notify customers whose information was exposed, or disclose the incident to U.S. regulators, such as filing a notice with the U.S.
Securities and Exchange Commission, as public companies are required to do for material cybersecurity incidents.
The researcher said Wyndham has no way to report security flaws, and asked for TechCrunch’s help in alerting the company.
Soon after TechCrunch made contact with Wyndham’s cybersecurity staff, the exposed credential was revoked, preventing any further access to the database.

“Our team has taken steps to address the issue,” a Wyndham spokesperson told TechCrunch. “Our security teams have no evidence of any unauthorized access,” the statement added, without providing any further details about the claim.
Wiggins told TechCrunch that the credential exposed personal information including customer names, email addresses, and Wyndham member numbers.
The database also stores customer login tokens ( called JWTs ) that keep customers logged-in to their apps without having to repeatedly enter their own passwords.
According to Wiggins, the database had millions of entries, but he was unable to determine an accurate number of exposed customer records.
Wyndham touts some 129 million enrolled rewards members.
For Wiggins, this is his second public discovery of hardcoded credentials in two weeks, after finding a near-identical vulnerability in Applebee’s app that exposed customer data.
This is the latest known security incident at Wyndham in recent years.

Bitcoin traded near $74,200 on November 10 as Bitcoin December Fed rate hike odds reached 84.4%. Global equity funds, meanwhile, took in $266 billion over four weeks. BTC ▼ $73,805.00 was down 1.4% since midnight UTC, according to CoinDesk .
Equity-fund inflows and rising rate expectations are both in focus for crypto traders. The 84.4% figure reflects market pricing, not a Fed decision: officials held rates at their October meeting.

Global equity funds drew a record $266 billion over four weeks, according to BeInCrypto , citing the Kobeissi Letter. The pace picked up last week, when funds attracted $89 billion worldwide, including $32 billion for U.S. equity funds.

Since 2020, U.S. equity funds have received $2.1 trillion, the Kobeissi Letter said. Of that, $1.5 trillion arrived since the start of 2024. Emerging-market Asia equity funds took in $470 billion over the longer period, while European equity funds saw $426 billion in outflows.
Bitcoin also lagged the Nasdaq rebound on Friday. The figures show a divergence in fund flows, but do not establish that equity buying drove Bitcoin lower.

passages: Jensen Huang, the CEO and co-founder of the world’s most prominent chip company, has allegedly been honey-trapped by a suspected Chinese spy, and the news has struck the internet like a match to gasoline.

Huang has long been seen as a wife guy (or so everyone assumed). He and his wife, Lori, have been together since the 1980s, and both of their children work at Nvidia. Huang has been the closest thing the tech world has to a rock star, with fans lining up for selfies and autographs. Of all the AI overlords, the leather-jacket wearing Huang has seemed like the most level-headed and least erratic, which is why this plot twist has hit so hard.

The potential fallout is mind-boggling. Nvidia looms so large over the U.S. stock market that even the company’s domestic drama is a market risk. Countless AI startups depend on Nvidia chips, so any shake-up at the top would ripple far beyond the company. And Nvidia has no publicly disclosed succession plan, so if Huang leaves, it’s unclear who’d take over.

Is this how the AI bubble bursts? It’s a question that will be answered in time, but in the meantime, a more pressing matter demands our attention: ranking the funniest memes about the scandal, with bonus points for AI images presumably generated using Nvidia chips.

There’s admittedly a lot to choose from, ranging from “500 Days of Summer” jokes to jokes about divorce lawyers to an AI-adaptation of the music video for Usher ‘s song “Confessions Pt. II,” a track about cheating. Another person created a viral AI video that recreates the Coldplay concert where a startup CEO was caught on the Jumbotron hugging a colleague.
Huang publicly confessed to the affair just yesterday, so the internet has the rest of the week to get creative.
For the sake of the US economy I really hope Jensen's wife can be chill about this.
Jensen, why would I deceive you? pic.twitter.com/KWz6S3mxUq
“AI will replace you”. I’d like to see AI become CEO of a multitrillion company and destroy its marriage and lose over $1.6T because it had an affair with a spy.
Not enough people talking about how betrayed Jensen Huang must feel right now. Found a mistress he can talk about semiconductors with and she was lying to him the whole time. He must be heartbroken
The real crisis: every SF founder now thinks he's worth spying on
Jensen Huang on Monday morning pic.twitter.com/y60dfyrVos
Me and Jensen Huang’s ex wife after she gets half his money in the divorce. pic.twitter.com/xWAOhzXYVk
Breaking News CIA reportedly deploying Sydney Sweeney to China 🇨🇳 pic.twitter.com/ss1trtBXaO
jensen what the fuck pic.twitter.com/E0g1tiwVGz
Jensen Huang’s wife divorce lawyers right now pic.twitter.com/QE3EEOtE71
Jensen Huang after learning about the Chinese honeypot scandal pic.twitter.com/HehLQ7zlB8
Yes, the internet is having a field day with this one.

As usual, AI-generated content is doing a lot of heavy lifting. Copyleaks, a software company that analyzes online content for signs of AI and digital manipulation, said Monday that it had seen “an explosion in AI-manipulated photos and videos of Huang and Alice Huang, ranging from memes to more subtle edits.” The tally includes at least 70 AI-related posts on X, which together drew around 8.42 million views and 64,362 engagements as of Monday morning. Those metrics have almost certainly climbed since.

That permissiveness isn’t the only thing drawing attackers.
The October attack on OpenCode , which targeted users’ third-party API keys and caused financial damage, is the latest example.
It follows an incident this summer in which an OpenAI agent swarm breached Hugging Face in an apparent attempt to cover its tracks after accessing answers to cybersecurity evaluations.
For now, Hugging Face is trying to avoid that route.
Solaiman said the company has been beefing up monitoring tools to catch hacks, as well as taking steps to prevent them.

She added that there’s a “danger of open source really closing down at a time when we’ve gotten so much public support.”
Other parts of the open source ecosystem are dealing with similar security-related tradeoffs.

extraction.body: The very qualities that make open AI platforms valuable, like open doors and rich data, might also make them vulnerable to more hacks, Irene Solaiman, chief policy officer and SVP of strategy at Hugging Face said on a recent episode of the Equity podcast. The October attack on OpenCode , which targeted users’ third-party API keys and caused financial damage, is the latest example. It follows an incident this summer in which an OpenAI agent swarm breached Hugging Face in an apparent attempt to cover its tracks after accessing answers to cybersecurity evaluations. The risks aren’t limited to platforms that invite open community contributions. On Monday, AI infrastructure startup Fireworks, which helps developers run and train open AI models, disclosed that attackers had accessed some customers’ model weights, datasets, and billing information. The company temporarily disabled certain self-service dataset functions as it investigates. While the attack isn’t necessarily due to Fireworks’ openness, it highlights how much valuable information is concentrated within AI infrastructure providers. “The things I worry about making an open community targeted are also what makes it special,” Solaiman said on Equity. “We are necessarily permissive. We want the average hobbyist in their basement who doesn’t have an institutional affiliation to be able to contribute.” “You want people to be able to just submit pull requests and allow anybody without a valid affiliation to contribute…but then you have some losers who ruin it for the rest,” she added in a separate conversation. That permissiveness isn’t the only thing drawing attackers. The wealth of information open platforms host also make them targets. Hugging Face became a temptation for OpenAI’s agent swarm because of the evaluation datasets it holds, whereas OpenCode’s target in this case came from its “juicy third-party API keys,” per Solaiman. “The combination of that makes us prime targets,” Solaiman told TechCrunch in a separate conversation. She added that there’s a “danger of open source really closing down at a time when we’ve gotten so much public support.” Much of the industry has come out recently in support of open AI models , including heavy hitters like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. And increasingly, governments, enterprises and startups are relying on open models to build. So what would a pullback actually look like? It could theoretically mean restrictions on who can upload models or datasets, more stringent identity verification, or additional vetting of developers before they can access certain features. While these moves could protect platforms from attackers, it could also make it more difficult for independent researchers and hobbyists to participate in communities they would have been welcomed in before. For now, Hugging Face is trying to avoid that route. Solaiman said the company has been beefing up monitoring tools to catch hacks, as well as taking steps to prevent them. But monitoring can be expensive to maintain, she noted, and not every platform will be able to afford it. “Administrative access tokens were part of what gave that agent swarm better access, so we just rotate them a lot more frequently than we used to,” Solaiman said. “We also now have stricter network controls.” In other words, the credentials that give admins broad access to Hugging Face’s systems now get changed more often, which means a stolen token would be useful for less time. Other parts of the open source ecosystem are dealing with similar security-related tradeoffs. GitHub, the world’s largest host for open-source projects, has been fighting off attackers who inject malicious code into projects to quickly spread malware. The company began tightening security requirements for publishing packages to the npm registry, revoking older authentication tokens, and limiting how long new ones remain valid. Zach Steindler, an engineer at GitHub who handles software supply chain security, told TechCrunch via email that while security measures can disrupt established workflows, the platforms can become more secure without fundamentally restricting participation. “It’s less about limiting functionality and more about going and fixing things that weren’t secure in the first place,” Steindler said. He noted that npm install scripts have existed for years, but recent attacks highlighted how dangerous they could be. GitHub worked with OpenJS — a nonprofit that hosts critical open-source projects built with JavaScript — on a safer approach. The same logic applies to where security teams put their effort, per Steindler: “Security is all about maximizing impact with the resources we have, and I would much rather invest in detecting suspicious behavior and containment capabilities: things that cover all accounts and access methods. Suspicious behavior is suspicious regardless of who is exhibiting it.” Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence. Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications. The October attack on OpenCode , which targeted users’ third-party API keys and caused financial damage, is the latest example. It follows an incident this summer in which an OpenAI agent swarm breached Hugging Face in an apparent attempt to cover its tracks after accessing answers to cybersecurity evaluations.

The risks aren’t limited to platforms that invite open community contributions. On Monday, AI infrastructure startup Fireworks, which helps developers run and train open AI models, disclosed that attackers had accessed some customers’ model weights, datasets, and billing information. The company temporarily disabled certain self-service dataset functions as it investigates. While the attack isn’t necessarily due to Fireworks’ openness, it highlights how much valuable information is concentrated within AI infrastructure providers.

“The things I worry about making an open community targeted are also what makes it special,” Solaiman said on Equity. “We are necessarily permissive. We want the average hobbyist in their basement who doesn’t have an institutional affiliation to be able to contribute.”

“You want people to be able to just submit pull requests and allow anybody without a valid affiliation to contribute…but then you have some losers who ruin it for the rest,” she added in a separate conversation.

That permissiveness isn’t the only thing drawing attackers. The wealth of information open platforms host also make them targets. Hugging Face became a temptation for OpenAI’s agent swarm because of the evaluation datasets it holds, whereas OpenCode’s target in this case came from its “juicy third-party API keys,” per Solaiman.

“The combination of that makes us prime targets,” Solaiman told TechCrunch in a separate conversation. She added that there’s a “danger of open source really closing down at a time when we’ve gotten so much public support.”

Much of the industry has come out recently in support of open AI models , including heavy hitters like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. And increasingly, governments, enterprises and startups are relying on open models to build.

So what would a pullback actually look like? It could theoretically mean restrictions on who can upload models or datasets, more stringent identity verification, or additional vetting of developers before they can access certain features. While these moves could protect platforms from attackers, it could also make it more difficult for independent researchers and hobbyists to participate in communities they would have been welcomed in before.

For now, Hugging Face is trying to avoid that route. Solaiman said the company has been beefing up monitoring tools to catch hacks, as well as taking steps to prevent them. But monitoring can be expensive to maintain, she noted, and not every platform will be able to afford it.

“Administrative access tokens were part of what gave that agent swarm better access, so we just rotate them a lot more frequently than we used to,” Solaiman said. “We also now have stricter network controls.”
In other words, the credentials that give admins broad access to Hugging Face’s systems now get changed more often, which means a stolen token would be useful for less time.

Other parts of the open source ecosystem are dealing with similar security-related tradeoffs. GitHub, the world’s largest host for open-source projects, has been fighting off attackers who inject malicious code into projects to quickly spread malware. The company began tightening security requirements for publishing packages to the npm registry, revoking older authentication tokens, and limiting how long new ones remain valid.

Zach Steindler, an engineer at GitHub who handles software supply chain security, told TechCrunch via email that while security measures can disrupt established workflows, the platforms can become more secure without fundamentally restricting participation.

“It’s less about limiting functionality and more about going and fixing things that weren’t secure in the first place,” Steindler said. He noted that npm install scripts have existed for years, but recent attacks highlighted how dangerous they could be. GitHub worked with OpenJS — a nonprofit that hosts critical open-source projects built with JavaScript — on a safer approach.

The same logic applies to where security teams put their effort, per Steindler: “Security is all about maximizing impact with the resources we have, and I would much rather invest in detecting suspicious behavior and containment capabilities: things that cover all accounts and access methods. Suspicious behavior is suspicious regardless of who is exhibiting it.”
